It is permissible for the agent in if to be the will to be estimated and indicate the will, meaning: the will was written upon you if. Fourth: The Almighty’s saying: Good. Good here means money without dispute, and they differed about its amount. Some said: A lot of money. It was narrated from Ali, Aisha, and Ibn Abbas. They said that seven hundred dinars are little. Qatadah from Al-Hasan: Good is a thousand dinars and above. Al-Sha’bi: Between five hundred dinars and a thousand. A will is anything that is ordered to be done and entrusted during life and after death. Custom has specified it to what is entrusted to be done and implemented after death. The plural is wills, like the plural of qadā’. The waḍī can be the testator and the one to whom it is entrusted. Its origin is from wasā’ī, lightened. The plant is tawāsā tawāsā if it is connected. And a wasīyah land: connected to plants. I bequeathed something to him and I bequeathed it to him if I made him your guardian. The noun is wasāyah and wasāyah with kasrah and fathah. I also entrusted him with a recommendation with the same meaning, and the noun is wasāṭah. The people entrusted each other. In the hadith: Treat women well, for they are prisoners in your care. To bequeath something to someone means to connect it to them. Fifth: The scholars differed regarding the obligation of a will on someone who left behind wealth, after their consensus that it is obligatory on someone who left behind deposits and owes debts. Most scholars are of the opinion that a will is not obligatory on someone who does not have any of that, which is the opinion of Malik, Al-Shafi’i and Al-Thawri, whether the testator is wealthy or poor. A group said: A will is obligatory according to the apparent meaning of the Qur’an: This was stated by Al-Zuhri and Abu Majlaz, whether the wealth is little or much. Abu Thawr said: A will is not obligatory except on a man who owes a debt or has money for some people, so it is obligatory for him to write his will and inform them of what he owes. As for someone who has no debt or deposit, it is not obligatory on him unless he wishes. Ibn Al-Mundhir said: This is good, because God has imposed the return of trusts to their owners, and whoever has no right or trust from him is not obligated to make a will. The first scholars cited as evidence what the imams narrated on the authority of Ibn Umar that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: It is not right for a Muslim who has something he wants to make a will to spend two nights without having his will written down with him. In another narration, to spend three nights. In this regard, Abdullah ibn Umar said: “Not a night has passed since I heard the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, say that, without having my will with him.” Those who do not make it obligatory have argued that if it were obligatory, he would not have made it up to the will of the testator, and that would be obligatory in any case. Then, if we assume that it appears to be obligatory, then the statement that it is obligatory rejects it. This is in the case of someone who has rights over people and fears that they will lose them, as Abu Thawr said. Likewise, if he has rights over people and fears that they will be lost to the heirs, then he must make a will, and there is no disagreement about that. If it is said: God Almighty said: It is prescribed for you and prescribed means imposed, so it indicates the obligation of making a will. It is said to them: The answer to this has already been given in the verse before, and the meaning is: If you want to make a will, and God knows best. Al-Nakha’i said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, died without making a will, and Abu Bakr made a will, so if he made a will, it is good, but if he did not make a will, then nothing is required of him. Sixth: God the Almighty did not specify in His Book the amount of money that should be bequeathed, but He said: If he leaves behind a bequest of wealth, and wealth is money, as in His saying: And whatever you spend of good, and For indeed, for the love of good. The scholars differed regarding the amount of that. It was narrated on the authority of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him, that he bequeathed a fifth. Ali, may God be pleased with him, said: From the spoils of the Muslims, a fifth. Muammar said on the authority of Qatadah: Umar bequeathed a quarter. Al-Bukhari mentioned it on the authority of Ibn Abbas. It was narrated on the authority of Ali, may God be pleased with him, that he said: For me to bequeath a fifth is more beloved to me than to bequeath a quarter, and for me to bequeath a quarter is more beloved to me than to bequeath a third. A group of people chose for those who have little wealth and have heirs to leave a will. This was narrated on the authority of Ali, Ibn Abbas, and Aisha, may God be pleased with them all. Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated on the authority of Ibn Abi Malekah on the authority of Aisha that a man said to her: I want to make a will. She said: How much is your wealth? He said: Three thousand. She said: How many are your dependents? He said: Four. She said: God Almighty says: If he leaves behind something good, and this is a small amount, so leave it for your dependents, for that is better for you. Seventh: The majority of scholars have held that it is not permissible for anyone to bequeath more than a third, except for Abu Hanifa and his companions, for they said: If the testator does not leave any heirs, it is permissible for him to bequeath all of his wealth. They said: Limiting the bequest to a third was only in order to leave his heirs rich, based on the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: It is better for you to leave your heirs rich than to leave them poor, begging from people. The hadith was narrated by the Imams. Whoever has no heirs is not one of those concerned with the hadith. This statement was narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas, and Abu Ubaidah and Masruq said the same. Ishaq and Malik agreed with it in one of their two opinions, and it was narrated on the authority of Ali. The reason for the disagreement with what we have mentioned is the disagreement over the treasury: is it an heir or a guardian of what is put in it? There are two opinions. Eighth: The scholars agreed that if a person dies and has heirs, he is not entitled to bequeath all of his money. It was narrated on the authority of Amr ibn al-Aas, may God be pleased with him, that when death approached him, he said to his son Abdullah: I wanted to make a will. He said to him: Make a will and your money is in my money. So he called a scribe and dictated. Abdullah said: I said to him: I see that you have already taken my money and your money. If I called my brothers, you would be permitted to do so. Ninth: They agreed that a person can change his will and return to whatever he wishes from it, except that they differed on that regarding the mudabbar. Malik, may God have mercy on him, said: The matter agreed upon among us is that if the testator makes a will in his health or illness in which there is the emancipation of a slave or something else, then he can change it as he wishes and do whatever he wishes with it until he dies. If he likes to discard that will and drop it, he can do so, except for the mudabbar. If he manages a slave, then he has no way to change what he has planned, and that is because the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: It is not right for a Muslim who has something to bequeath to spend two nights without having his will written down with him. Abu al-Faraj al-Maliki said that the mudabbar is like the manumitted slave for a month, because it is a term that will inevitably come. They agreed that he cannot go back on an oath by manumission or manumission for a term, and so is the mudabbar, and Abu Hanifa said the same. Al-Shafi’i, Ahmad and Ishaq said: It is a will, because they agreed that it is for a third like all other wills. And in their permitting intercourse with the mudabbar, there is what is missing from their analogy of the mudabbar to manumission for a term, and it has been proven: “The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, sold a slave girl,” and Aisha sold a slave girl who had been set free and then sold her. This is the opinion of a group of the Tabi’in. A group said: A man may change whatever he wants from his will except for manumission. This is what Al-Sha’bi, Ibn Sirin, Ibn Shubramah, and Al-Nakha’i said, and it is the opinion of Sufyan Al-Thawri. Tenth: They differed about a man who says to his slave: You are free after my death, and he wanted to make a will, then he has the right to return it according to Malik. If he says: So-and-so is a mudabbar after my death, then he does not have the right to return it. If he wanted to manage it with his first statement, then he does not have the right to return it according to most of Malik’s companions. As for al-Shafi’i, Ahmad, Ishaq, and Abu Thawr, then all of this is a will according to them, because it is in the third, and everything that is in the third is a will, except that al-Shafi’i said: There is no return in the mudabbar except by removing him from his ownership by selling or gifting him. And his saying: I have returned it is not a return, and if the mudabbar does not leave his ownership until he dies, then he is freed by his death. And he said in al-Qadeem: There is a return in the mudabbar as one returns in a will. Al-Muzani chose it based on their consensus on returning in the case of someone who bequeathed his freedom. Abu Thawr said: If he says I have returned in the case of the mudabbar, then the management is void, and if he dies, he is not freed. Ibn Al-Qasim and Ashab differed about the one who said: My slave is free after my death, and he did not mean a will or management. Ibn Al-Qasim said: It is a will. Ashab said: He is a manager even if he did not mean a will. Eleventh: The scholars differed regarding this verse, whether it was abrogated or decisive. It was said: It is decisive. Its apparent meaning is general, but its meaning is specific to the parents who do not inherit, such as the disbelievers and slaves, and to the relatives who are not heirs. This was said by Ad-Dahhak, Tawus, and Al-Hasan, and it was chosen by Al-Tabari. Al-Zuhri said that the will is obligatory in matters of little or much. Ibn Al-Mundhir said: All the scholars from whom we have preserved agreed that the will for the parents who do not inherit and the relatives who do not inherit is permissible. Ibn Abbas, Al-Hasan, and Qatadah said: The verse is general, and the ruling was established by it for a period of time, and everyone who inherits was abrogated by the verse of inheritance. It was said: The verse of inheritance was not abrogated independently, but by another addition, which is the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: God has given to every person with a right his right, so there is no bequest for an heir. Narrated by Abu Umamah, and At-Tirmidhi said: This is a good and authentic hadith. The verse was abrogated by the established Sunnah, not by inheritance, according to the correct opinion of the scholars. If it were not for this hadith, it would have been possible to reconcile the two verses by taking the money from the deceased by a will, or by inheritance if he did not make a will, or what remains after the will, but this hadith and consensus prevented that. Even though Ash-Shafi’i and Abu Al-Faraj prevented the abrogation of the Qur’an by the Sunnah, the correct opinion is that it is permissible, based on the fact that all of it is the ruling of God, the Most High, and from Him, even if the names differ. This meaning has been mentioned above. Although this report has reached us as a single narration, it has been joined by the consensus of the Muslims that it is not permissible to make a bequest for an heir. It has become clear that the obligation of making a bequest for the closest heirs has been abrogated by the Sunnah, and it is the basis of those who agree. And God knows best. Ibn Abbas and Al-Hasan said: The will to the parents was abrogated by obligation in Surat An-Nisa and was confirmed for the closest relatives who do not inherit. This is the view of Al-Shafi’i, most of the Malikis and a group of scholars. In Al-Bukhari, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, he said: The money was for the child and the will was for the parents, so he abrogated that as he wished, so he made for the male the share of two females, and he made for the two repentant children each one of them a sixth, and he made for the woman an eighth and a quarter, and for the husband a half and a quarter. Ibn Omar, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Zayd said: The entire verse was abrogated, and the will remained as a recommendation. Something similar to this is the statement of Malik, may God have mercy on him, and it was mentioned by Al-Nahhas on the authority of Al-Sha’bi and Al-Nakha’i. Al-Rabi’ bin Khathim said: There is no will. Urwah bin Thabit said: I said to Rabi’ bin Khathim: Bequeath me your copy of the Qur’an. He looked at his son and read: And those of kinship are nearer to one another in the Book of God. Something similar to this is what Ibn Omar, may God be pleased with him, did. Twelfth: The Almighty said: And the nearest relatives. The nearest is the plural of nearest. Some people said that the will to the nearest relatives is more appropriate than to the strangers, because of the explicit text of God regarding them, so Ad-Dahhak said: If he wills to someone other than his relatives, then his work has ended with disobedience. It was narrated from Ibn Omar that he willed to the mothers of his children, each one of his relatives with four thousand. It was narrated that Aisha willed to a female slave of hers the furniture of the house. It was narrated from Salim bin Abdullah something similar. Al-Hasan said: If he wills to someone other than his relatives, the will is returned to the nearest relatives, but if it is for a stranger, then it is with them, and it is not permissible for others if they are left alone. When Abu Al-Aaliyah died, people said: How strange! A woman from Riyah freed him and he willed his money to the Prophet of Hashim. Al-Sha’bi said: He had no right to that nor any honor. Tawus said: If he wills to someone other than his relatives, the will is returned to his relatives and his action is nullified. Jabir bin Zaid said the same, and something similar was narrated from Al-Hasan as well, and Ishaq bin Rahawayh said the same. Malik, Al-Shafi’i, Abu Hanifa and their companions, Al-Awza’i and Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: Whoever makes a will to someone other than his relatives and leaves his relatives in need, then what a bad thing he has done! His action is permissible and valid for everyone to whom he made a will, whether rich or poor, near or far, Muslim or infidel. This is the meaning of what was narrated from Ibn Umar and Aisha, and it is the statement of Ibn Umar and Ibn Abbas. I said: The first statement is better. As for Abu Al-Aaliyah, may God be pleased with him, perhaps he considered that the Banu Hashim were more deserving than his emancipator, because he had Ibn Abbas as his guardian, taught him, and included him among the ranks of scholars in this world and the next. Although this fatherhood was spiritual, it was the real one, and the ultimate goal of his emancipator was to include him among the free in this world, so the reward of her emancipation was sufficient for her, and God knows best. Thirteenth: The majority of scholars have said that a sick person is to be placed under guardianship over his wealth, and the scholars of the apparent meaning have deviated and said: He is not to be placed under guardianship, and it is like the correct view. The hadith and its meaning are rebutted. “Saad said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, visited me during the Farewell Pilgrimage when I was suffering from an illness from which I almost died, so I said: O Messenger of God, what you see has afflicted me with the illness I have, and I have wealth and no one inherits from me except one daughter. Should I give two-thirds of my wealth in charity? He said: No. I said: Should I give half of it in charity? He said: No, a third, and a third is a lot. If you leave your heirs rich, it is better than leaving them poor, begging from people.” The hadith. The people of the apparent meaning also forbade a will of more than a third, even if the heirs approved it. All of them approved it if the heirs approved it, and this is correct, because the sick person was only prevented from bequeathing more than a third due to the right of the heir. So if the heirs waive their right, it is permissible and valid, and it is like a gift from them. Al-Darqutni narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: A will is not permissible for an heir unless the heirs wish it. It was narrated on the authority of Amr bin Kharijah who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: There is no will for an heir unless the heirs approve. Fourteenth: They differed regarding the revocation of those who permit the will to the heir during the life of the testator after his death. A group said: It is permissible for them and they do not have the right to revoke it. This is the opinion of Ata’ ibn Abi Rabah, Tawus, Al-Hasan, Ibn Sirin, Ibn Abi Laila, Al-Zuhri, Rabia, and Al-Awza’i. A group said: They have the right to revoke it if they like. This is the opinion of Ibn Mas’ud, Shuraih, Al-Hakam, Tawus, Al-Thawri, Al-Hasan ibn Salih, Abu Hanifa, Al-Shafi’i, Ahmad, and Abu Thawr, and it was chosen by Ibn Al-Mundhir. Malik made a distinction and said: If they gave permission when he was healthy, then they have the right to revoke it. If they gave permission to him when he was sick when he was prevented from his money, then that is permissible for them. This is the opinion of Ishaq. The people of the first opinion argued that the prevention only occurred for the sake of the heirs, so if they permitted it, it is permissible. They agreed that if he bequeathed more than a third of his estate to a stranger, it is permissible with their permission, and so it is here. The second opinion argued that they had permitted something that they did not own at that time, and that the money is only owned after his death. The heir who asked permission may die before him and not be an heir, and someone else may inherit it. So he permitted someone who had no right to it, and nothing is required of him. Malik argued by saying: If a man is healthy, he is more entitled to all of his money and can do with it as he pleases. So if they permitted him when he was healthy, they have left something that was not due to them. And if they permitted him when he was sick, they have seen what was due to them from the right, so they do not have the right to go back on it if he has already implemented it because it has passed. Fifteenth: If the patient does not carry out that, then the heir has the right to revoke it because he did not fulfill it, as stated by Al-Abhari. Ibn Al-Mundhir mentioned on the authority of Ishaq bin Rahawayh that the statement of Malik on this issue is more similar to the Sunnah than others. Ibn Al-Mundhir said: The statement of Malik, Al-Thawri, the Kufians, Al-Shafi’i, and Abu Thawr is more correct, that if they permit that after his death, then it is binding on them. Sixteenth: They differed about a man who bequeaths money to some of his heirs, and says in his will: If the heirs approve it, it is his, and if they do not approve it, it is for the sake of God, but they did not approve it. Malik said: If the heirs do not approve it, it returns to them. According to the statement of Al-Shafi’i, Abu Hanifa, and Muammar, the companion of Abd Al-Razzaq, it goes on in the way of God. Seventeenth: There is no disagreement regarding the will of an adult who is sane and not under guardianship. There is disagreement regarding others. Malik said: The matter agreed upon among us is that the wills of the weak in mind, the foolish, and the afflicted who sometimes regains consciousness are permissible if they have enough reason to know what they are bequeathing. The same applies to a young boy if he understands what he has bequeathed and does not say anything reprehensible, then his will is valid and binding. Abu Hanifa and his companions said: The will of a young boy is not permissible. Al-Muzani said: This is based on the opinion of Al-Shafi’i, and I did not find anything Al-Shafi’i mentioned or stated explicitly about that. His companions differed on two opinions: one of them is like Malik’s opinion, and the second is like Abu Hanifa’s opinion. Their argument is that his divorce or emancipation is not permissible, and he is not subject to retaliation for a crime or to the prescribed punishment for slander, so he is not like an adult who is under guardianship, so his will is the same. Abu Omar said: They agreed that the will of an adult who is under guardianship is permissible. It is known that if a boy of sound mind makes a will, his situation is the same as that of one who is wronged in his money. The reason for being forbidden is the squandering and destruction of money, and that reason is removed by death. He is more like one who is forbidden in his money than a madman who is not of sound mind. Therefore, his will must be permissible, in accordance with the matter that came in it from Omar, may God be pleased with him. Malik said: It is the matter agreed upon among them in Madinah, and success is from God. Muhammad ibn Shuraih said: Whoever makes a will, young or old, and he gets it right, God has decreed it through his tongue. There is no repelling the truth. Eighteenth: The Almighty’s saying: with what is right means with justice, with no laxity or excess in it, and that this is entrusted to the deceased’s effort and the testator’s consideration, then God Almighty took charge of determining that through the tongue of His Prophet, peace be upon him, so he, peace be upon him, said: A third, and a third is a lot. The scholars have already stated this. The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: God has given you a third of your wealth as charity when you die, as an addition to your good deeds, so that He may make it a form of zakat for you. Narrated by Ad-Daraqutni on the authority of Abu Umamah on the authority of Muadh ibn Jabal on the authority of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace. Al-Hasan said: It is not permissible to make a will except for a third, and Al-Bukhari agreed with him and used as evidence the words of God the Almighty: And judge between them by what God has revealed. The ruling of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, that a third is a lot is the ruling by what God has revealed. So whoever exceeds the limit set by the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, and exceeds a third has committed what the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, prohibited, and by doing so he is a sinner if he is knowledgeable in the ruling of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace. Ash-Shafi’i said: His statement, A third is a lot, means that it is not a little. Nineteenth: The Almighty’s saying: Truly means established with the establishment of consideration and fortification, not the establishment of obligation and necessity, as evidenced by His saying: upon the righteous. This indicates that it is recommended, because if it were an obligation, it would be upon all Muslims. So when God singled out those who are righteous, that is, who fear negligence, it indicates that it is not obligatory except in what is expected to be lost if he dies, so it is obligatory for him to rush to write it down and bequeath it, because if he is silent about it, it would be a waste of it and negligence on his part. This meaning has already been presented. And truly is in the accusative case as a confirmed source, and it is permissible in other than the Qur’an to say truth in the meaning of that truth. Al-Muwaffiyah 20: The scholars said: The initiative to write a will is not taken from this verse, but rather from the hadith of Ibn Umar. Its benefit is: to exaggerate in increasing the security and for it to be written and witnessed, and it is the will that is agreed upon to be acted upon. So if just men bear witness and perform that testimony verbally, it is to be acted upon even if it is not written in writing. So if he writes it with his own hand and does not bear witness, then there is no difference in the statement of Malik that it is not to be acted upon except in what it contains of an acknowledgment of a right for someone who is not accused of it, in which case he is obligated to implement it. Twenty-first: Al-Daraqutni narrated on the authority of Anas bin Malik, who said: They used to write at the top of their wills: This is what so-and-so, son of so-and-so, has willed: He bears witness that there is no god but God alone, without partner, and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger, and that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt about it, and that God will resurrect those in the graves. And he will command those of his family he left behind to fear God as He should be feared, and to reconcile their differences, and to obey God and His Messenger if they are believers. And he commanded them with what Abraham commanded his sons, and so did Jacob: O my sons, God has chosen for you this religion, so do not die except as Muslims.
2:181: God Almighty says: “But whoever changes it after he has heard it, then the sin is only upon those who have changed it. Indeed, God is Hearing and Knowing.” There are four issues: The first: The Almighty’s saying: So whoever changes it is a condition, and its answer is Then the sin is only upon those who change it and what is a collective noun for in about the action. And his sin is raised by the beginning, upon those who change it is the place of the predicate. The pronoun in badalahu refers to the will, because the will is in the meaning of the will, and likewise the pronoun in hears it, and it is like His saying: So whoever receives an admonition from his Lord meaning admonition, and His saying: And when he attends the division meaning the money, as evidenced by His saying from it. And similar to it is the saying of the poet: What is this sound? Any shout. Imru Al-Qais said: A dream come true for a girl like a crazy person The swollen, leafy one, which is the softest, went to the rod and left the word kharoobah. And his hearing may have been from the executor himself, and it may have been from someone who could prove it to him, and that is two just men. And the pronoun in his sin refers to the change, meaning the sin of the change is on the one who was changed, not on the dead person, because the testator was exempted from blame by the will and it was directed at the heir or guardian. And it was said: If this testator changed and left the will or did not perform it as prescribed for him in the law, then the sin is upon him. Second: This verse is evidence that if a deceased person bequeaths a debt, it will be removed from his responsibility and the guardian will obtain what he is required to pay. He will be rewarded for paying it, but he will bear the burden of delaying it. Judge Abu Bakr Ibn al-Arabi said: This is only valid if the deceased did not neglect to pay it. However, if he was able to pay it and left it and then bequeathed it, then the guardian’s neglect of it will not remove it from his responsibility. Third: There is no disagreement that if he bequeaths something that is not permissible, such as bequeathing wine, pork, or something sinful, then it is permissible to change it but it is not permissible to carry it out, just as it is not permissible to carry out what exceeds a third, as Abu Omar said. Fourth: The Almighty’s saying: Indeed, God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing. These are two attributes of God Almighty that do not conceal anything about the injustice of those who recommend and the change of those who transgress.
2:182: God Almighty says: “But if anyone fears injustice or wrongdoing on the part of a testator and brings about a settlement between them, there is no sin upon him. Indeed, God is Forgiving and Merciful.” There are six issues: The first: The Almighty’s saying: So whoever fears from a condition, and fear means feared. It was said: knew. The original is fear, the waw was changed to an alif because it is moving and what precedes it is moving. The people of Kufa incline fear to indicate the kasra of fa’ala. From muwas with emphasis, the reading of Abu Bakr from Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa’i, and the rest lightened it, and lightening is clearer, because most grammarians say muwas for multiplication. It may be permissible for it to be like karama and akram. Janfan from janafa yajnaf if he is unfair, and the noun from it is jinnaf and janaf, from an-Nahhas. It was said: janf is inclination. Al-A’ash said: My camel turned away from the stone of Yamamah, and I did not seek anyone from its people except you. In Al-Sahah: Al-Janf means inclination. And it is said that Janfah with a kasra means to lean, and from this is the saying of God Almighty: But whoever fears from a testator deviation The poet said: They are our masters, even if they are unfair to us. We are indeed afraid of meeting them. Abu Ubaidah said: The mawla here is in the place of the mawālī, meaning the paternal cousins, as in the Almighty’s saying: Then He brings you forth as a child. And Labid said: I am a man who has prevented the descendants of Amir from oppressing me, and my enemies have wronged me. Abu Ubaidah said: “Likewise, the jinni’ with a hamza is also the one who leans. It is said: a man is ajnaf, meaning he came with the junuf. Just as it is said: alaam, meaning he came with something he is blamed for. And akhs, meaning he came with a base thing. And tajanaf lithman, meaning he leaned. And a man is ajnaf, meaning he has a bent back. And janfa on fa’la with a damma on the fa’ and a fatha on the ‘ayn: is the name of a place, on the authority of Ibn al-Sikkit. It was narrated on the authority of Ali that he read haifa with a ha’ and a ya’, meaning oppression. Mujahid said: “So whoever fears” means whoever fears that the testator will be ajnaf and cut off the inheritance of a group and intentionally harm them, or come to them without intention, and that is the junf without sin, but if he does it intentionally, then it is the junf in sin. So the meaning is whoever is admonished about that and it is returned from him, so he reconciles with that what is between him and his heirs and between the heirs themselves, then there is no sin upon him. Indeed, God is Forgiving of the testator if he is admonished and he refrains from what he intended of harm. Ibn Abbas, Qatada, Al-Rabi’ and others said: The meaning of the verse is: “Whoever fears, knows, sees, and his knowledge comes to him after the death of the testator that the testator has been unjust and deliberately harmed some of his heirs, and he corrects the confusion and discord that occurred between the heirs, “there is no sin upon him,” meaning that the sin of the previously mentioned change will not befall him. Even if there is some change in his action, it is a change for the sake of benefit. The change in which there is sin is only a change of desire. Second: The address in His saying: But whoever fears is to all Muslims. It was said to them: If you fear that a testator will deviate in his will and go away from the truth and fall into sin and he does not spend it in a reasonable manner, such as by bequeathing the money to his daughter’s husband or to his daughter’s son so that the money goes to his daughter, or to his son’s son with the intention that the money goes to his son, or he bequeathed to someone distant and left out the one who is close, then hasten to strive to reconcile between them. If reconciliation occurs, the sin is dropped from the one who reconciled. Reconciliation is a communal obligation, so if one of them does it, it is dropped from the rest, but if they do not do it, then everyone is sinful. Third: This verse is evidence of ruling based on suspicion, because if corruption is suspected, then it is necessary to strive for reform. If corruption is confirmed, then it is not a reconciliation, but rather a ruling to repel, nullify and put an end to corruption. The Almighty’s saying: “Then make peace between them” is in apposition to feared, and the metaphor refers to the heirs. They were not mentioned because the meaning was known, and the answer to the condition is that there is no sin upon him. Fourth: There is no disagreement that charity when alive and healthy is better than charity when dead, based on the statement of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, when he was asked: Which charity is best? He said: If you give charity when you are healthy and stingy. The hadith was narrated by the people of Sahih. Al-Darqutni narrated on the authority of Abu Saeed Al-Khudri that the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said: It is better for a person to give charity of one dirham during his life than to give charity of one hundred at his death. Al-Nasa’i narrated on the authority of Abu al-Darda’ that the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: The example of the one who spends or gives charity at the time of his death is like the example of the one who gives gifts after he is full. Fifth: If someone does not cause harm in his will, it is an expiation for what he left behind of his zakat. Al-Darqutni narrated on the authority of Muawiyah bin Qurrah on the authority of his father who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: Whoever is on the verge of death and makes a will, and his will is in accordance with the Book of God, it will be an expiation for what he left behind of zakat. If there is harm in the will, which is: Sixth: Al-Darqutni also narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas, on the authority of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, who said: Harming in a will is a major sin. Abu Dawud narrated on the authority of Abu Hurairah, may God be pleased with him, that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: A man or woman may work in obedience to God for sixty years, then death comes to them and they are harmed in their will, so Hell is obligatory for them. Al-Nasa’i included a translation of the prayer for one who deviates in his will: Ali ibn Hajar informed us, Hisham informed us, on the authority of Mansur, who is Ibn Zadan, on the authority of Al-Hasan, on the authority of Amrat ibn Husayn, may God be pleased with him: “A man freed six of his slaves when he died, and he had no other wealth. report of that reached the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, and he became angry and said: ‘I was thinking of not praying over him.’ Then he called his slaves and divided them into three parts. Then he cast lots among them, so he freed two and enslaved four.” Muslim narrated it with the same meaning, except that he said at the end: And he said to him a harsh word, instead of saying: I was thinking of not praying over him.
2:183: It has six issues: First: The Almighty’s saying: O you who have believed, decreed upon you is fasting. When He mentioned what was decreed upon those who are accountable regarding retaliation and wills, He also mentioned that He decreed upon them fasting and made it obligatory upon them and made it obligatory upon them, and there is no disagreement about that. The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: “Islam is built on five pillars: the testimony that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God, establishing prayer, paying zakat, fasting Ramadan, and Hajj.” Narrated by Ibn Umar. Its meaning in the language is: abstaining from moving from one state to another. Silence is called fasting because it is abstaining from speech. God the Almighty said, informing about Maryam 19:Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast, meaning silence from speech. Fasting is the stagnation of the wind, which is its abstention from blowing. The animal fasted on its hump: it stood and stood still and did not feed. The day fasted: it was moderate. The sun’s fast is when it is at its zenith in the middle of the day. From this is the saying of Al-Nabigha: Fasting horses, non-fasting horses in the dust, and horses chewing on bridles Any horse that is stable and unable to run or move, as he said: As if the chandelier was suspended in its place That is, it is fixed in its place and does not move. And his saying: And the fasting girls are greedy It means that it does not rotate. Imru Al-Qais said: So leave it and ask the worries away from you with a strong, humble heart when the day is fasting and deserted. That is, the sun slowed down in moving and setting, so it became like a handicap due to its slowness. Another said: Even if the day fasted and became moderate and the sun began to salivate, then it descended Another said: Yellow-cheeked ostrich, which only eats sleep when fasting Any list. And poetry in this sense is abundant. Fasting in Islamic law means abstaining from things that break the fast, with the intention to do so, from sunrise to sunset. Its completion and perfection is achieved by avoiding prohibitions and not falling into forbidden things, as the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: Whoever does not give up false speech and acting upon it, God has no need for him to give up his food and drink. Second: The virtue of fasting is great, and its reward is immense. Many authentic and good hadiths have been reported about this, which the imams mentioned in their Musnads, and some of them will come. It is sufficient for you now, from them, regarding the virtue of fasting, that God has singled it out with an attribute to Him, as it was proven in the hadith from the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, that he said, informing about his Lord: “God, the Blessed and Exalted, says: ‘Every deed of the son of Adam is for him except fasting, for it is for Me and I will reward for it.’” The hadith. He specifically mentioned fasting as being for Him, even though all acts of worship are for Him. The two matters distinguish fasting from all other acts of worship. One of them: Fasting prevents the pleasures and desires of the soul in a way that other acts of worship do not prevent. Second: Fasting is a secret between the servant and his Lord, and is only revealed to Him. Therefore, it is specific to Him. Other acts of worship are apparent, and may be done out of affectation and hypocrisy. Therefore, it is more specific to fasting than other acts. Others have been said. Third: The Almighty’s saying: As it was written Al-Kafi is in the accusative case as an adjective, meaning a book as, or fasting as. Or as a state of fasting, meaning fasting was written upon you similar to what was written upon those before you. Some grammarians said: Kaf is in the nominative case as an adjective for fasting, since its definition is not purely specific, due to the ambiguity in it as explained by the Shari’ah. Therefore, it is permissible to describe it with as, since it is only used to describe indefinite nouns, so it is like fasting was written upon you. This statement has been weakened. Ma is in the genitive case, and its connection is: It was written upon those before you. The pronoun in Kabe refers back to ma. The people of interpretation differed regarding the place of the simile, which is: Fourth: Al-Sha’bi, Qatada and others said: The comparison goes back to the time of fasting and the amount of fasting. God Almighty prescribed the fast of Ramadan for the people of Moses and Jesus, but they changed it. Their rabbis increased it by ten days. Then one of their rabbis fell ill and vowed that if God healed him, he would increase their fast by ten days, so he did. So the Christians fasted for fifty days. It was difficult for them in the heat, so they moved it to spring. Al-Nahhas chose this statement and said: It is more similar to what is in the verse. And in it is a hadith that indicates its authenticity, which he attributed to Daghfal bin Hanzalah, “On the authority of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, who said: The Christians were required to fast for a month, then one of them fell ill, so they said: If God heals him, we will increase it by ten. Then there was another who ate meat and his mouth hurt, so they said: If God heals him, we will increase it by seven. Then there was another king, so they said: Let us wish for these seven days and make our fast in spring. He said: So it became fifty.” Mujahid said: God Almighty prescribed the fasting of the month of Ramadan for every nation. It was said: They took the document and fasted before the thirty days and after it one day, century after century, until their fasting reached fifty days. It was difficult for them in the heat, so they moved it to the solar season. Al-Naqqash said: There is a hadith on this from Daghfal bin Hanzala, Al-Hasan Al-Basri, and Al-Suddi. I said: And for this reason - and God knows best - it is disliked now to fast the Day of Doubt and the six days of Shawwal following the Day of Breaking the Fast, connected to it. Al-Sha'bi said: If I fasted the whole year, I would break my fast on the Day of Doubt. This is because the Christians were required to fast the month of Ramadan as it was required of us, so they changed it to the solar season because it coincided with the summer, so they counted thirty days. Then a generation came after them and they took the document for themselves and fasted before the thirty days and a day after it. Then the other generation continued to follow the example of those who came before them until they reached fifty days. This is what God the Almighty said: As it was prescribed for those before you. It was said: The likening refers to the origin of its obligation upon those who came before, not to the time and manner. It was said: The likening is to the nature of the fast that was upon them, which prevented them from eating, drinking and sexual intercourse. So when the time to break the fast came, the one who slept would not do these things. And this was also the case with the Christians at first and at the beginning of Islam, then God abrogated it by saying: Lawful to you on the night of the fast is the approach to your wives as will be explained, as stated by Al-Suddi, Abu Al-Aaliyah and Al-Rabi’. Muadh ibn Jabal and Ata’ said: The likening is to fasting, not to the description or the number, even though the two fasts differ in terms of increase and decrease. The meaning is: Fasting has been prescribed for you i.e. at the beginning of Islam, three days of every month and the day of Ashura, as it was prescribed for those before you and they are the Jews - according to Ibn Abbas - three days and Ashura. Then this was abrogated in this nation by the month of Ramadan. Muadh ibn Jabal said: This was abrogated by for a specified number of days then the days were abrogated by Ramadan. Fifth: Perhaps you will become righteous. Perhaps it is hoped that this is true for them, as mentioned above. And be righteous it was said that its meaning here is that you will become weak, because when eating decreased, desire weakened, and whenever desire weakens, sins decrease. This is a good metaphorical meaning. It was also said: So that you will become righteous from sins. It was also said that it is general, because fasting, as the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: Fasting is a shield and a means of piety, because it kills desires.
2:184: Sixth: The Almighty’s saying: A numbered number of days. Days is the second object of wrote, as Al-Farra’ said. It was said: It is an accusative of circumstance for wrote, meaning fasting was prescribed for you in days. The numbered days are the month of Ramadan, and this indicates the opposite of what was narrated from Muadh, and God knows best. The Almighty said: But whoever among you is ill or on a journey - then an equal number of other days. There are sixteen issues in this. First: The Almighty’s saying: sick. There are two cases for a sick person: One of them is that he is not able to fast under any circumstances, so he must break his fast as an obligation. Second: That he is able to fast with harm and hardship, so it is recommended for him to break his fast, and no one fasts except the ignorant. Ibn Sirin said: When a person finds himself in a condition that deserves the name of sickness, then it is permissible for him to break his fast, by analogy with the traveler, perhaps because of travel, even if there is no necessity for breaking his fast. Tarif ibn Tamam al-Attardi said: I entered upon Muhammad ibn Sirin in Ramadan while he was eating, and when he finished he said: This finger of mine hurts. The majority of scholars said: If he has an illness that is causing him pain and harm, or he fears its continuation or increase, then it is permissible for him to break his fast. Ibn Atiyyah said: This is the doctrine of the most skilled followers of Malik, and they debate it. As for the wording of Malik, it is an illness that is difficult for a person and causes him great suffering. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: There are different narrations from Malik regarding the illness that permits breaking the fast. He said once: It is the fear of being ruined by fasting. He said once: Severe illness, its increase, and great hardship. This is his correct school of thought and is what is apparent, because he did not specify one illness from another, so it is permissible in every illness, except what the evidence specifies, such as headache, fever, and a minor illness for which there is no burden in fasting. Al-Hasan said: If he is unable to pray standing due to illness, he breaks his fast. Al-Nakha’i said: A group said: He does not break his fast due to illness except for the one who is compelled by the necessity of the illness itself to break his fast, and whenever he tolerates the necessity with it, he does not break his fast. This is the opinion of Al-Shafi’i, may God have mercy on him. I said: The statement of Ibn Sirin is the most just thing in this regard, God willing. Al-Bukhari said: I fell ill in Nishapur with a minor illness, and that was in the month of Ramadan. Ishaq ibn Rahawayh visited me with a group of his companions and said to me: Have you broken your fast, O Abu Abdullah? I said: Yes, because I feared that I would be too weak to accept the concession. I said: Abdun narrated to us on the authority of Ibn al-Mubarak on the authority of Ibn Jurayj who said: I said to Ata’: Whoever sees that he is sick should break his fast? He said: From whatever illness, as God Almighty said: And whoever among you is ill [al-Bukhari] Al-Bukhari said: This hadith was not narrated by Ishaq. Abu Hanifa said: If a man fears for himself while he is fasting that if he does not break his fast, his eye will become more severe or his fever will become more severe, then he should break his fast. Second: The Almighty’s saying: Or on a journey. Scholars differed about the journey in which breaking the fast and shortening the prayer is permissible, after their consensus on the journey of obedience such as Hajj and Jihad. Connected to these two is the journey to maintain kinship ties and to seek a necessary livelihood. As for travelling for trade and permissible purposes, there is a difference of opinion regarding its prohibition and permission, and the opinion regarding its permissibility is stronger. As for the journey of a sinner, there is a difference of opinion regarding its permissibility and prohibition, and the opinion regarding its prohibition is stronger, as stated by Ibn Atiyyah. The distance of breaking the fast according to Malik is where the prayer is shortened. Scholars differed about its amount. Malik said: A day and a night, then he changed his mind and said: Forty-eight miles. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: This is the apparent meaning of his school of thought. He said once: Forty-two miles, and he said once: Thirty-six miles, and he said once: A day and a night’s journey, and it was narrated from him two days, and this is the opinion of Al-Shafi’i. He once distinguished between land and sea, saying that at sea it is a day and a night’s journey, and on land it is forty-eight miles, and in a way it is thirty miles, and in a way other than that it is three miles. Ibn Amr, Ibn Abbas, and Al-Thawri said: The breaking of the fast is for a journey of three days, as narrated by Ibn Atiyah. Third: The scholars agreed that the traveler in Ramadan is not permitted to spend the night breaking his fast, because the traveler is not a traveler by intention, unlike the resident, but rather he is a traveler by work and getting up, and the resident does not need work, because if he intends to stay, he is a resident at the time, because residence does not need work, so they differ. There is also no disagreement among them regarding the one who hopes to travel, that he is not permitted to break his fast before he leaves, and if he breaks his fast, Ibn Habib said: If he has prepared for his travel and has taken the means of movement, then nothing is upon him. This was narrated from Asbagh and Ibn Al-Majishun, but if an obstacle prevents him from traveling, then he must pay expiation, and it is sufficient for him to be saved if he travels. Isa narrated from Ibn Al-Qasim that he only has to make up a day, because he interpreted his breaking of the fast. Ashhab said: He does not have to pay expiation whether he travels or not. Sahnun said: He has to pay expiation whether he travels or not, and he is like a woman who says: My period will come tomorrow, so she breaks her fast for that reason. Then he returned to the words of Abdul Malik and Asbagh and said: It is not like a woman, because a man may menstruate while traveling if he wants, but a woman does not menstruate. I said: The statement of Ibn Al-Qasim and Ashab in denying the expiation is good, because it is not permissible for him to do it, and the conscience is innocent, so nothing is proven in it except with certainty, and there is no certainty with disagreement, then it is required by the saying of God the Almighty: or on a journey. Abu Omar said: This is the most correct of their statements in this matter, because he did not violate the sanctity of fasting with the intention of doing so, but rather he interpreted it, and if eating with the intention of traveling would require expiation from him, because before he left, his departure would have absolved him of it, so reflect on that and you will find it to be so, God willing. Al-Darqutni narrated: Abu Bakr Al-Naysaburi told us, Ismail bin Ishaq bin Sahl told us in Egypt, he said: Ibn Abi Maryam told us, Muhammad bin Jaafar told us, Zaid bin Aslam told me, he said: Muhammad bin Al-Munkadir told me, on the authority of Muhammad bin Kaab, that he said: I came to Anas bin Malik in Ramadan while he wanted to travel, and his mount had been saddled and he had put on his travel clothes and the sun was about to set, so he called for food and ate from it then he got on. So I said to him: Is it a Sunnah? He said: Yes. It was also narrated from Anas that he said: Abu Musa said to me: Did I not tell you that when you go out, you go out fasting, and when you enter, you enter fasting, so when you go out, go out breaking your fast, and when you enter, go in breaking your fast? Al-Hasan al-Basri said: He may break his fast if he wishes in his house on the day he wants to go out. Ahmad said: He may break his fast when he leaves the houses. Ishaq said: No, but when he places his foot in his saddle. Ibn al-Mundhir said: Ahmad’s statement is correct, because they say to someone who wakes up healthy and then becomes ill: He breaks his fast for the rest of the day. Likewise, if he wakes up in the city and then sets out to travel, he may also break his fast. A group said: He does not break his fast that day even if he gets up for his journey. This is what al-Zuhri, Makhul, Yahya al-Ansari, Malik, al-Awza’i, al-Shafi’i, Abu Thawr and the people of opinion said. They differed about whether he does so, and all of them said that he should make up for it and not offer expiation. Malik said: Because travel is an urgent excuse, so it is like an illness that befalls him. It was narrated from some of the companions of Malik that he should make up the fast and offer expiation. This is the opinion of Ibn Kinanah and Al-Makhzoumi. Al-Baji narrated it from Al-Shafi’i, and Ibn Al-Arabi chose it and said it. He said: Because travel is an excuse that arose after the obligation of worship, and it is different from sickness and menstruation, because sickness permits him to break the fast, and menstruation prohibits her from fasting, and travel does not permit him to do so, so expiation is required of him for violating its sanctity. Abu Omar said: This is nothing, because God, the Exalted, has permitted him to break the fast in the Book and the Sunnah. As for their saying that he should not break the fast, this is only recommended for what he has stipulated. If he takes advantage of God’s dispensation, then he must make it up. As for expiation, there is no basis for it, and whoever requires it has required something that God and His Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace, did not require. It was narrated from Ibn Omar on this issue: He may break the fast if he wishes on that day if he sets out on a journey. This is the opinion of Al-Sha’bi, Ahmad and Ishaq. I said: Al-Bukhari, may God have mercy on him, has addressed this issue in the chapter on the one who breaks his fast while traveling so that people can see him, and he cited the hadith: “On the authority of Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, left Medina for Mecca and fasted until he reached Usfan, then he called for water and raised it to his hands so that people could see him, and he broke his fast until he reached Mecca, that was in Ramadan.” Muslim also narrated it on the authority of Ibn Abbas, and he said in it: Then he called for a vessel containing a drink and drank it during the day so that people could see him, then he broke his fast until he entered Mecca. This is a text in the chapter, so what contradicts it is dropped, and God is the Grantor of success. It also contains an argument against those who say: Fasting is not valid while traveling. It was narrated on the authority of Umar, Ibn Abbas, Abu Hurairah, and Ibn Umar. Ibn Umar said: Whoever fasts while traveling must make up for it while at home. And on the authority of Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf: The one who fasts while traveling is like the one who breaks his fast while at home. Some of the people of the apparent meaning said this, and they argued with the words of God, the Most High: Then an equal number of other days, as will be explained, and with what Ka’b ibn Asim narrated, who said: I heard the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, say: It is not righteousness to fast while traveling. This also provides evidence against those who say: Whoever intends to fast while traveling may break his fast even if he has no excuse. This is the view of Mutarrif, and it is one of the two opinions of al-Shafi’i, and a group of the people of hadith agree with him. Malik used to require him to make up the fast and offer expiation because he had a choice between fasting and breaking the fast. When he chose to fast and stay home, it was obligatory for him, but he was not allowed to break the fast. If he broke the fast intentionally without an excuse, he must make up the fast and offer expiation. It has been narrated from him that he does not have to offer expiation, and this is the view of most of his companions except for Abd al-Malik, who said: “If he breaks his fast by having sexual intercourse, he has disbelieved, because he does not have the strength to travel and has no excuse, because the traveler is only permitted to break his fast so that he may have the strength to travel.” The rest of the jurists in Iraq and Hijaz said: He does not have to offer expiation, including al-Thawri, al-Awza’i, al-Shafi’i, Abu Hanifah, and the rest of the jurists of Kufa. This was stated by Abu ‘Umar. Fourth: The scholars differed about what is better, breaking the fast or fasting while traveling. Malik and al-Shafi’i said in some of what was narrated from them: Fasting is better for those who are able to do it. Most of Malik’s school of thought is that there is a choice, as does al-Shafi’i’s school of thought. Al-Shafi’i and those who followed him said: He has a choice, and he did not specify. So did Ibn Ulayyah, based on the hadith of Anas who said: “We traveled with the Prophet (peace and blessings of God be upon him) during Ramadan, and the fasting person did not criticize the one who broke the fast, nor did the one who broke the fast criticize the fasting person.” Narrated by Malik, al-Bukhari and Muslim. It was narrated on the authority of Uthman ibn Abi al-‘As al-Thaqafi and Anas ibn Malik, the two companions of the Messenger of God (peace and blessings of God be upon him), that they said: Fasting while traveling is better for whoever is able to do so. This is the opinion of Abu Hanifa and his companions. It was narrated on the authority of Ibn ‘Umar and Ibn ‘Abbas: A concession is better. This was also said by Sa’id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Sha’bi, ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-‘Aziz, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Awza’i, Ahmad and Ishaq. All of these said that breaking the fast is better, because God the Almighty says interpretation of the meaning: God intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship. Fifth: The Almighty’s statement: then a number of days is omitted in the statement, meaning whoever among you is sick or traveling and breaks his fast, let him make it up. The majority of scholars are of the opinion that if the people of a country fast twenty-nine days and there is a sick man in the country who did not recover, then he must make up for twenty-nine days. Some people, including Al-Hasan bin Salih bin Hayy, said: He should make up for a month without considering the number of days. Al-Kaya Al-Tabari said: This is far-fetched, because the Almighty said: then a number of other days and did not say then a month of other days. His statement: then a number requires completing the number of days in which he broke his fast, and there is no doubt that if he broke his fast for some of Ramadan, then he must make up for the number of days he broke his fast after it, and likewise the ruling on breaking his fast as a whole must be based on its number. Sixth: The Almighty’s saying: So a number. “So a number” is raised as a predicate of the subject, its meaning is So the ruling or So the duty is a number, and it is correct for him to fast a number. Al-Kisa’i said: So a number is permissible, meaning let him fast a number of days. It was also said: The meaning is fasting a number, so the complement was deleted and the number was established in its place. The number is a verb from count, and it means what is counted, like grinding in the sense of what is ground. You say: I hear a noise but I do not see any grinding. And from this is the woman’s number. From other days “Akhir” was not declined according to Sibawayh, because it is modified from the alif and lam, because the way of a verb in this category is to come with the alif and lam, like al-kabr and al-fadl. Al-Kisa’i said: It is modified from akhir, as you say: hamra’ and hamra’, and that is why it was not declined. It was also said: It was prevented from being declined because it is on the weight of a plural and it is an attribute of ayam, and akhir was not brought so that it would not be confused as an attribute of the number. It was also said: Akhir is the plural of akhir as if it were ayam, then it became more numerous, so it was said: Ayyam Akhar. It was said: The description of days is feminine, so it was described by another. Seventh: People differed on the necessity of performing it consecutively, with two opinions mentioned by Al-Daraqutni in his Sunan. He narrated on the authority of Aisha, may God be pleased with her, who said: It was revealed on several consecutive days, then it was dropped consecutively. He said: This is a sound chain of transmission. It was narrated on the authority of Abu Hurairah, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: Whoever owes a fast from Ramadan, let him complete it and not break it. In its chain of transmission is Abd al-Rahman ibn Ibrahim, who is weak in hadith. And he narrated it on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding making up Ramadan: Fast it however you wish. And Ibn Umar said: Fast it as you broke it. And he narrated on the authority of Abu Ubaidah ibn al-Jarrah, Ibn Abbas, Abu Hurayrah, Muadh ibn Jabal, and Amr ibn al-Aas. And “On the authority of Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, he said: It reached me that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, was asked about breaking up the fast of Ramadan, so he said: That is up to you. Tell me, if one of you had a debt and paid off a dirham or two, would he not have paid it off? God is more deserving of pardoning and forgiveness.” Its chain of transmission is good, except that it is mursal and cannot be proven as connected. In the Muwatta of Malik, on the authority of Nafi’ that Abdullah ibn Umar used to say: Whoever breaks it off consecutively due to illness or travel should fast Ramadan consecutively. Al-Baji said in al-Muntaqa: It is possible that he meant to inform about the obligation, and it is possible that he meant to inform about the desirability, and the majority of jurists are of the view that it is desirability. If he does it separately, it is sufficient for him, and Malik and Al-Shafi’i said the same. The evidence for the correctness of this is the statement of God the Almighty: Then a number of other days, and He did not specify separate days from consecutive days. If he does it separately, then he has fasted a number of other days, so it is obligatory for him to do it. Ibn Al-Arabi said: Consecutive days are only obligatory in the month because it is specific, and there is no specification in making up, so separating them is permissible. Eighth: When God Almighty said: Then a number of other days, this indicates the obligation to make up for it without specifying a time, because the wording is general in its meaning and does not refer to some of them over others. In the two Sahihs, on the authority of Aisha, may God be pleased with her, she said: I have to fast from Ramadan, but I cannot make it up except in Shaban, because I am busy with the Messenger of God, or with the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace. In another narration: “Because of the position of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace.” This is the text and further clarification of the verse. This refutes Dawud’s statement that he must make it up on the second of Shawwal. Whoever does not fast it and then dies is sinful in his eyes. Based on this, if he is obligated to free a slave and finds a slave being sold for a price, he does not have the right to go beyond that and buy another, because the obligation upon him is to free the first slave he finds, so no other will suffice. If he has a slave, it is not permissible for him to buy another, and if the one he has dies, the manumission is not invalidated, just as it is invalidated in the case of someone who vows to free a specific slave and she dies, his vow is invalidated, and this invalidates his statement. Some of the scholars of the principles of jurisprudence said: If he dies after the passing of the eighth day of Shawwal, he does not disobey the condition of intention. The correct view is that he is not sinful or negligent, and this is the view of the majority. However, it is recommended for him to hasten to make up for it so that death does not overtake him and the obligation remains upon him. Ninth: If someone had to make up days of Ramadan and the number of days passed after breaking the fast, during which he could have fasted, but he delayed it, then something happened to prevent him from making it up until another Ramadan, then he is not required to feed, because he did not break his fast when he did what was permissible for him to delay. This is the opinion of the Malikis of Baghdad, and they see it as the opinion of Ibn al-Qasim in al-Mudawwana. Tenth: If he delays making up for it until after Sha’ban, which is the last period in which he can make up for Ramadan, is he required to make up for it or not? Malik, Al-Shafi’i, Ahmad, and Ishaq said: Yes. Abu Hanifa, Al-Hasan, Al-Nakha’i, and Dawud said: No. I said: Al-Bukhari went to this for his statement, and he mentions on the authority of Abu Hurairah, without a chain of transmission, and Ibn Abbas that he feeds, and God did not mention feeding, rather He said: Then a number of other days. I said: It was narrated on the authority of Abu Hurairah with a chain of transmission regarding someone who neglected to make up for Ramadan until another Ramadan came upon him. He said: This one should fast with the people, and he should fast the one he neglected, and he should feed a poor person for each day. Ad-Daraqutni narrated it and said: Its chain of transmission is sound. It was narrated on his authority with a chain of transmission traceable back to the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace: “A man broke his fast in Ramadan due to illness, then recovered and did not fast until another Ramadan came. He said: He should fast the month he caught up with, then fast the month in which he broke his fast, and feed a poor person for each day.” Its chain of transmission includes Ibn Nafi’ and Ibn Wajih, both of whom are weak. Eleventh: If his illness persists and he does not recover until the next Ramadan comes, then Al-Daraqutni narrated on the authority of Ibn Umar that he should feed a poor person a mudd of wheat for each day, then he does not have to make it up. It was also narrated on the authority of Abu Hurairah who said: If he does not recover between two Ramadans, he should fast for this and feed for the second, and he does not have to make it up. If he recovers but does not fast until the next Ramadan comes, he should fast for this and feed for the last, and when he breaks his fast, he should make it up. The chain of transmission is sound. Our scholars said: The statements of the Companions that contradict analogy may be used as evidence. It was narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas that a man came to him and said: You were sick for two Ramadans? Ibn Abbas said to him: Did your illness continue, or did you recover between them? He said: Rather, you recovered. He said: Fast two Ramadans and feed sixty poor people. This is in exchange for his statement: If his illness persists, he does not have to make it up. This is similar to their doctrine regarding the pregnant and breastfeeding woman, that they should feed and do not have to make it up, as will come. Twelfth: Those who are obligated to feed differed regarding the amount that must be fed. Abu Hurairah, Al-Qasim bin Muhammad, Malik, and Al-Shafi’i said: He should feed a mudd for each day. Al-Thawri said: He should feed half a sa’ for each day. Thirteenth: They differed about what is obligatory for someone who broke his fast or had intercourse while making up for Ramadan. Malik said: Whoever breaks his fast one day while making up for Ramadan by mistake, he does not have to do anything except make it up. It is recommended for him to continue with it due to the difference of opinion and then make it up. If he broke his fast intentionally, he has sinned and he does not have to do anything except make up for that day. He should not continue with it, because there is no point in refraining from what the fasting person refrains from here, since he is not fasting according to the majority of scholars because he broke his fast intentionally. As for expiation, there is no disagreement among Malik and his companions that it is not obligatory for that, and this is the opinion of the majority of scholars. Malik said: Whoever breaks his fast one day while making up for Ramadan by having intercourse with his wife or otherwise does not have to make expiation, but he has to make up for that day. Qatada said: Whoever has intercourse while making up for Ramadan has to make up for it and make up for it. Ibn al-Qasim narrated on the authority of Malik that whoever breaks his fast while making up for a missed Ramadan fast must make up for two days. Ibn al-Qasim used to issue a fatwa on this, then he changed his mind and said: If he breaks his fast intentionally while making up for a missed fast, he must fast for two days instead, like someone who spoils a Hajj by visiting his wife, and performs Hajj the following year and spoils his Hajj by visiting his wife again, he must make up for two Hajjs. Abu Omar said: Ibn Wahb and Abd al-Malik disagreed with him regarding Hajj, and analogy is not necessary based on a principle that is disputed. The correct view in my opinion - and God knows best - is that he only has to make up for one day in both cases, because it is one day that he spoiled twice. I said: This is required by the Almighty’s saying: Then a number of other days. So whenever he brings a full day in place of what he broke in making up for Ramadan, then he has fulfilled what is required of him, and nothing else is required of him, and God knows best. Fourteenth: The majority of scholars agree that if someone breaks his fast in Ramadan due to an illness and dies from that illness, or travels and dies during his journey, then nothing is due on him. Tawus and Qatada said about a sick person who dies before he recovers: Food should be fed on his behalf. Fifteenth: They differed concerning someone who died and had not made up for Ramadan fasts. Malik, Ash-Shafi’i and Ath-Thawri said: No one should fast. Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Thawr, Al-Layth, Abu Ubaid and the apparent scholars said: Fasting should be done on his behalf, except that they specified it as a vow. The same was narrated from Ash-Shafi’i. Ahmad and Ishaq said concerning making up Ramadan: Feeding should be done on his behalf. Those who said that fasting is permissible provided evidence with what Muslim narrated on the authority of Aisha that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: Whoever dies and owes fasting, his guardian should fast on his behalf. However, this is general in fasting, and is specified by what Muslim also narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas, who said: “A woman came to the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, and said: O Messenger of God, my mother has died and she had to fast as a vow - and in another narration, fast for a month - should I fast on her behalf? He said: Tell me, if your mother had a debt and you paid it off, would that be fulfilled on her behalf? She said: Yes. He said: Then fast on behalf of your mother.” Malik and those who agreed with him cited as evidence the words of God, the Most High: And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another and His words: And that man shall have nothing but what he strives for and His words: And no soul earns except against itself and what al-Nasa’i narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas, on the authority of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, that he said: No one should pray on behalf of anyone else, and no one should fast on behalf of anyone else, but a mudd of wheat should be fed on his behalf every day. I said: This hadith is general, so it is possible that what is meant by his saying: No one should fast on behalf of another is the fast of Ramadan. As for fasting a vow, it is permissible, based on the hadith of Ibn Abbas and others. It also came in Sahih Muslim from a hadith of Buraydah similar to the hadith of Ibn Abbas, and in some of its chains of transmission: Fasting for two months, should I fast on her behalf? He said: Fast on her behalf. She said: She has never performed Hajj, should I perform Hajj on her behalf? He said: Perform Hajj on her behalf. Her saying: Two months is unlikely to be Ramadan, and God knows best. The strongest evidence for Malik is that it was the practice of the people of Medina, and it is supported by clear analogy, which is that it is a physical act of worship in which money has no role, so it should not be done on behalf of someone upon whom it is obligatory, like prayer. This is not nullified by Hajj, because money has a role in it. Sixteenth: This verse was used as evidence by those who said that fasting is not valid while traveling and that one must make up for it. God Almighty says: But whoever among you is ill or on a journey - then an equal number of other days. That is, he must make up for it. There is no omission or implication in the speech. And with his saying, may the peace and blessings of God be upon him: It is not righteousness to fast while traveling. He said: Whatever is not righteousness is sinful. This indicates that fasting Ramadan while traveling is not permissible. The majority say: There is something omitted in it, so break your fast, as mentioned above. This is correct, based on the hadith of Anas, who said: “We traveled with the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, during Ramadan, and the fasting person did not criticize the one who broke his fast, nor did the one who broke his fast criticize the fasting person.” Narrated by Malik on the authority of Humayd al-Tawil on the authority of Anas. Muslim narrated it on the authority of Abu Sa`id al-Khudri, who said: We went on a military expedition with the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, sixteen days before the end of Ramadan. Some of us fasted and some of us broke our fast. The fasting person did not criticize the one who broke his fast, nor did the one who broke his fast criticize the fasting person. God Almighty says: “And for those who can do it [with hardship] is a ransom - the feeding of a poor person. But whoever volunteers good, it is better for him. And that you fast is better for you, if you only knew.” There are five issues in this: The first: The Almighty’s saying: And upon those who are able to bear it. The majority read it with a kasra on the ta’ and a sukoon on the ya’. Its original form is yatuquhu, the kasra was transferred to the ta’ and the waw was changed to a ya’ because of the kasra of what preceded it. Hamid read it according to the original form without any defect, and the analogy is defect. The well-known reading of Ibn Abbas is yatuquhu with a fatha on the ta’ and a shaddah on the waw, meaning they burden him. Mujahid narrated yatuquhu with a ya’ after the ta’ in the form yakilunu, which is invalid and impossible, because the verb is taken from tawq, so the waw is obligatory and there is no role for the ya’ in this example. Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: Ahmad bin Yahya al-Nahwi recited to us for Abu Dhu’ayb: It was said that it is more than you can bear. It is a printing press. Whoever visits it will not be harmed by it. So he showed the waw in the word tawq, and it is correct that the one who puts the ya in its place differs from the correct. Ibn al-Anbari narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas, yatuqunuhu with the fatha on the ya and the shaddah on the ta, and the ya with the fatha on it means yatuqunuhu, it is said: taaq, atataaq, and atiq with the same meaning. And on the authority of Ibn Abbas also, Aisha, Tawus, and Amr ibn Dinar, yatuqunuhu with the fatha on the ya and the shaddah on the ta, open, and it is correct in the language, because the original is yatuqunuhu, so the ta was made quiescent and assimilated into the ta, so it became a shaddah on the ta, and it is not from the Qur’an, contrary to those who confirmed it as a Qur’an, but it is a reading based on interpretation. The people of Madinah and Ash-Sham read fidya food with an addition, masakin as a plural. Ibn Abbas read ta’am miskin in the singular, as mentioned by al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud, and al-Nasa’i on the authority of Ata’ on his authority. It is a good reading, because it clarifies the ruling on the day, and Abu Ubaid chose it, and it is the reading of Abu Amr, Hamza, and al-Kisa’i. Abu Ubaid said: So it was made clear that each day there is one person to feed, so one person translates from all, but not all translate from one person. And the plural of the poor is not known how many of them there are in a day except from another verse. And the plural reading in poor is derived from the fact that those who are able to do it are a plural and each one of them is required to have a poor person, so the word is plural, as God Almighty said: And those who accuse chaste women but do not produce four witnesses - flog them with eighty lashes meaning flog each one of them with eighty lashes, so the eighty are not scattered among all of them, rather each one has eighty, Abu Ali said its meaning. And An-Nahhas chose the plural reading, and he said: What Abu Ubaid chose is rejected, because this is only known by indication, and it is known that the meaning of And upon those who are able to do it is a ransom to feed poor people is that for each day there is a poor person, so this reading was chosen to refer plural to plural. Al-Nahhas said: Abu Ubaid chose to read it as a food ransom. He said: Because the food is the ransom, and it is not permissible for food to be an adjective because it is a substance, but it is permissible as a substitute. It is clearer than that to read it as a food ransom with the addition, because a vague ransom applies to food and other things, so it becomes like your saying: This is a silk garment. Second: The scholars differed about the meaning of the verse. Some said: It is abrogated. Al-Bukhari narrated: Ibn Numayr said: Al-A’mash told us: Amr ibn Murrah told us: Ibn Abi Laila told us: The companions of Muhammad (peace be upon him) told us: Ramadan was revealed and it was difficult for them. So whoever fed a poor person every day, those who were able to fast, left fasting. They were given permission to do so, but it was abrogated by and that you fast is better for you. According to this, the majority read they are able to do it, because the obligation of fasting is as follows: Whoever wants to fast, let him fast, and whoever wants to feed a poor person, let him feed. Ibn Abbas said: This verse was revealed as a permission for the elderly and the infirm in particular if they broke their fast while they were able to fast. Then it was abrogated by His statement: And whoever among you witnesses the month, let him fast it. So the permission was removed except for those who were unable to do so. Al-Farra’ said: The pronoun in they are able to fast may refer to fasting, meaning that those who are able to fast should feed when they break their fast. Then it was abrogated by His statement: and that you fast. It is permissible to refer to the ransom, i.e., and for those who are able to ransom, a ransom.
