As for the reading of yatuqunuhu, it means they are burdened with the hardship that will follow them, such as the sick and the pregnant, for they are able to do it but with hardship that will follow them in themselves, so if they fast, it will suffice them and if they ransom themselves, then they may do so. Ibn Abbas - if the chain of transmission from him is sound - interpreted yatuqunuhu as yatuqunuhu and yatuqulunuhu, so some of the narrators included it in the Qur’an. Abu Dawud narrated from Ibn Abbas, and for those who are able to do it, he said: It was proven for the pregnant and breastfeeding woman. And it was narrated from him, And for those who are able to do it, a ransom of feeding a poor person, he said: It was a concession for the elderly who are able to fast to break their fast and feed a poor person for each day, and the pregnant and breastfeeding woman, if they fear for their children, they break their fast and feed. Al-Daraqutni also narrated from him, he said: It was concession for the elderly man to break his fast and feed a poor person for each day, and he does not have to make it up. This is a sound chain of transmission. It was also narrated from him that he said: And upon those who are able to fast is a ransom of food that has not been abrogated, namely the elderly man and the elderly woman who are unable to fast, so they feed a poor person for each day. This is authentic. It was also narrated from him that he said to his mother, whether she was pregnant or breastfeeding: You are among those who are not able to fast, you must make up for it but you do not have to make it up. This is an authentic chain of transmission. In another narration: He had a mother of his who was breastfeeding - without a doubt - and she became exhausted, so he ordered her to break her fast and not make it up. This is authentic. I said: It has been proven with authentic chains of transmission on the authority of Ibn Abbas that the verse is not abrogated and that it is decisive for those mentioned. The first statement is also correct, except that it is possible that abrogation there means specification, as the ancients often used the term abrogation in this sense, and God knows best. Al-Hasan al-Basri, Ata’ ibn Abi Rabah, al-Dahhak, al-Nakha’i, al-Zuhri, Rabi’ah, al-Awza’i and the people of opinion said: The pregnant and breastfeeding woman break the fast and do not have to feed the poor, just as the sick person breaks the fast and makes up for it. Abu Ubaid and Abu Thawr said the same. Abu Ubaid narrated that on the authority of Abu Thawr, and Ibn al-Mundhir chose it. It is the statement of Malik regarding the pregnant woman who breaks the fast, but as for the breastfeeding woman, if she breaks the fast, she must make it up and feed the poor. Al-Shafi’i and Ahmad said: They break the fast, feed the poor and make it up. They agreed that the elderly and old women who cannot fast or can do so with great difficulty should break the fast. They differed about what they are required to do. Rabia and Malik said: They are not required to do anything. However, Malik said: If they fed a poor person for each day, that would be more pleasing to me. Anas, Ibn Abbas, Qays ibn al-Sa’ib and Abu Hurayrah said: They are required to pay the ransom. This is the opinion of al-Shafi’i, the People of Opinion, Ahmad and Ishaq, following the opinion of the Companions may God be pleased with them all, and the words of God the Almighty: But whoever among you is ill or on a journey - the same number of days should be made up from other days (al-Anbiya’ 1:10). Then He said: And upon those who can afford it is a ransom of feeding a poor person (al-Anbiya’ 1:10). These people are neither ill nor travelling, so the ransom is required of them. The evidence for Malik’s opinion is that this person breaks the fast due to an excuse that exists in him, which is old age and decrepitude, so he is not required to feed the poor like the traveller and the sick person. This was narrated from al-Thawri and Makhul, and Ibn al-Mundhir chose it. Third: Those who made the ransom obligatory differed regarding its amount. Malik said: A mudd of the Prophet’s mudd for each day he broke his fast, and Al-Shafi’i said the same. Abu Hanifa said: The expiation for each day is a sa’ of dates or half a sa’ of wheat. It was narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas: Half a sa’ of wheat, as mentioned by Al-Daraqutni. It was narrated on the authority of Abu Hurairah that he said: Whoever is overtaken by old age and is unable to fast, must pay a mudd of wheat for each day. It was narrated on the authority of Anas bin Malik that he was too weak to fast for a year, so he made a bowl of food, then called for thirty poor people and fed them. Fourth: The Almighty’s saying: But whoever volunteers good, it is better for him. Ibn Shihab said: Whoever intends to feed along with fasting. Mujahid said: Whoever feeds more than a mudd. Ibn Abbas: Whoever volunteers good, he said: Another poor person, it is better for him. Al-Daraqutni mentioned it and said: A sound and proven chain of transmission. The second good is an adjective of preference, as is the third and the first good. Isa bin Omar, Yahya bin Waththab, Hamza and Al-Kisa’i read yataw’u khairan with a shaddah and the ‘ayn was jazm to mean yutaw’u, the rest read tataw’u with a ta’ and a light ta’ and a fathah on the ‘ayn for the past tense. Fifth: The Almighty said: And that you fast is better for you. That is, fasting is better for you. And this is how my father read it, that is, than breaking the fast with the ransom, and this was before the abrogation. And it was said: And that you fast while traveling and sick, but not while it is difficult, and God knows best. In short, it requires urging fasting, that is, so know that and fast.
2:185: God Almighty says: “The month of Ramadan is that in which the Qur’an was revealed, a guidance for mankind and clear proofs of guidance and criterion. So whoever sights the month shall fast it. And whoever is ill or on a journey - then an equal number of other days. God intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship and [that] you may complete the number and glorify God for having guided you; and perhaps you will be grateful.” It contains twenty-one issues: First: The Almighty’s saying: The month of Ramadan. Historians said: The first to fast Ramadan was Noah, peace be upon him, when he got out of the ship. Mujahid’s statement was mentioned earlier: God prescribed Ramadan for every nation, and it is known that Noah had nations, and God knows best. The word month is derived from publicizing because it is well-known and it is not difficult for anyone who wants to know it. From this it is said: I drew the sword if you unsheathed it. Ramadan is taken from the word ramadh the fasting person who burns his stomach from intense thirst. Ramada extended means intense heat, and from this the hadith: The prayer of the repentant when the camels are scorched. Narrated by Muslim. The scorching of the camels is when the sand burns and they are blessed due to its intense heat. Ramadan - according to what they mentioned - coincides with the intense heat, so it is taken from the scorching sun. Al-Jawhari said: The month of Ramadan is pluralized as Ramadanat and irmadaa. It is said that when they transferred the names of the months from the ancient language, they named them according to the times in which they fell, so this month coincided with the days of the scorching sun, so it was called that. It was also said: It was called Ramadan because it scorches sins, that is, it burns them with good deeds, from irmad, which means burning, and from this, his foot was scorched from the sand, meaning it was burned. And the sand scorched me, meaning it burned me, and from this it was said: The matter scorched me. It was also said: Because the hearts take from it the heat of admonition and contemplation of the matter of the Hereafter, just as sand and stones take from the heat of the sun. And scorching means hot stones. It was said: It is from رمضاطan-Nasl, which means to grind it between two stones to make it thin. From this comes the wordرمضضذ andرمضضوذ- according to Ibn al-Sikkit - and the month was named after it because they used to grind their weapons in Ramadan to fight with them in Shawwal before the sacred months began. Al-Mawardi narrated that its name in the pre-Islamic era was Natiq, and he recited for al-Mufaddal: In Natiq, the knights of Khatham fled in the heat of battle. The word month is in the nominative case, as per the group’s reading, as a subject, and the predicate is in which the Qur’an was revealed. Or it is in the nominative case with an implied subject, meaning: the month of Ramadan is obligatory upon you, or among what is prescribed for you is the month of Ramadan. It is permissible for month to be a subject, and in which the Qur’an was revealed is an adjective, and the predicate is so whoever witnesses the month. The month is mentioned again for emphasis, as in the Almighty’s saying: “The Inevitable. What is the Inevitable?” It is permissible for the meaning of reward to enter into it, because the month of Ramadan, even if it is a definite noun, is not a specific definite noun because it is common throughout the future, as Abu Ali said: It was narrated from Mujahid and Shahr bin Hawshab that Shahr was in the accusative case, and Harun al-A’war narrated it from Abu Amr, and its meaning is: stick to the month of Ramadan or fast. And in which the Qur’an was revealed is an adjective for it, and it is not permissible for it to be in the accusative case with fast, so as not to separate the relative clause from the relative pronoun with the predicate of that and it is better for you. Al-Rumani: It is permissible to put it in the accusative case as a substitute for his saying numbered days. Second: There is a difference of opinion as to whether it is said Ramadan without adding it to the month. Mujahid disliked that and said: It is said as God Almighty said. And in the hadith: Do not say Ramadan, but attribute it as God attributed it in the Qur’an, saying the month of Ramadan. He used to say: I have heard that it is one of the names of God. He disliked that the word be combined for this meaning. He used to cite as evidence what was narrated: Ramadan is one of the names of God the Most High, and this is not correct, as it is from the hadith of Abu Ma’shar Najih, who is weak. What is correct is that it is permissible to use Ramadan without adding it, as is proven in the Sahihs and other books. Muslim narrated on the authority of Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: When Ramadan comes, the gates of mercy are opened, the gates of Hell are closed, and the devils are chained up. In Sahih Al-Basti, it is narrated on his authority that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: When Ramadan comes, the gates of mercy are opened for him, the gates of Hell are closed, and the devils are chained. It was narrated on the authority of Ibn Shihab on the authority of Anas ibn Abi Anas that his father told him that he heard Abu Hurairah say…, and he mentioned it. Al-Basti said: This Anas ibn Abi Anas is the father of Malik ibn Anas, and the name of Abu Anas is Malik ibn Abi Amir, one of the trustworthy people of Madinah, and he is Malik ibn Abi Amir ibn Amr ibn al-Harith ibn Uthman ibn Khathil ibn Amr from Dhi Asbah, one of the chiefs of Yemen. Al-Nasa’i narrated on the authority of Abu Hurairah that he said: “The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: Ramadan has come to you, a blessed month, in which God the Almighty has made fasting obligatory upon you. In it the gates of heaven are opened, the gates of Hell are closed, and the rebellious devils are chained for God. In it is a night better than a thousand months. Whoever is deprived of its goodness is indeed deprived.” Abu Hatim al-Basti also narrated it and said: His saying: the rebellious devils is a qualification of his saying: the devils are chained and chained. Al-Sana’i also narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas, who said: “The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said to a woman from the Ansar: ‘When Ramadan comes, perform Umrah, for an Umrah in it is equal to a Hajj.’” Al-Nasa’i also narrated on the authority of Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: “God the Almighty has imposed the fasting of Ramadan upon you and has made it a Sunnah for you to stand in prayer during it. Whoever fasts and stands in prayer during it out of faith and in the hope of reward will emerge from his sins as on the day his mother bore him.” There are many reports on this, all of which omit the month. Perhaps the Arabs omitted the mention of the month from Ramadan. The poet said: A slave girl in her loose white armor from the sister of the Banu Ibadh Last Ramadan, she interrupted the conversation by nodding. The virtue of Ramadan is great, and its reward is immense. This is indicated by the meaning of the derivation of it being a burner of sins, and the hadiths we have written. Third: God imposed fasting during Ramadan, that is, the duration of its crescent moon, and the month was named after it, as stated in the hadith: If the month is hidden from you meaning the crescent, it will come, and the poet said: Brothers from Najd, trustworthy and famous as a nail clipping Until it is completed in its roundness in four more than ten And He has imposed upon us, when the crescent moon is cloudy, the completion of the number of Sha’ban as thirty days, and the completion of the number of Ramadan as thirty days, so that we may enter into worship with certainty and depart from it with certainty. He said in His Book, And We have sent down to you the message that you may make clear to the people what was sent down to them. And the Imams of the proof have narrated on the authority of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, who said: “Fast when it is seen and break your fast when it is sighted. If it is cloudy, complete the number.” In another narration, If the month is cloudy, count thirty. Mutraf ibn Abdullah ibn Ash-Shakheer, one of the senior Tabi’een, and Ibn Qutaybah, one of the linguists, said: One relies on calculations when it is cloudy by estimating the mansions and considering their calculations in fasting Ramadan, so that if it is clear, it will be seen, based on the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): If it is cloudy, estimate it, meaning infer it from mansions, and estimate the completion of the month by calculating it. The majority said: The meaning of estimate it is to complete the amount, as explained by the hadith of Abu Hurayrah: Then complete the number. Al-Dawudi mentioned that it was said about the meaning of his saying estimate it: meaning estimate the mansions. We do not know of anyone who said this except some of the companions of Al-Shafi’i that the saying of astrologers is considered in this, and consensus is an argument against them. Ibn Nafi’ narrated on the authority of Malik that the imam does not fast upon sighting the crescent moon nor break his fast upon sighting it, but rather fasts and breaks his fast based on calculations: he is not to be imitated or followed. Ibn al-Arabi said: Some of our companions made a mistake and narrated on the authority of al-Shafi’i that he said: He relies on calculations, and it is a stumbling block, not a fault. Fourth: Malik and Al-Shafi’i differed as to whether the crescent of Ramadan is proven by the testimony of one or two witnesses. Malik said: The testimony of one witness is not accepted because it is testimony on a crescent, so less than two witnesses are not accepted in it. Its origin is testimony on the crescent of Shawwal and Dhul-Hijjah. Al-Shafi’i and Abu Hanifa said: One witness is accepted, based on what Abu Dawud narrated on the authority of Ibn Umar who said: The people saw the crescent, so I informed the Messenger of God (blessings and peace of God be upon him) that I saw it, so he fasted and ordered the people to fast. Al-Darqutni narrated it and said: Marwan bin Muhammad is the only one who narrated it on the authority of Ibn Wahb, and he is trustworthy. Al-Darqutni narrated: A man testified before Ali bin Abi Talib that he had seen the crescent of Ramadan, so he fasted. I think he said: And he ordered the people to fast, and he said: I would rather fast one day of Sha’ban than break my fast one day of Ramadan. Al-Shafi’i said: If the people did not see the crescent of Ramadan and a just man saw it, I saw that I should accept it for the sake of the hadith and precaution. Al-Shafi’i said: After that: It is not permissible for Ramadan to be witnessed except by two witnesses. Al-Shafi’i said: Some of our companions said: I do not accept it except with two witnesses, and this is the analogy for everything that is absent. Fifth: They differed regarding the one who saw the crescent of Ramadan alone or the crescent of Shawwal. Al-Rabi’ narrated from Al-Shafi’i: Whoever sees the crescent of Ramadan alone should fast, and whoever sees the crescent of Shawwal alone should break his fast, and he should be careful about that. Ibn Wahb narrated from Malik regarding the one who sees the crescent of Ramadan alone that he should fast, because he should not break his fast while he knows that that day is from the month of Ramadan. And whoever sees the crescent of Shawwal alone should not break his fast, because people are accused of breaking their fast if someone among them is not trustworthy, then they say when it appears to them: We have seen the crescent. Ibn Al-Mundhir said: Al-Layth bin Sa’d and Ahmad bin Hanbal said this. Ata’ and Ishaq said: He should neither fast nor break his fast. Ibn Al-Mundhir said: He should fast and break his fast. Sixth: They differed if he reported the sighting of a country, so it is either close or far. If it is close, then the ruling is the same, and if it is far, then the people of each country have their own sighting. This was narrated from Ikrimah, Al-Qasim, and Salim, and it was narrated from Ibn Abbas, and Ishaq said the same, and Al-Bukhari referred to it when he classified the sighting of the people of each country. Others said: If it is proven among the people that the people of a country have seen it, then they must make up for what they broke their fast. This is what Al-Layth bin Saad and Al-Shafi’i said. Ibn Al-Mundhir said: I do not know of any other statement than the statement of Al-Muzani and Al-Kufi. I said: Al-Kaya al-Tabari mentioned in his book Ahkam al-Qur’an: The companions of Abu Hanifa agreed that if the people of a country fast thirty days due to the sighting, and the people of another country fast twenty-nine days, then those who fasted twenty-nine days must make up for one day. The companions of al-Shafi’i do not see that, since the sightings in the countries may differ. The argument of the companions of Abu Hanifa is the Almighty’s saying: And that you may complete the number. It is proven by the sighting of the people of a country that the number is thirty, so it is obligatory for these people to complete it. And their opposition is supported by the saying of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace: Fast when you see it and break your fast when you see it, the hadith. This requires taking into account the custom of each people in their country. Abu Omar narrated the consensus that the sighting is not taken into account in countries further away, such as Andalusia from Khurasan. He said: Each country has its own sighting, except for what is like Greater Egypt and the countries of the Muslims whose regions are close together. Muslim narrated on the authority of Kurayb that Umm al-Fadl bint al-Harith sent him to Muawiyah in Syria. He said: So I went to Ash-Sham and completed my need, and Ramadan began for me while I was in Ash-Sham. I saw the crescent moon on Friday night. Then I went to Madinah at the end of the month and Abdullah ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, asked me, then he mentioned the crescent moon and said: When did you see the crescent moon? I said: We saw it on Friday night. He said: Did you see it? I said: Yes, and the people saw it and fasted, and Muawiyah fasted. He said: But we saw it on Saturday night, so we will not stop fasting until we complete thirty or we see it. I said: Is it sufficient for us to see Muawiyah and fast? He said: No, this is what the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) commanded us to do. Our scholars said that the statement of Ibn Abbas, this is what the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) commanded us to do, is a clear statement that this should be reported to the Prophet (peace be upon him) and by his command. It is evidence that if the countries are far apart, such as the distance between Syria and Hijaz, then it is obligatory for the people of each country to act upon its sighting without the sighting of any other country, even if this is proven by the Grand Imam, as long as the people are not forced to do so. If this is forced, then it is not permissible to disobey him. Al-Kaya al-Tabari said: His statement, this is what the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) commanded us to do, may be interpreted as the statement of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him): Fast upon its sighting and break your fast upon its sighting. Ibn al-Arabi said: There is disagreement regarding the interpretation of this statement of Ibn Abbas. It was said: It was rejected because it is a single report. It was also said: It was rejected because the countries differ in their risings, and this is correct, because Kurayb did not testify, but rather he reported a ruling that was proven by testimony, and there is no disagreement regarding the established ruling that a single report is sufficient. Its equivalent is if it is proven that the people of Aghmat saw the crescent on Friday night and the people of Seville saw it on Saturday night, then the people of each country will have their own sighting, because Suhayl is seen from Aghmat and not from Seville, and this indicates a difference in the risings. I said: As for the doctrine of Malik, may God have mercy on him, in this issue, Ibn Wahb and Ibn Al-Qasim narrated from him in Al-Majmu’ah that if the people of Basra see the crescent of Ramadan and then it reaches the people of Kufa, Medina and Yemen, then they must fast or make up for it if they missed it. Judge Abu Ishaq narrated from Ibn Al-Majshun that if it is proven in Basra by a common and widespread matter that does not require testimony or verification, then it is necessary for others from the people of the country to make up for it. But if it is only proven before their ruler by the testimony of two witnesses, then it is not necessary for anyone from the country except those who are subject to the ruling of that ruler from those under his jurisdiction, or it is proven before the Commander of the Faithful, then it is necessary for the Muslim community to make up for it. He said: This is the opinion of Malik. Seventh: The majority of people read Shahr in the nominative case as a predicate of an implied subject, meaning that is a month, or that which is obligatory upon you to fast is the month of Ramadan, or the fasting or the days. It was said: It was raised as a direct object whose agent was not named with Kutub meaning upon you is the month of Ramadan. Ramadan is not declined because the nun in it is redundant. It is permissible for it to be raised as a subject, and its predicate is in which the Qur’an was revealed. It was said: Its predicate is whoever witnessed, and which was revealed is an adjective for it. It was said: It was raised as a substitute for fasting. So whoever said: The fasting in His statement Fasting is prescribed upon you is three days and Ashura, said here as a subject. And whoever said: The fasting there is Ramadan, said here as a subject or as a substitute for fasting, meaning the month of Ramadan was prescribed upon you. Mujahid and Shahr ibn Hawshab read Shahr in the accusative case. Al-Kisa’i said: The meaning is that fasting is prescribed upon you, and that you fast the month of Ramadan. Al-Farra’ said: That is, fasting is prescribed upon you, meaning that you fast the month of Ramadan. Al-Nahhas said: It is not permissible to make the month of Ramadan the object of fast, because it enters into the relative clause and then separates between the relative clause and the relative pronoun. Likewise, if you make it the object of fasting, but it is permissible to make it the object of enticement, meaning, adhere to the month of Ramadan, and fast the month of Ramadan. This is also far-fetched because the month was not mentioned before, so it would be enticing. I said: His statement, Fasting has been prescribed for you, indicates the month, so it is permissible to use ijrā’, which is the choice of Abu Ubaid. Al-Akhfash said: It is in the accusative case as an adverb. It was reported from Al-Hasan and Abu Amr that the ra’ was assimilated into the ra’, and this is not permissible lest two quiescent letters come together. It is permissible to change the vowel of the ra’ to the ha’, so that the ha’ is made a damma and then assimilated, which is the opinion of the Kufians.
2:186: It has four issues: The first: The Almighty’s saying: And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near. It was said: When they ask you about the One to be worshipped, then tell them that He is near, rewards obedience, answers the caller, and knows what the servant does of fasting, prayer, and other things. There is a difference of opinion about the reason for its revelation. Muqatil said: Umar, may God be pleased with him, had intercourse with his wife after the Isha prayer, then regretted it and cried, and came to the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, and informed him of that, then returned sad. This was before the permission was revealed, so this verse was revealed: And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near. It was said: When it was obligatory upon them at the beginning to refrain from eating after sleeping, some of them ate and then regretted it, so this verse was revealed to accept repentance and abrogate that ruling, as will be explained. Al-Kalbi narrated on the authority of Abu Salih on the authority of Ibn Abbas, who said: The Jews said: How can our Lord hear our supplication, while you claim that there are five hundred years between us and the heavens, and the thickness of each heaven is the same? So this verse was revealed. Al-Hasan said: The reason for this is that some people said to the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace: Is our Lord near so that we may speak to Him, or is He far so that we may call upon Him? So it was revealed. Ata’ and Qatada said: When this verse was revealed: And your Lord says, ‘Call upon Me; I will respond to you,’ some people said: At what hour should we call upon Him? So it was revealed. Second: The Almighty’s saying: I am near, meaning with the answer. It was also said with knowledge. It was also said: I am near to My friends with favor and blessings. Third: The Almighty’s saying: I answer the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me. That is, I accept the worship of whoever worships Me. Supplication means worship, and answering means acceptance. Its evidence is what Abu Dawud narrated on the authority of An-Nu’man ibn Bashir on the authority of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, who said: “Supplication is worship. Your Lord said, ‘Call upon Me; I will respond to you.’” So supplication was called worship, and from this is the saying of God Almighty: Indeed, those who disdain My worship will enter Hell [rendered] contemptible. That is, My supplication. So God Almighty commanded supplication and urged it and called it worship, and promised that He would respond to them. Laith narrated on the authority of Shahr ibn Hawshab on the authority of Ubadah ibn al-Samit who said: I heard the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, say: “My nation has been given three things that were given only to the prophets. When God sent a prophet, He said, ‘Call upon Me and I will respond to you.’ And He said to this nation, ‘Call upon Me and I will respond to you.’ And when God sent a prophet, He said to him, ‘He has not placed any difficulty upon you in religion.’ And He said to this nation, ‘He has not placed any difficulty upon you in religion.’ And when God sent a prophet, He made him a witness over his people and made this nation witnesses over the people.” Khalid Al-Ra’i used to say: I am amazed at this nation, in ‘Call upon Me and I will respond to you.’ He ordered them to supplicate and promised them that He would respond, and there is no condition between them. Someone asked him, Like what? He said, Like His statement, ‘And give good tidings to those who believe and do righteous deeds.’ Here, there is a condition. His statement, And give good tidings to those who believe that they will have a firm footing. There is no condition of action in it. And like His statement, So call upon God, sincere to Him in religion. Here, there is a condition. And His statement, Call upon Me and I will respond to you. There is no condition in it. And the nations would resort to their prophets in their needs, until they would ask the prophets for that. If it is said: What is the reason for a supplicant who calls and is not answered? The answer is to know that His statement, the Truth, in the two verses, I respond, I answer does not necessitate an answer absolutely for every supplicant in detail, nor for every request in detail. Our Lord, the Blessed and Exalted, said in another verse: “Call upon your Lord in humility and secretly. Indeed, He does not like transgressors.” And everyone who persists in committing a major sin, knowingly or ignorantly, is an aggressor. And He has informed us that He does not like transgressors, so how can He answer him? And the types of transgression are many, and they will be explained here and in Al-A’raf, God willing. Some scholars said: I respond if you wish, as He said: He will remove that for which you call, if He wills. So this is from the category of the absolute and the restricted. The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, supplicated in three cases, and he was given two and denied one, as will be explained in Al-An’am, God willing. It was said: The purpose of this report is to inform all believers that this is a description of their Lord, glory be to Him, that He answers the supplications of those who supplicate in general, and that He is close to the servant, hears his supplication and knows his distress, so He answers him with whatever He wishes and however He wishes. And who is more astray than he who calls upon others besides God who does not respond to him? The verse. A master may answer his servant or a father his son, but then not give him what he asked for. So the answer was inevitably obtained when the supplication occurred, because I answered and I respond is report that cannot be abrogated, so the informant becomes a liar. Evidence for this interpretation is what Ibn Umar narrated on the authority of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, who said: Whoever has his supplications opened for him, the doors of response will be opened for him. And God Almighty revealed to David: Tell the oppressors among My servants not to call upon Me, for I have made it obligatory upon Myself to answer those who call upon Me, and if I answer the oppressors, I will curse them. Some people said: God answers every supplication, and either the answer appears in this world, or He expiates it, or He stores it up for him in the Hereafter, based on what Abu Sa`id Al-Khudri narrated, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: There is no Muslim who supplicates with a supplication in which there is no sin or severing of family ties, but God will give him one of three things: either He will hasten his supplication, or He will store it up for him, or He will avert from him an evil equivalent to it. They said: Then we should increase it? He said: God is more abundant. Narrated by Abu `Umar ibn `Abd Al-Barr, and Abu Muhammad `Abd Al-Haqq authenticated it. It is in Al-Muwatta’ with an interrupted chain of transmission. Abu `Umar said: This hadith is included in the explanation of the chain of transmission of God’s statement: Call upon Me, I will respond to you. All of this is from the answer. Ibn Abbas said: Every servant who prays will have his supplication answered. If what he prays for is provision for him in this world, it will be given to him. If it is not provision for him in this world, it will be stored up for him. I said: The hadith of Abu Saeed Al-Khudri, even if it was permission to answer in one of three cases, it indicated to you the validity of what preceded from avoiding the exception that prevents answering, where he said in it: As long as he does not ask for sin or the severing of family ties. Muslim added: As long as he is not impatient. It was narrated on the authority of Abu Hurairah on the authority of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, that he said: The servant’s supplication will continue to be answered as long as he does not supplicate for a sin or for severing family ties, as long as he is not impatient. It was said: O Messenger of God, what is impatience? He said: He says, ‘I supplicated but did not see that I was answered.’ Then he becomes frustrated and stops supplicating. Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and Abu Dawud narrated on the authority of Abu Hurairah that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: One of you will be answered as long as he does not hasten and say, ‘I called and I was not answered.’ Our scholars, may God have mercy on them, said: His statement, One of you will be answered, may be interpreted as informing about the necessity of the response occurring, or informing about the possibility of its occurring. If it means informing about the necessity and occurrence, then the response would mean the three aforementioned things. If he says, I called and I was not answered, then the occurrence of one of these three things is invalidated and the supplication is devoid of all of them. If it means the possibility of the response, then the response in that case is by doing what he called for specifically, and what prevents the supplicant from saying, I called and I was not answered, is because that is a form of despair, weak certainty, and discontent. I said: Eating forbidden food and anything similar to it also prevents the supplication from being answered. The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: “A man who travels far, disheveled and covered in dust, stretches his hands to the sky, ‘O Lord, O Lord,’ while his food is unlawful, his drink is unlawful, his clothing is unlawful, and he is nourished with unlawful things. How can that be answered?” This is a question that excludes the acceptance of a supplication from someone of this description, because the answer to a supplication requires conditions in the supplicant, the supplication, and the thing for which he is supplicating. Among the conditions of the supplicant is that he should know that no one is able to meet his need except God, and that the intermediaries are in His grasp and subject to His subjugation. He should supplicate with sincere intention and presence of heart, because God does not answer the supplication of a heedless, distracted heart. He should also avoid eating unlawful food and not get tired of supplicating. Among the conditions of the thing for which he is supplicating is that it is permissible to ask for and do something according to Islamic law, as God said: As long as he does not supplicate for a sin or severing family ties. So sin includes everything that one commits a sin for, and all the rights and injustices of Muslims are included in the category of kinship ties. Sahl ibn Abdullah al-Tustari said: The conditions of supplication are seven: The first is humility, fear, hope, persistence, humility, generality, and eating lawful food. Ibn Ata’ said: Supplication has pillars, wings, causes, and times, but its causes are the most successful. Its pillars are presence of heart, compassion, submission, and humility. Its wings are truthfulness, its times are the pre-dawn hours, and its causes are prayers upon Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace. It was said: Its conditions are four: The first is to protect the heart when alone, to protect the tongue with people, to protect the eyes from looking at what is not lawful, and to protect the stomach from what is unlawful. It was said: One of the conditions of supplication is that it be free from mistakes, as one of them recited: He calls upon his Lord in a low tone, but when he calls upon Him, He does not answer. It was said to Ibrahim bin Adham: Why do we supplicate but are not answered? He said: Because you knew God but did not obey Him, and you knew the Messenger but did not follow his Sunnah, and you knew the Quran but did not act upon it, and you ate God’s blessings but did not give thanks for them, and you knew Paradise but did not seek it, and you knew Hell but did not flee from it, and you knew Satan but did not fight him and agreed with him, and you knew death but did not prepare for it, and you buried the dead but did not learn from it, and you left your faults and occupied yourself with the faults of others. Ali may God be pleased with him said to Nawf Al-Bakali: O Nawf, God revealed to David to command the Children of Israel not to enter any of My houses except with pure hearts, humble eyes, and clean hands, for I will not answer any of you as long as any of My creation has injustice. O Nouf, do not be a poet, a chief, a policeman, a tax collector, or a tax-collector, for David stood up at one hour of the night and said: This is an hour in which no servant supplicates except that his supplication will be answered, unless he is a chief, a policeman, a tax collector, or the owner of an ‘urtaba a tambourine or a kubba a drum. Our scholars said: The supplicant should not say: O God, give me if You will, O God, forgive me if You will, O God, have mercy on me if You will. Rather, he should strip his supplication and prayer of the wording of the will, and ask as one who knows that He will not do anything except that He wills. Also, in his saying: If You will, there is a kind of independence from His forgiveness, giving, and mercy, like the saying of the one who says: If You will give me such and such, then do it. This is only used with one who is independent of it. As for the one who is compelled to do so, he is determined in his question and asks as a poor person compelled to ask for what he asked for. The imams narrated, and the wording is from Bukhari, on the authority of Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: When one of you supplicates, let him be determined in his supplication and not say, ‘O God, if You will, then give me,’ for there is no one who can force Him. In Al-Muwatta’ it says, O God, forgive me if You will, O God, have mercy on me if You will. Our scholars said: His saying, Let him be determined in his supplication is evidence that the believer should strive in supplication and have hope of an answer, and not despair of God’s mercy, for he is supplicating to the Generous One. Sufyan ibn ‘Uyaynah said: No one should be prevented from supplicating because of what he knows about himself, for God answered the supplication of the worst of creation, Iblis, He said, ‘My Lord, then respite me until the Day they are resurrected.’ He said, ‘Indeed, you are among those granted respite.’ Supplication has times and conditions in which it is most likely to be answered, such as the pre-dawn hours, the time of breaking the fast, between the call to prayer and the iqama, between noon and afternoon prayers on Wednesday, times of distress, when traveling or sick, when it is raining and when standing in the ranks for the sake of God. All of this has been reported in the reports, and their explanation will come in their proper places. Shahr bin Hawshab narrated that Umm Al-Darda’ said to him: O Shahr, don’t you feel goosebumps? I said: Yes. She said: Then pray to God, for prayers are answered at that time. Jabir bin Abdullah said: “The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, supplicated in the Masjid al-Fath three times, on Monday and Tuesday, and his supplication was answered on Wednesday between the two prayers. I saw the joy on his face.” Jabir said: Whenever an important or difficult matter befell me, I would choose that hour to supplicate at it and know that it would be answered. Fourth: The Almighty’s saying: So let them respond to me. Abu Raja’ al-Khurasani said: So let them supplicate to me. Ibn Atiyyah said: The meaning is: So let them ask that I respond to them. This is the chapter of istaf’ala, meaning to ask for something except for what is exceptional, such as istaghna God God is independent. Mujahid and others said: The meaning is: So let them respond to me in what I have called them to of faith, meaning obedience and action. It is said: ajaba and istajaba have the same meaning, and from this is the saying of the poet: No one responded to him at that time. That is, he did not answer him. The seen is redundant and the lam is the lam of command. And so is and to believe. The lam of command is made jussive because it makes the verb future and nothing else, so it is similar to in which is for condition. And it was said: because it only occurs with the verb. And guidance is the opposite of misguidance. And he has guided, guides, guides, guidance with kasra guides, guidance, a dialect for it. And God guided him. And the paths are the ends of the roads. And the most righteous path is like the most axis. And you say: it is for guidance, unlike saying: for fornication. And Umm Rashid is a nickname for the mouse. And Banu Rashdan are a clan of Arabs, according to al-Jawhari. And al-Harawi said: guidance, guidance, and rightness, and from it is his saying: so that they may be guided.
2:187: God Almighty says: “Lawful to you on the night of the fast is the approach to your wives. They are your clothing and you are their clothing. God knows that you were deceiving yourselves, so He turned to you in forgiveness and pardoned you. So now have intercourse with them and seek what God has ordained for you. And eat and drink until the white thread of dawn becomes distinct to you from the black thread [of night]. Then complete the fast until the nightfall. And do not have intercourse with them while you are staying in the mosques. These are the limits set by God, so do not approach them. Thus does God make clear His verses to the people that they may fear God.” It contains thirty-six issues: First: The Almighty’s statement: Lawful to you The word lawful indicates that it was forbidden before that and then abrogated. Abu Dawud narrated on the authority of Ibn Abi Laila who said: Our companions told us: If a man broke his fast and slept before eating, he would not eat until morning. He said: Then Umar came and wanted his wife, but she said: I have fallen asleep. He thought that she was making an excuse, so he went to her. Then a man from the Ansar came and wanted food, but they said: Until we heat something for you. So he slept. When morning came, this verse was revealed, and in it: Lawful to you on the night of the fast is the intimacy with your wives. Al-Bukhari narrated on the authority of Al-Baraa who said: The companions of the Prophet (peace and blessings of God be upon him), if a man was fasting and the time for breaking the fast came and he slept before breaking the fast, he would not eat that night or that day until he walked. Qays ibn Sarmah al-Ansari was fasting - and in another narration: he used to work in the palm trees during the day and he was fasting - and when the time for breaking the fast came, he came to his wife and said to her: Do you have any food? She said: No, but I will go and get some for you. He worked all day, but his eyes overcame him. His wife came to him and when she saw him, she said: What a disappointment! At noon, he fainted. This was mentioned to the Prophet (peace and blessings of God be upon him), and this verse was revealed: Lawful to you on the night of the fast is the approach to your wives. They were extremely happy, and this verse was revealed: And eat and drink until the white thread of dawn becomes distinct to you from the black thread. And in Bukhari also on the authority of al-Baraa’, he said: When the fast of Ramadan was revealed, they would not approach women the entire month of Ramadan, and there were men who betrayed themselves, so God revealed: God knows that you were betraying yourselves, so He turned to you in forgiveness and pardoned you. It is said: Khan and ikhtan have the same meaning as betrayal, meaning you betray yourselves by having intercourse during the nights of fasting. Whoever disobeys God has betrayed himself, as he has brought punishment upon himself. Al-Qutbi said: The root of betrayal is when a man is entrusted with something and does not fulfill the trust. Al-Tabari said: “That Omar, may God be pleased with him, returned from the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, and he had spent the night with him, and he found that his wife had fallen asleep, so he wanted to see her, but she said to him: I slept, so he said to her: I did not sleep, so he had intercourse with her. Ka’b bin Malik did the same, so Omar went to the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, the next day and said: I apologize to God and to you, for my soul made it seem good to me, so I had intercourse with my wife, so do you find any concession for me? He said to me: You were not worthy of that, O Omar. So when he reached his house, he sent for him and informed him of his excuse in a verse of the Qur’an.” An-Nahhas and Makki mentioned that Omar slept and then had intercourse with his wife, and that he came to the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, and told him, so the verse was revealed: God knows that you were deceiving yourselves, so He has turned to you in forgiveness and pardoned you, so now have intercourse with them 1:13. Second: The Almighty’s saying: The night of fasting is sexual intercourse. Night is an accusative of circumstance, and it is a generic noun, so it was singled out. And sexual intercourse is a euphemism for sexual intercourse, because God Almighty is generous and euphemistic, as Ibn Abbas and Al-Suddi said. Al-Zajjaj said: Sexual intercourse is a comprehensive word for everything a man wants from his wife, and Al-Azhari also said this. Ibn Arafa said: Sexual intercourse here is sexual intercourse. And sexual intercourse is explicitly mentioning sexual intercourse and expressing it. The poet said: They see Anas talking to adulterers and they are averse to the obscenities of men. It was said: The origin of rifth is saying obscenities. It is said: rafath and arfath if he speaks something ugly. From this comes the saying of the poet: And the flocks of pilgrims refrain from idle talk and obscene speech. And the verb rafth is transitive with ila in the words of God the Almighty: the intimacy with your women. You do not say rafthat ila an-nisa, but it was brought with the meaning of ifdaa which means attachment in the example of His words: and some of you have gone in unto others. And from this meaning is: and when they are alone with their devils, as mentioned above. And His words: the day it will be heated means it will be lit, because you say: the iron was heated in the fire, and it will come. And from this is His words: so let those beware who oppose his command was carried with the meaning of deviating from his command or turning away from his command, because you say: I opposed Zayd. And similar to it is His words the Almighty: and was to the believers Most Merciful was carried with the meaning of kind in the example of to the believers Kind and Merciful. Don’t you see that you say: I was kindled with him, and you do not say I had mercy on him, but because it agreed with it in meaning, it was lowered to its position in transitivity. And from this type is the saying of Abu Kabir al-Hudhali: She became pregnant with him on a dark night out of hatred, and her marriage was tied without being permissible. Adi carried him with the preposition baa, and it should have reached the object by itself, as it came in the revelation: His mother carried him with hardship and gave birth to him with hardship. But he said: She carried him, because it is in the meaning of she became pregnant with him. The second: The Almighty’s saying: They are clothing for you is a subject and predicate. The nun in hunna is stressed because it is like the mim and waw in the masculine. And you are clothing for them The origin of clothing is clothes, then the mixing of each of the spouses with the other was called clothing, because the bodies are joined together and mixed and intertwined, likening them to a garment. Al-Nabigha Al-Ja’di said: If the deceased dies, her neck is bent, and she collapses and becomes his clothing. He also said: I wore people and destroyed them, and after people I destroyed people Some of them said: What covers and conceals something is called clothing. So it is permissible for each of them to be a cover for the other from what is not permissible, as mentioned in the hadith. And it was said: Because each of them is a cover for the other from the sight of people in what happens between them of intercourse. Abu Ubaid and others said: It is said of the woman that she is your clothing, your bed, and your garment. A man said to Umar ibn al-Khattab: Shall I not deliver a messenger to Abu Hafs, may my trustworthy brother redeem you for my sake? Abu Ubaid said: That is, my women. It was also said: My soul. Al-Rabi’ said: They are your bed, and you are their blanket. Mujahid: That is, a dwelling place for you, that is, you dwell with one another. Fourth: The Almighty’s statement: God knows that you were betraying yourselves means that some of you would ask each other to commit forbidden acts such as sexual intercourse and eating after sleeping during the nights of fasting, as in the statement of God the Almighty: You kill yourselves meaning that some of you kill each other. It is possible that He means by this each one of them in his own self that he betrays it, and He called him a traitor to himself from a hadith whose harm would return to him, as mentioned above. His statement: Then He turned to you has two possible meanings: One of them: Accepting their repentance from their betrayal of themselves. The other is easing their burden by granting them permission and allowing them, as in the statement of God the Almighty: He knew that you would not be able to count it, so He turned to you meaning He made it easier for you. His statement after unintentional killing: But whoever cannot find [that], then a fast of two consecutive months as repentance from God means an alleviation, because the unintentional killer did not do anything that requires him to repent. God the Almighty said: God has already forgiven the Prophet and the Muhajireen and the Ansar who followed him during the time of hardship even though there was nothing from the Prophet (peace and blessings of God be upon him) that would require repentance. His statement: And pardoned you may mean pardoning the sin, or it may mean expansion and facilitation, like the Prophet (peace and blessings of God be upon him) saying: The beginning of the time is the pleasure of God and its end is the pardon of God meaning facilitating and expanding it. So the meaning of God knew is that He knew that this would happen from you, So He pardoned you after it had happened, meaning He lightened your burden. And pardoned means made it easy. You betray comes from betrayal, as mentioned above. Ibn al-Arabi said: Our ascetic scholars said: And so let the care and honor of status be. Umar may God be pleased with him betrayed himself, so God the Almighty made it a law, and made the burden easier for the nation because of him, so God was pleased with him and satisfied with him. The Almighty’s saying: Now have sexual intercourse with them is a metaphor for sexual intercourse, meaning that what was forbidden to you has been made lawful for you. And intercourse is called direct intercourse because of the contact of the two skins during it. Ibn al-Arabi said: This indicates that the reason for the verse was the intercourse of Umar, may God be pleased with him, and not Qais’s hunger, because if the reason had been Qais’ hunger, he would have said: Now eat, he began with it because it is the important thing for which the verse was revealed. Fifth: The Almighty’s saying: And seek what God has decreed for you. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Al-Hakam bin Uyaynah, Ikrimah, Al-Hasan, Al-Suddi, Al-Rabi’ and Al-Dahhak said: Its meaning is and seek children, which is indicated by the fact that it follows His saying: So now have sexual relations with them. Ibn Abbas said: What God has decreed for us is the Qur’an. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, seek the Qur’an with what is permitted to you in it and what you have been commanded to do. It was narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas and Muadh bin Jabal that the meaning is and seek the Night of Decree. It was said: The meaning is seek permission and expansion, as Qatada said. Ibn Atiyyah said: It is a good statement. It was said: And seek what God has decreed for you of female slaves and wives. Al-Hasan Al-Basri and Al-Hasan bin Qurra read and they followed from following, and Ibn Abbas permitted it, and preferred Ibtaghaw from seeking. Sixth: The Almighty’s saying: And eat and drink. This is the answer to Qais’s case, and the first is Omar’s answer. He began with Omar’s case because he is the important one and he is the one who takes precedence. Seventh: The Almighty’s saying: Until the white thread of dawn becomes distinct to you from the black thread. Until is the limit of distinction, and it is not correct for distinction to occur to someone and for him to be forbidden from eating until a certain amount of time has passed since the rising of dawn. There is a difference of opinion regarding the limit upon which abstaining from eating is obligatory. The majority said: It is the dawn crossing the horizon to the right and left. This is how the reports came and the countries followed. Muslim narrated on the authority of Samurah ibn Jundub, may God be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: Do not be deceived by Bilal’s call to prayer, nor by the whiteness of the horizon, which is rectangular like this until it flies like this. Hammad narrated it with his own hands, saying: He means interrupting. And in the hadith of Ibn Masoud: “The dawn is not the one who says like this - and he gathered his fingers and then lowered them to the ground - but the one who says like this - and he placed the rosary on the rosary and stretched out his hands.” Al-Daraqutni narrated on the authority of Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Thauban that he was informed that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: “They are two dawns. As for the one that looks like the tail of a scorpion, it does not make anything permissible or forbidden. As for the one that is oblong and faces the horizon, prayer is permissible in it and food is forbidden.” This is a mursal. A group said: That is after the dawn has risen and is visible in the roads and houses. This was narrated on the authority of Umar, Hudhayfah, Ibn Abbas, Talq ibn Ali, Ata ibn Abi Rabah, Al-A’mash Sulayman and others that abstaining from eating is obligatory when the dawn is visible in the roads and on the tops of mountains. Masruq said: They did not consider the dawn to be your dawn, rather they considered the dawn that fills the houses. An-Nasa’i narrated on the authority of Asim on the authority of Zur who said: We said to Hudhayfah: At what time did you eat suhoor with the Messenger of God (blessings and peace of God be upon him)? He said: It was during the day, except that the sun had not risen. Ad-Darqutni narrated on the authority of Talq ibn Ali that the Prophet of God (blessings and peace of God be upon him) said: “Eat and drink, and do not be deceived by the rising sun. Eat and drink until you see red.” Ad-Daraqutni said: Qays ibn Talq is not strong. Abu Dawud said: This is something that was unique to the people of Yamamah. At-Tabari said: What led them to this is that fasting is during the day, and the day for them is from sunrise to sunset. The difference of opinion on this has already passed among the linguists. The explanation of the Messenger of God (blessings and peace of God be upon him) is his saying: It is only the blackness of the night and the whiteness of the day, which is the decisive factor in that, and his saying: for a numbered number of days. Ad-Daraqutni narrated on the authority of Aisha may God be pleased with her on the authority of the Prophet (blessings and peace of God be upon him) who said: Whoever does not intend to fast before dawn, his fast is not valid. This was narrated by Abdullah ibn Abbad alone on the authority of al-Mufaddal ibn Fadalah with this chain of transmission, and all of them are trustworthy. It was narrated on the authority of Hafsah that the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: Whoever does not intend to fast before dawn, his fast is not valid. It was narrated by Abdullah bin Abi Bakr, who is one of the trustworthy and distinguished narrators, and it was narrated on the authority of Hafsa, with her saying suspended. In these two hadiths is evidence of what the majority said about dawn, and the prohibition of fasting without the intention before dawn, contrary to the saying of Abu Hanifa, which is: Eighth: Fasting is one of the acts of worship and is not valid without intention. The Lawgiver has set its time before dawn, so how can it be said that eating and drinking after dawn is permissible? Al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated on the authority of Sahl ibn Sa`d who said: The verse And eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread was revealed before dawn. When men wanted to fast, one of them would tie a white thread and a black thread to his feet, and he would continue eating and drinking until he could clearly see them. Then God revealed after dawn, so they knew that He meant the whiteness of the day. And “On the authority of Adi bin Hatim, he said: I said: O Messenger of God, what is the white thread and the black thread? Are they the two threads? He said: Your back is wide if you see the two threads - then he said: No, it is the blackness of the night and the whiteness of the day.” Narrated by Al-Bukhari. And dawn is called a thread because what appears of the whiteness is seen as an extended thread. The poet said: The white thread is the light of dawn, and the black thread is the darkness of the night, hidden. In their speech, the thread refers to the color. Fajr is the source of the word fajrat al-ma’ afjaruhu fajr, meaning it flowed and erupted. Its origin is the crack, so that is what is said about the one who rises from the first signs of the sun’s light from its rising: fajr, because of the emanation of its light. It is the first whiteness of the day, apparent and scattered in the spreading horizon. The Arabs call it the white thread, as we have explained. Abu Dawud al-Ayadi said: When a curtain lit up for us and a thread of light appeared from the morning Another said: It almost appeared and she began to touch him, and the dark night covered him. It may also be called the crack, and from it they say: The dawn has cracked. Bishr bin Abi Khazim or Amr bin Ma’dikarib said: You see Al-Sarhan spreading his hands as if the whiteness of his skin is cracked Al-Shamakh likened it to the parting of the head, saying: If the night is the morning, it is more difficult than the parting of the hair with oil. They say about something that is clear: This is like the break of dawn, the beginning of the day, and the first signs of dawn. The poet said: It came before dawn, and the son of intelligence is hidden in Kafr Ninth: The Almighty’s saying: Then complete the fast until the night. God, the Exalted, made the night a time for eating, drinking, and sexual intercourse, and the day a time for fasting. He made the rulings of the two times clear and distinguished between them. Nothing that He permitted at night is permissible during the day except for a traveler or a sick person, as was explained above. So whoever breaks the fast in Ramadan other than those mentioned, he is either intentional or forgetful. If it is the former, then Malik said: Whoever breaks the fast in Ramadan intentionally by eating, drinking, or sexual intercourse must make up for it and offer expiation, based on what Malik narrated in his Muwatta’ and Muslim in his Sahih on the authority of Abu Hurayrah: “A man broke his fast in Ramadan, so the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, ordered him to make expiation by freeing a slave, or fasting two consecutive months, or feeding two consecutive months, or feeding sixty poor people,” the hadith. This is what Al-Sha’bi said. Al-Shafi’i and others said: This expiation is only for the one who broke his fast by having sexual intercourse, based on the hadith of Abu Hurayrah who also said: “A man came to the Messenger of God (peace and blessings of God be upon him) and said: ‘I am ruined, O Messenger of God!’ He said: ‘What ruined you?’ He said: ‘I had intercourse with my wife during Ramadan.’” The hadith mentions the expiation in order, narrated by Muslim. They interpreted this issue as the first issue and said: It is one. This is not accepted, rather they are two different issues, because their context is different. The expiation was made conditional on the one who broke the fast without restrictions, so it is binding absolutely. This is what Malik and his companions, Al-Awza’i, Ishaq, Abu Thawr, Al-Tabari, and Ibn Al-Mundhir said. It was narrated from ‘Ata’ in one narration, and from Al-Hasan and Al-Zuhri. Al-Shafi’i is obligated to say this, because he says: Failing to inquire about the matter when circumstances are conflicting indicates the generality of the ruling. Al-Shafi’i made it obligatory for him, along with the judgement, to punish him for violating the sanctity of the month. Tenth: They also differed regarding what is obligatory for a woman whose husband has intercourse with her during the month of Ramadan. Malik, Abu Yusuf, and the people of opinion said: She has the same obligation as the husband. Al-Shafi’i said: She only has to pay one expiation, whether she consented to him or he forced her, because the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, answered the questioner with one expiation and did not specify. It was narrated from Abu Hanifa: If she consented to him, then each of them has to pay an expiation, and if he forced her, then he has to pay one expiation and nothing more. This is the opinion of Sahnun ibn Sa’id al-Maliki. Malik said: He has to pay two expiations, and this is the conclusion of his school of thought according to a group of his companions. Eleventh: They also differed about someone who had intercourse while forgetting that he was fasting or had eaten. Al-Shafi’i, Abu Hanifa and his companions, and Ishaq said: There is nothing upon him in both cases, neither making up for it nor expiation. Malik, Al-Layth, and Al-Awza’i said: He has to make up for it but not expiate. The same was narrated from Ata’. It was narrated from Ata’ that he has to make expiation even if he had intercourse. He said: A person like this does not forget. Some of the people of the apparent meaning said: Whether he had intercourse forgetfully or intentionally, he has to make up for it and expiate. This is the opinion of Ibn Al-Majishun Abd Al-Malik, and Ahmad Ibn Hanbal agreed with him, because the hadith requiring expiation did not differentiate between the one who forgot and the one who did it intentionally. Ibn Al-Mundhir said: There is nothing upon him. Twelfth: Malik, Al-Shafi’i, Abu Thawr and the people of opinion said: If someone eats forgetfully and thinks that he has broken his fast and then has sexual intercourse intentionally, he must make up for it and there is no penalty on him. Ibn Al-Mundhir said: We say the same. It was said in the school of thought: He must make up for it and pay expiation if he intended to violate the sanctity of his fast out of boldness and negligence. Abu Omar said: According to Malik’s principle, he should not pay expiation, because whoever eats forgetfully is, in his view, someone who has broken his fast and must make up for that day. So what sanctity has he violated while he is breaking his fast? According to other than Malik: Not everyone who eats forgetfully is breaking his fast. I said: This is correct, and the majority said the same: If someone eats or drinks forgetfully, he does not have to make up for it, and his fast is complete, according to the hadith of Abu Hurairah, who said that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: “If a fasting person eats or drinks forgetfully, then it is a provision that God has brought to him and he does not have to make it up - in one narration - so let him complete his fast, for God has fed him and given him drink.” Narrated by Al-Daraqutni. He said: Its chain of transmission is sound and all of them are trustworthy. Abu Bakr Al-Athram said: I heard Abu Abdullah being asked about someone who eats forgetfully in Ramadan. He said: There is nothing upon him according to the hadith of Abu Hurairah. Then Abu Abdullah Malik said: They claimed that Malik says he has to make it up! And he laughed. Ibn Al-Mundhir said: There is nothing upon him, “because the Prophet (peace and blessings of God be upon him) said to someone who eats or drinks forgetfully: His fast is completed. If he says, “His fast is completed,” then he completes it, and it is a complete and perfect fast. I said: If someone breaks his fast forgetfully, he does not have to make it up and his fast is a complete fast, then if he has sexual intercourse intentionally, he must make it up and offer expiation - and God knows best - like someone who did not break his fast forgetfully. Our scholars have argued for the obligation of making it up by saying: What is required of him is to fast a complete day in which there is no breach, based on the statement of God the Almighty: Then complete the fast until the night. This is not done in its entirety, so it remains upon him. Perhaps the hadith is about voluntary fasting because of its lightness. It was stated in the two Sahihs of Bukhari and Muslim: Whoever forgets while he is fasting and eats or drinks, let him complete his fast. He did not mention making up for it nor did he address it. Rather, what he addressed was the removal of blame and the command to continue with his fast and complete it. If this was obligatory, then it indicates what we mentioned about making up for it. As for voluntary fasting, there is no making up for it for someone who ate by mistake, because the Prophet (peace and blessings of God be upon him) said: He does not have to make it up. I said: This is what our scholars have used as evidence, and it is correct. If it were not for what is authentic from the Lawgiver, we would not have mentioned it. It came with the clear, correct text, which is what Abu Hurairah narrated on the authority of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, who said: Whoever breaks the fast in the month of Ramadan out of forgetfulness does not have to make up for it or offer expiation. Narrated by Al-Daraqutni, who said: It was narrated by Ibn Marzuq, who is trustworthy, on the authority of Al-Ansari alone. Thus, the possibility is removed and the problem is resolved. Praise be to God, the Majestic and the Perfect. Thirteenth: Since God, the Almighty, mentioned the prohibitions of fasting, which are eating, drinking, and sexual intercourse, and did not mention direct contact, which is skin-to-skin contact, such as kissing, holding hands, and others, this indicates the validity of the fast of the one who kisses and touches, because the meaning of the speech only indicates the prohibition of what the night permitted, which are the three things, and there is no indication in it for anything else, rather it is suspended on evidence, and for this reason differences became widespread in it, and the scholars of the Salaf differed in it, including direct contact. Our scholars said: It is disliked for the one who does not feel safe about himself and does not control himself, lest he be a cause of something that spoils the fast. Malik narrated from Nafi’ that Abdullah ibn Umar, may God be pleased with them both, used to forbid kissing and direct contact for the fasting person, and this - and God knows best - is for fear of what would happen from them, so if he kisses and greets, there is no blame on him, and likewise if he touches. Al-Bukhari narrated from Aisha, who said: “The Prophet (peace be upon him) used to kiss and have intercourse while he was fasting.” Among those who disliked kissing for a fasting person were Abdullah ibn Masoud and Urwah ibn al-Zubayr. It was narrated from Ibn Masoud that he would make up a day in its place, and the hadith is evidence against them. Abu Omar said: I do not know of anyone who permitted it for someone who knows that it will cause him to have an erection that would spoil his fast. If he kisses and ejaculates, he must make up for it and there is no expiation. This was stated by Abu Hanifa and his companions, al-Thawri, al-Hasan, and al-Shafi’i. Ibn al-Mundhir chose this view and said: It is not an evidence that he must make up for it. Abu Omar said: If he kisses and ejaculates, there is nothing against him according to them. Ahmad said: If someone kisses and ejaculates or has intercourse, he must make up for it and there is no expiation against him, except for someone who has intercourse and penetrates intentionally or forgetfully. Ibn al-Qasim narrated from Malik that if someone kisses or has intercourse and becomes erect but no fluid comes out of him at all, he must make up for it. Ibn Wahb narrated from him that he does not have to make up for it until he ejaculates. Judge Abu Muhammad said: Our companions agreed that he does not have to make up for it. If it was semen, is he required to make up the fast and make up for it? It could be that he kissed once and ejaculated, or he kissed and enjoyed himself and then ejaculated again. If he kissed once or had intercourse or touched once, Ashhab and Sahnoon said: He does not have to make up for it until he repeats it. Ibn al-Qasim said: He should make up for it, except for looking, in which case he does not have to make up for it until he repeats it. Among those who said that he must make up for it if he kisses, has intercourse, plays with his wife, or has intercourse without intercourse and ejaculates are: al-Hasan al-Basri, Ata’, Ibn al-Mubarak, Abu Thawr, and Ishaq. It is the opinion of Malik in al-Mudawwana. The evidence for Ashhab’s opinion is that touching, kissing, and intercourse do not break the fast in and of themselves, but rather they can be interpreted as something that breaks the fast. If he does it once, he did not intend to ejaculate or spoil the fast, so he does not have to make up for it, just like looking at her. If he repeats it, he intended to spoil his fast, so he must make up for it, as if he looked repeatedly. Al-Lakhmi said: They all agreed that there is no expiation for ejaculation from looking, unless he repeats it. The basic principle is that expiation is only required of one who intended to break the fast and violate the sanctity of fasting. If that is the case, then the habit of the person who did that must be considered. If it is his habit to ejaculate from kissing or direct contact once, or his habit is different: sometimes he ejaculates and sometimes he does not ejaculate, then expiation is required of him, because the one who did that intended to violate his fast or is exposed to it. If his habit is to be safe, then it is possible that what he did was contrary to his habit, then expiation is not required of him. Malik’s statement regarding the obligation of expiation may be possible, and it is possible that what he did was contrary to his habit, then expiation is not required of him. Malik’s statement regarding the obligation of expiation may be possible, because that only happens to someone who is in that nature and is satisfied with what appears from him. Ashhab interpreted the matter as most people being safe from that, and their statement regarding consideration is evidence of that. I said: What he narrated about the agreement in looking and making it a principle is not like that. Al-Baji narrated in Al-Muntaqa: If he looked once with the intention of pleasure and ejaculated, then Sheikh Abu Al-Hasan said: He must make up for it and pay expiation. Al-Baji said: This is correct in my opinion, because if he intended enjoyment by it, then it is like a kiss and other types of enjoyment, and God knows best. Jabir bin Zaid, Al-Thawri, Al-Shafi’i, Abu Thawr and the people of opinion said about the one who looked at a woman repeatedly until he ejaculated: He does not have to make up for it or pay expiation. This was said by Ibn Al-Mundhir. Al-Baji said: Ibn Nafi’ narrated in Al-Madinah from Malik that if he looked at a naked woman and enjoyed it and ejaculated, he must make up for it but not pay expiation. Fourteenth: The majority of scholars agree that the fast of someone who wakes up in a state of ritual impurity is valid. Judge Abu Bakr Ibn al-Arabi said: This is permissible by consensus. There was some discussion about it among the Companions, then it was settled that the fast of someone who wakes up in a state of ritual impurity is valid. I said: As for what was mentioned about the occurrence of speech, it is correct and well-known, and that is the saying of Abu Hurayrah: Whoever wakes up in a state of ritual impurity has no fast. It was narrated by Al-Muwatta’ and others. In the book of Al-Nasa’i, it is mentioned that he said when he was consulted: By God, I did not say that, Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, said it. There is a difference of opinion about his going back on it, and the most well-known of his two opinions among the people of knowledge is that he has no fast. It was narrated by Ibn Al-Mundhir, and it was narrated from Al-Hasan bin Salih. And from Abu Hurayrah also a third saying, he said: If he knows about his crime and then sleeps until morning, then he has broken his fast, and if he does not know until morning, then he is fasting. This was narrated from Ata’, Tawus, and Urwah bin Al-Zubayr. It was narrated from Al-Hasan and Al-Nakha’i that this is sufficient for a voluntary fast and makes up for an obligatory fast. I said: These are four sayings of scholars regarding someone who wakes up in a state of ritual impurity, and the correct one is the opinion of the majority, based on the hadith of Aisha, may God be pleased with her, and Umm Salamah: “The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, would wake up in a state of ritual impurity from sexual intercourse, not a wet dream, and then he would fast.” On the authority of Aisha, may God be pleased with her, she said: “The dawn of Ramadan would come upon the Messenger of God (blessings and peace of God be upon him) while he was in a state of ritual impurity, not having had a wet dream. He would perform ghusl and fast.” Narrated by al-Bukhari and Muslim. This is what is understood from the necessity of God’s statement: Now have intercourse with them al-Baqarah 2:17, because since He extended the permissibility of sexual intercourse until dawn, it is necessary to know that dawn would come upon him while he was in a state of ritual impurity, and ghusl is only possible after dawn. Al-Shafi’i said: If the penis was inside and he pulled it out at dawn, he does not have to make it up. Al-Muzani said: He has to make it up because it is part of the act of sexual intercourse. The first is more correct, based on what we have mentioned, and it is the opinion of our scholars. Fifteenth: They differed regarding a menstruating woman who becomes pure before dawn and leaves purification until morning. The majority of them are of the opinion that fasting is obligatory for her and is valid, whether she leaves it intentionally or inadvertently, like someone who is junub. This is the opinion of Malik and Ibn al-Qasim. Abdul Malik said: If a menstruating woman becomes pure before dawn and delays her ritual bath until dawn comes, then her day is a day of breaking the fast, because she is not pure in part of it, and she is not like someone who is junub because a wet dream does not break the fast, but menstruation does. This is what Abu al-Faraj said in his book on the authority of Abdul Malik. Al-Awza’i said: She must make up for it because she neglected to perform ritual bathing. Ibn al-Jalab mentioned on the authority of Abdul Malik that if she becomes pure before dawn at a time when she can perform ritual bathing, then she neglects and does not perform ritual bathing until morning, it does not harm her, like someone who is junub. If the time is short and she cannot perform ritual bathing, then her fast is not valid and her day is a day of breaking the fast. Malik said the same, and she is like someone who is menstruating when dawn comes upon her. Muhammad bin Maslama said about this: You fast and make up for it, like what Al-Awza’i said. It was narrated from him that he was an anomaly and made it obligatory for the one who purified herself before dawn and was negligent, procrastinated, and delayed until morning to pay expiation and make up for it. Sixteenth: If a woman becomes pure at night in Ramadan and does not know whether that was before dawn or after it, she should fast and make up that day as a precaution, and she does not have to make up for it. Seventeenth: It was narrated on the authority of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, that he said: The cupper and the one being cupped have broken their fast. From the hadith of Thawban, the hadith of Shaddad ibn Aws, and the hadith of Rafi’ ibn Khadij. Ahmad and Ishaq said the same. Ahmad authenticated the hadith of Shaddad ibn Aws, and Ali ibn al-Madini authenticated the hadith of Rafi’ ibn Khadij. Malik, al-Shafi’i, and al-Thawri said: He does not have to make up for it, but it is disliked for him to do so because of the deception. In Sahih Muslim, it is narrated that it was said to him: Did you dislike cupping for a fasting person? He said: No, except for weakness.
