He narrated from al-Shafi’i that he said: He should not pray until he reaches Muzdalifah, and if midnight comes upon him before he reaches Muzdalifah, he should pray them. Thirteenth: Whoever hastens to reach Muzdalifah before sunset, Ibn Habib said: There is no prayer for whoever hastens to Muzdalifah before sunset, whether for an imam or anyone else, until sunset, based on the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: The prayer is in front of you, then he prayed it in Muzdalifah after sunset. From the meaning, the time for this prayer is after sunset, so it is not permissible to perform it before it. If it had a time before sunset, it would not have been delayed. Fourteenth: As for the one who comes to Arafat after the Imam has left, or has an excuse from those who stood with the Imam, Ibn Al-Mawaz said: Whoever stands after the Imam should pray each prayer at its time. Malik said about the one who has an excuse that prevents him from being with the Imam: He should pray the two prayers when the twilight disappears, combining them. Ibn Al-Qasim said about the one who stands after the Imam: If he hopes to reach Muzdalifah a third of the night before, then he should delay the prayer until he reaches Muzdalifah, otherwise he should pray each prayer at its time. Ibn Al-Mawaz made delaying the prayer to Muzdalifah for the one who stands with the Imam and not others. Malik considered the time and not the place, and Ibn Al-Qasim considered the chosen time for the prayer and the place. If he fears missing the chosen time, then considering the place is invalid, and considering its chosen time is more appropriate. Fifteenth: The scholars differed regarding the form of prayer in Muzdalifah in two aspects: One of them: the call to prayer and the call to prayer. The other: Is it permissible to combine them together in a continuous manner without separating them by work, or is it permissible to work between them and set down the luggage and the like? As for the call to prayer and the call to prayer, it has been established: “The Messenger of God (peace and blessings of God be upon him) prayed Maghrib and Isha’ prayers in Muzdalifah with one call to prayer and two iqamas.” Narrated by Sahih from the long hadith of Jabir, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Abu Thawr, and Ibn al-Mundhir said the same. Malik said: He prays them with two calls to prayer and two iqamas, and the same applies to Dhuhr and Asr prayers in Arafat, except that this is at the beginning of the time of Dhuhr, according to consensus. Abu ‘Umar said: I do not know of any hadith of what Malik said that is traced back to the Prophet (peace and blessings of God be upon him) in any way, but it was narrated from ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab, and Ibn al-Mundhir added Ibn Mas’ud. One of the arguments for Malik in this regard from a theoretical perspective is that the Messenger of God (peace and blessings of God be upon him) established the Sunnah for the prayers in Muzdalifah and Arafat that the time for both of them is the same. If their time is the same and each prayer is prayed at its proper time, then neither of them is more deserving of the call to prayer and the iqama than the other, because neither of them is to be made up, rather it is a prayer that is prayed at its proper time, and the Sunnah for every prayer that is prayed at its proper time is that the call to prayer and the iqama are given in congregation, and this is clear, and God knows best. Others said: As for the first of them, it is prayed with the call to prayer and the iqama, and as for the second, it is prayed without the call to prayer or the iqama. They said: Omar ordered the second call to prayer because the people had dispersed for their dinner, so he called to prayer to gather them. They said: And we say the same when the people disperse from the Imam for dinner or something else, he orders the muezzins to call to prayer to gather them, and when he calls to prayer, he calls to prayer. They said: This is the meaning of what was narrated from Omar, and they mentioned the hadith of Abd al-Rahman ibn Yazid who said: Ibn Masoud used to pray the dinner prayer in Muzdalifah between the two prayers, and in another chain of transmission he prayed with the call to prayer and the iqama, mentioned by Abd al-Razzaq. Others said: Both prayers are prayed in Muzdalifah with the iqama and no call to prayer in either of them, narrated from Ibn Umar and al-Thawri said the same. Abd al-Razzaq and Abd al-Malik ibn al-Sabah mentioned from al-Thawri from Salamah ibn Kuhayl from Sa`id ibn Jubayr from Ibn Umar who said: “The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, combined the Maghrib and Isha prayers together. He prayed the Maghrib prayer as three rak’ahs and the Isha prayer as two rak’ahs with one call to prayer.” Others said: Both prayers are performed together between the Maghrib and Isha prayers together with one call to prayer and one call to prayer. They went in that regard to what Hisham narrated on the authority of Yunus ibn Ubayd on the authority of Sa’id ibn Jubayr on the authority of Ibn Umar: He combined Maghrib and Isha’ with one call to prayer and one Iqamah, without making anything between them. A similar hadith was narrated with a chain of transmission traceable to the Prophet (peace and blessings of God be upon him) from Khuzaymah ibn Thabit, but it is not strong. Al-Jawzajaani narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan from Abu Yusuf from Abu Hanifa that they are prayed with one call to prayer and two Iqamahs, with the call to prayer for Maghrib and the Iqamah for Isha’ only. This is what al-Tahawi adopted based on the hadeeth of Jabir, and it is the first opinion and is relied upon. Others said: They are prayed with two Iqamahs without the call to prayer for either of them. Among those who said this were al-Shafi’i and his companions, Ishaq, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal in one of his two opinions, which is the opinion of Salim ibn ‘Abdullah and al-Qasim ibn Muhammad. They cited as evidence what ‘Abd al-Razzaq mentioned from Mu’ammar from Ibn Shihab from Salim from Ibn ‘Umar, “When the Prophet (peace and blessings of God be upon him) came to Muzdalifah, he combined Maghrib and ‘Isha’, prayed Maghrib three rak’ahs and ‘Isha’ two rak’ahs with one Iqamah for each of them, and he did not pray anything between them.” Abu Omar said: The narrations from Ibn Omar in this statement are among the most authentic of what was narrated from him in this chapter, but they are open to interpretation. The hadith of Jabir was not disputed, so it is more appropriate. There is no room for consideration in this issue, but rather it is a matter of following. Sixteenth: As for separating the two prayers by doing something other than prayer, it was proven from Usamah bin Zaid: “When the Prophet (peace and blessings of God be upon him) came to Muzdalifah, he dismounted, performed ablution and performed it thoroughly. Then the Iqamah for prayer was pronounced and he prayed Maghrib. Then each person made his camel kneel in his place. Then the Iqamah for prayer was pronounced and they prayed it and did not pray anything between them.” In another narration: And they did not become free from ihram until the Isha prayer was pronounced, so he prayed and then became free from ihram. We mentioned earlier on the authority of Ibn Mas`ud that he used to make Isha prayer between the two prayers. This indicates the permissibility of separating the two prayers by combining them. Malik was asked about someone who came to Muzdalifah: Should he start with the prayer or delay it until he dismounts from his mount? He said: As for the light saddle, there is no problem in starting with it before the prayer. As for the mounts and the Zawamil, I do not see that. He should start with the two prayers and then dismount from his mount.” Ashhab said in his books: He may dismount his saddle before the prayer, and I prefer dismounting it after he prays Maghrib, unless he is forced to do so because of the weight of his mount or some other excuse. As for the voluntary prayer between the two prayers, Ibn al-Mundhir said: I do not know of any disagreement among them that it is a sin not to perform a voluntary prayer between them, and in the hadith of Usama: And he did not pray anything between them. Seventeenth: As for spending the night in Muzdalifah, it is not a pillar of Hajj according to the majority of scholars. They differed regarding what is obligatory for someone who did not spend the night in Muzdalifah on the night of sacrifice and did not stand in Jam’ah. Malik said: Whoever did not spend the night there must offer a blood sacrifice, and whoever stayed for more than one night does not have to do anything, because spending the night there on the night of sacrifice is a confirmed Sunnah according to Malik and his companions, and not an obligation. A similar opinion is given by Ata’, Az-Zuhri, Qatadah, Sufyan Ath-Thawri, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Thawr and the people of opinion regarding someone who did not spend the night. Ash-Shafi’i said: If he leaves it after midnight, nothing is required of him, and if he leaves before midnight and does not return to Muzdalifah, he must pay a ransom, and the ransom is a sheep. Ikrimah, Ash-Sha’bi, An-Nakha’i and Al-Hasan Al-Basri said: Standing in Muzdalifah is obligatory, and whoever misses Jam’ah and does not stand has missed Hajj, and his ihram should be made into an ‘Umrah. This was narrated from Ibn Az-Zubayr and it is the opinion of Al-Awza’i. The same was narrated from Ath-Thawri, and the most correct opinion from him is that standing there is a confirmed Sunnah. Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman said: Whoever misses the Ifadah from Jam’ has missed Hajj, and he should perform Umrah and then perform Hajj the following year. They cited as evidence the apparent meaning of the Qur’an and Sunnah. As for the Qur’an, it is the saying of God the Almighty: And when you depart from ‘Arafat, remember God at Al-Mash’ar Al-Haram 10:13. As for the Sunnah, it is the saying of the Prophet (peace and blessings of God be upon him): Whoever witnesses Jam’ah and stands with the people until he departs has indeed witnessed it, but whoever does not witness that has no Hajj. This was mentioned by Ibn Al-Mundhir. Ad-Darqutni narrated: “On the authority of Urwah ibn Mudarris, he said: I came to the Prophet (peace and blessings of God be upon him) while he was at Jam’ah and said to him: O Messenger of God, is there any Hajj for me? He said: Whoever prays this prayer with us and stands with us until we depart, and has departed from ‘Arafat before that, by night or by day, has completed his Hajj and fulfilled his obligation.” Al-Sha’bi said: Whoever does not stand at Jam’ah should consider it as Umrah. Those who cited as evidence for the majority responded by saying: As for the verse, it does not provide evidence for the obligation of standing or spending the night, since that is not mentioned in it, rather it merely mentions it. And everyone has agreed that if he stands in Muzdalifah and does not remember God, his Hajj is complete. So if the remembrance that is commanded is not part of Hajj, then witnessing the place of sacrifice is more deserving of not being so. Abu Omar said: And they have also agreed that if the sun rises on the Day of Sacrifice, then the time for standing in Jam’ has passed, and whoever stands there before sunrise has done so, according to some who say that it is obligatory, and others who say that it is Sunnah. As for the hadith of Urwah ibn Mudris, some of its chains of transmission state that standing in Arafah is not spending the night in Muzdalifah. Similar to it is the hadith of Abd al-Rahman ibn Ya’mar al-Dayli, who said: I witnessed the Messenger of God (blessings and peace of God be upon him) in Arafah, and some people from Najd came to him and asked him about Hajj, so the Messenger of God (blessings and peace of God be upon him) said: Hajj is Arafah. Whoever reaches it before dawn on the night of Jam’ has completed his Hajj. Narrated by al-Nasa’i, who said: Ishaq ibn Ibrahim told us, who said: Waki’ told us, who said: Sufyan - meaning al-Thawri - told us on the authority of Bakir ibn Ata’ on the authority of Abd al-Rahman ibn Ya’mar al-Dayli, who said: I witnessed..., and he mentioned it. Narrated by Ibn Uyaynah on the authority of Bakir on the authority of Abd al-Rahman ibn Ya`mar al-Dailami who said: I witnessed the Messenger of God (peace and blessings of God be upon him) saying: “Hajj is Arafat. Whoever reaches Arafat before dawn has reached it. The days of Mina are three. Whoever hastens to do so in two days, there is no sin upon him, and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him.” And his saying in the hadith of Urwah: Whoever prays this prayer of ours. So he mentioned the prayer at Muzdalifah. The scholars have agreed that if he spends the night there and stands and sleeps through the prayer and does not pray with the imam until he misses it, then his Hajj is complete. Since attending the prayer with the imam is not part of Hajj, standing at the place where the prayer is performed is more likely to be the same. They said: This hadith does not fulfill this obligation except at Arafat specifically. Eighteenth: The Almighty said: And remember Him as He has guided you. He repeated the command for emphasis, as you say: Throw, throw. It was said: The first is a command to remember at the sacred monument. The second is a command to remember according to the rule of sincerity. It was said: What is meant by the second is to enumerate the blessing and command to thank for it, then He reminded them of their state of misguidance to show the extent of the blessing, so He said: And if you were before that among those astray. The kaf in kama is a description of an omitted source, and ma is a source or a collective. The meaning is: Remember Him with a good remembrance as He has guided you with a good guidance, and remember Him as you know how to remember Him, do not deviate from it. An is a lightened form of the heavy one, and this is indicated by the inclusion of the lam in the predicate, as Sibawayh said. Al-Farra’: It is a negative meaning what, and the lam means except, as he said: May your mother be bereaved of you, if you kill a Muslim, the punishment of the Most Merciful will befall you. Or it means had, meaning you were, three sayings. The pronoun in before refers to guidance. It was said to refer to the Qur’an, meaning you were nothing but astray before its revelation. If you wish, it refers to the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, as a metaphor for something not mentioned, and the first is more apparent, and God knows best.
2:199: It has four issues: The first: The Almighty’s saying: Then hasten from where the people hasten. It was said that the address is to the Hams, for they did not stand with the people at Arafat, but they stood at Muzdalifah, which is one of the red mountains, and they used to say: We are the two of God, so it is appropriate for us to honor the Sacred Sanctuary, and not to honor anything in the Sanctuary. And despite their knowledge and acknowledgement that Arafat was the place of Abraham’s (peace be upon him) standing, they did not leave the Sacred Sanctuary, and they would stand in groups and hasten from it, and the people would stand at Arafat. So it was said to them: Hasten with the group. And then is not in this verse for order, but rather it is to connect a sentence of speech that is separate from it. Ad-Dahhak said: The one addressed in the verse is the entire nation, and what is meant by the people is Abraham (peace be upon him), as he said: Those to whom the people said, and he meant one. And it is possible based on this that they were commanded to hasten from Arafat, and it is possible that it was another hasten, which is the one from Muzdalifah, so then comes according to this possibility in its chapter, and on this possibility At-Tabari relied. Meaning: Go forth from where Abraham went forth from Muzdalifah, meaning then go forth to Mina because the going forth from Arafat is before the going forth from Jam’a. I said: This is an argument for those who make standing at Muzdalifah obligatory, because of the command to leave from it, and God knows best. The correct interpretation of this verse of the two opinions is the first opinion. Al-Tirmidhi narrated on the authority of Aisha, who said: The Quraysh and those who followed their religion, the Hums, would stand at Muzdalifah saying: We are the Qutayyin of God. Those other than them would stand at Arafat. Then God the Almighty revealed: Then proceed from where the people proceed. This is a good and authentic hadith. In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Aisha, she said: The Hams are those about whom God revealed: Then hasten from where the people hasten. She said: The people used to hasten from Arafat, and the Hams used to hasten from Muzdalifah, saying: We do not hasten except from the Haram. So when the verse: Then hasten from where the people have departed was revealed, they returned to Arafat. This is a clear text and there are many similar ones that are correct, so no reliance should be placed on any other statement. And God is the source of help. Saeed bin Jubair read al-Naasi and its interpretation is Adam, peace be upon him, because God Almighty said: Then he forgot, and We found in him no firm resolve. Some of them allow the ya’ to be softened and say al-Nas, like al-Qadi and al-Haadi. Ibn Atiyyah said: As for its permissibility in Arabic, Sibawayh mentioned it, but as for its permissibility as read, I do not remember it. God commanded seeking forgiveness because it is its place, and the place of acceptance and the place of mercy. A group said: The meaning is seek forgiveness from God for your action that was contrary to the Sunnah of Abraham in your standing at Qazh from Muzdalifah rather than Arafat. Second: Abu Dawud narrated on the authority of Ali, who said: When morning came, he - meaning the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace - stood at Qahzah and said: This is Qahzah, which is the place of standing, and all of it is a place of standing, and the sacrifice was made here, and all of Mina is a place of sacrifice, so sacrifice in your dwellings. So the ruling for the pilgrims when they set out from Arafat to Muzdalifah is that they spend the night there, then the imam leads the people in the early morning and they stand at the sacred monument. Qahzah is the mountain on which the imam stands, and they continue to remember God and supplicate until close to sunrise, then they set out before sunrise, in opposition to the Arabs, for they used to set out after sunrise and say: Thabir has risen, so that we may raid, meaning so that we may come close to being released from the state of ihram and be able to raid. Al-Bukhari narrated on the authority of Amr ibn Maymun, who said: I witnessed Umar praying the Fajr prayer, then he stood up and said: The polytheists would not leave until the sun had risen, and they would say: Thabir has risen. The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, differed from them and left before the sun had risen. Ibn Uyaynah narrated on the authority of Ibn Jurayj on the authority of Muhammad ibn Qays ibn Makhramah on the authority of Tawus on the authority of his father: The people of the Jahiliyyah used to leave Arafat before sunset, and they used to leave from Muzdalifah after sunrise. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, delayed this one and hastened this one. He delayed leaving from Arafat and hastened leaving from Muzdalifah, contrary to the guidance of the polytheists. Third: If they set out before sunrise, then the ruling is that they set out in the manner of setting out from Arafat, which is that the imam leads the people at the pace of the neck, and if one of you finds a space, he should add something to the pace of the neck. The pace of the neck is a well-known gait of the animals, and it is not unknown. The text says: Above the neck, like the trot, or above that. In Sahih Muslim: On the authority of Usamah ibn Zayd, may God be pleased with them both, who was asked: How did the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, walk when he left Arafat? He said: He walked at a distance of about the neck, and when he found a gap, he would move. Hisham said: The distance is above the neck, and it has been mentioned before. It is recommended for him to move in the valley of Muhsar at a distance of a stone’s throw, but if he does not do that, there is no blame, and it is from Mina. Al-Thawri and others narrated on the authority of Abu al-Zubayr, on the authority of Jabir, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, pushed them away, and he was calm, and he said to them: Settle down in the valley of Muhsar, and he said to them: Learn your rituals from me. When they come to Mina, which is the morning of the Day of Sacrifice, they throw pebbles at Jamrat al-Aqabah there in the morning, riding if they are able. It is not recommended to ride at any other Jamrat. They throw seven pebbles, each pebble the size of a throwing pebble, as will be explained later. When they throw them, everything that was forbidden to them of clothing and all manner of clothing is permissible for them, except women, perfume, and hunting, according to Malik and Ishaq in the narration of Abu Dawud al-Khaffaf from him. Umar ibn al-Khattab and Ibn Umar said: Everything is permissible for him except women and perfume. According to Malik, whoever perfumes himself after throwing pebbles and before leaving is not required to pay a ransom, due to what was mentioned in that regard. Whoever hunts in his presence after throwing pebbles at Jamrat al-Aqabah and before leaving is required to pay a penalty. Ash-Shafi’i, Ahmad, and Ishaq Abu Thawr said: Everything is permissible for him except women. This was narrated from Ibn Abbas. Fourth: The pilgrim ends the Talbiyah with the first pebble he throws at Jamrat al-Aqaba. This is the opinion of most scholars in Madinah and elsewhere. It is permissible and permitted according to Malik. What is well-known from him is that he ends it at noon on the Day of Arafah, according to what was mentioned in his Muwatta’ on the authority of Ali, and he said: This is the order according to us. I said: The basis for this sentence in the Sunnah is what Muslim narrated: On the authority of Al-Fadl ibn Abbas, who was riding behind the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, that he said on the eve of Arafah and the morning of the gathering of the people when they set out: Be calm, and he restrained his camel until he entered Muhassar which is from Mina. He said: Be calm, and he threw pebbles at the Jamarat, and he said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, continued to recite the Talbiyah until he threw the Jamarat Al-Aqaba. In another narration: “And the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, was pointing with his hand as a person throws pebbles.” And in Al-Bukhari on the authority of Abdullah He reached the Great Jamarat, with the Kaaba on his left and Mina on his right, and threw seven stones and said: This is how the one upon whom Surat Al-Baqarah was revealed threw stones, may God bless him and grant him peace. Al-Daraqutni narrated on the authority of Aisha that she said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: If you have stoned the Kaaba, shaved your head, and slaughtered your animals, then everything is permissible for you except women, and clothing and perfume are permissible for you. In Bukhari, “On the authority of Aisha, she said: I perfumed the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, with these two hands of mine when he entered ihram, and when he exited ihram before he performed tawaf, and she spread out her hands.” This is the lesser tahallul according to the scholars. The greater tahallul is the tawaf al-ifada, which is the one that permits women and all the prohibitions of ihram, and it will be mentioned in Surat al-Hajj, God willing.
2:200: There are two issues: First: The Almighty’s saying: And when you have completed your rites. Mujahid said: The rites are the sacrifices and the shedding of blood. It was said: They are the rituals of Hajj, because the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: Learn from me your rites. The meaning is: So when you perform a rite of Hajj, remember God and praise Him for His blessings upon you. Abu Amr assimilates the Kaf into the Kaf, and so does your rites, because they are two similar words. Qadatum here means you have performed and finished. God the Almighty said: And when you have completed the prayer, meaning you have performed the Friday prayer. Qada’ may also be used to refer to acts of worship performed outside of their specific time. The second: The Almighty’s saying: So remember God as you remember your fathers. It was the custom of the Arabs, when they completed their Hajj, to stand at the Jamrah, boast about their fathers, and remember the days of their ancestors of bravery, generosity, and other things, to the point that one of them would say: O God, my father had a great dome, a great bowl, and much wealth, so give me what You gave him, and he would not remember anyone but his father. So the verse was revealed so that they would commit themselves to remembering God more than they committed themselves to remembering their fathers during the days of ignorance. This is the saying of the majority of commentators. Ibn Abbas, Ata’, Ad-Dahhak, and Ar-Rabi’ said: The meaning of the verse: And remember God as children remember their fathers and mothers: father and mother, meaning seek help from Him and turn to Him as you used to do with your fathers when you were young. A group said: The meaning of the verse is: Remember God and glorify Him and defend His sanctity, and repel whoever wants to associate partners with God in His religion and feelings, just as you remember your fathers with goodness if one of them is angry, and you protect their sides and defend them. Abu al-Juza’ said to Ibn Abbas: A man today does not remember his father, so what is the meaning of the verse? He said: It is not like that, but that you become angry for the sake of God if he is disobeyed is more intense than your anger for your parents if they curse you. The kaf in His statement, like your remembrance is in the accusative case, meaning a remembrance like your remembrance. Or more intense Al-Zajjaj said: Or more intense is in the genitive case in apposition to your remembrance, meaning: or more intense remembrance. It was not declined because af’al is an adjective, and it is permissible for it to be in the accusative case meaning or remember Him more intensely. Remembrance is in the accusative case for clarification. God the Almighty said: And among the people is he who says, ‘Our Lord, give us in this world’ “Min” is in the nominative case as a subject, or as an adjective if you wish. He says, ‘Our Lord, give us in this world’ is the relative clause of min, and what is meant are the polytheists. Abu Wa’il, Al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd said: The Arabs in the Age of Ignorance used to supplicate for worldly interests only. They used to ask for camels, sheep, and victory over the enemy, and they did not ask for the Hereafter, since they did not know it or believe in it. So they were forbidden from that supplication that was specific to worldly matters, and the prohibition came in the form of a report about them. It is permissible for this threat to include the believer as well if he limits his supplications to this world. Based on this, and he will have no share in the Hereafter means like the share of the one who asks for the Hereafter. And the share is the portion. Min is redundant and has been mentioned before.
2:201: God Almighty says: And among them are those who say, ‘Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter and protect us from the punishment of the Fire.’ There are three issues: First: The Almighty’s saying: And among them meaning among the people, and they are the Muslims who seek the good of this world and the hereafter. There are many interpretations of the two good deeds. It was narrated on the authority of Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, that the good deed in this world is a beautiful woman, and in the hereafter it is the houris. And save us from the punishment of the Fire means the bad woman. I said: This is far-fetched, and is not authentically reported from Ali, because the Fire is the reality of the burning Fire, and the woman’s expression about the Fire is permissible. Qatada said: The good of this world is well-being in health and sufficient wealth. Al-Hasan said: The good of this world is knowledge and worship. Other than this has been said. What most scholars agree on is that what is meant by the two good deeds is the good of this world and the Hereafter. This is correct, because the wording requires all of this, because the word good is indefinite in the context of the supplication, so it is possible for every good deed of the good deeds as a substitute. The good of the Hereafter is Paradise by consensus. It has been said: He did not mean a single good deed, but rather he meant: Give us a good gift in this world, so the noun was omitted. Second: The Almighty’s saying: And save us from the punishment of the Fire. The root of qana is awqana. The waw was deleted as it was deleted in yaqee and yashee, because it is between a yaa and a kasra, like ba’d. This is the opinion of the Basrans. The Kufians said: It was deleted to differentiate between the intransitive and transitive. Muhammad bin Yazid said: This is a mistake, because the Arabs say waram yarmu, so they delete the waw. What is meant by the verse is a supplication that a person not be among those who enter it through his sins and are expelled by intercession. It is possible that it is a supplication emphasizing the request to enter Paradise, so that the desire is in the meaning of salvation and victory from both sides, as: One of the companions said to the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace: I only say in my supplication: O God, admit me into Paradise and save me from the Fire, and I do not know what your humming is or what Muadh’s humming is. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said to him: We hum around it. Narrated by Abu Dawud in his Sunan and Ibn Majah as well. Third: This verse is one of the comprehensive supplications that cover both this world and the Hereafter. Anas was asked: Supplicate to God for us. He said: O God, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter and save us from the punishment of the Fire. They said: Give us more. He said: What do you want? I have asked for this world and the Hereafter. In the two Sahihs, on the authority of Anas, he said: The most common supplication that the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, would make was: O God, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and save us from the punishment of the Fire. He said: When Anas wanted to supplicate, he would supplicate with it, and when he wanted to supplicate with a supplication, he would supplicate with it in it. In the hadith of Umar: “He used to circumambulate the Kaaba and say: ‘Our Lord, give us in this world that which is good and in the Hereafter that which is good and protect us from the punishment of the Fire.’” He had no other migration than this, as mentioned by Abu Ubaid. Ibn Jurayj said: “I have been told that he used to order that the Muslim’s most frequent supplication in the gathering be this verse: ‘Our Lord, give us in this world that which is good and in the Hereafter that which is good and protect us from the punishment of the Fire.’” Ibn Abbas said: “There is an angel standing at the corner since God created the heavens and the earth, saying, ‘Ameen.’ So say, ‘Our Lord, give us in this world that which is good and in the Hereafter that which is good and protect us from the punishment of the Fire.’” ‘Ata’ ibn Abi Rabah was asked about the Yemeni Corner while circumambulating the Kaaba, so ‘Ata’ said: “Abu Hurairah told me that the Prophet (peace and blessings of God be upon him) said: ‘Seventy angels are assigned to it, so whoever says, ‘O God, I ask You for forgiveness and well-being in this world and the Hereafter. Our Lord, give us in this world that which is good and in the Hereafter that which is good and protect us from the punishment of the Fire,’ they say, ‘Ameen.’” It was included by Ibn Majah in Sunan, and its complete chain of transmission will be included in Hajj, God willing.
2:202: There are three issues: The first: The Almighty’s statement: For those will be a share of what they have earned. This refers to the second group, the group of Islam, meaning that they will have the reward of Hajj or the reward of supplication, because the supplication of the believer is an act of worship. It was said: These refer to both groups, so the believer will have the reward of his work and supplication, and the disbeliever will have the punishment of his polytheism and his shortsightedness towards this world, and it is like the statement of the Almighty: And for all are degrees according to what they have done. The second: The Almighty’s saying: And God is swift in account. From the root word sara’a yusra’a - like ‘azaama ya’zam - sara’a and sira’a, so He is swift. Accountability is a noun like accounting, and what is calculated may be called accounting. And accounting is counting, it is said: hasaba yuhisab hisaban wa hisabahu wa hisaban wa hisaban wa hisaban, meaning he counted. Ibn al-A’rabi recited: Oh camel, may the King of Hassan al-Rabab give you a drink without account. You killed me with your charm and charm Lineage: what is considered one of a person’s glories. It is said: His religion is his lineage. It is also said: His wealth. From this comes the hadith: Nobility is wealth and generosity is piety. Narrated by Samurah ibn Jundub, narrated by Ibn Majah and also in Ash-Shihab. A man is a hasib, and he has calculated his account with dammah, like he gave a sermon. The meaning of the verse is that God, the Exalted, is quick to take account. He does not need to count, or to conclude, or to think as an account does. For this reason He said, and His word is the truth: And sufficient are We as accountants. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: O God, the Sender down of the Book, Swift in Reckoning. Hadith. God, the Almighty, the Majestic, knows what is for and against His servants, so He does not need to remember and ponder, since He knows what is for and against the accountant, because the benefit of the reckoning is knowing its reality. It was said: He is swift in rewarding the servants for their deeds. It was also said: The meaning is that one matter does not distract Him from another matter, so He holds them accountable in one instance, as He said, and His word is the truth: He did not create you and resurrect you except as a single soul. Al-Hasan said: His reckoning is faster than the blink of an eye. In the hadith, God holds accountable in the amount of milking a sheep. It was also said: It is that if He holds one person accountable, He has held all of creation accountable. It was said to Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him: How does God hold His servants accountable in one day? He said: As He provides for them in one day. The meaning of reckoning is God informing His servants of the amounts of recompense for their deeds, and reminding them of what they may have forgotten, as evidenced by His statement, the Almighty: "On the Day when God will resurrect them all and inform them of what they did. God has enumerated it, but they have forgotten it." It was said: The meaning of the verse is that the Day of Reckoning will come quickly, so the purpose of the verse is to warn of the Day of Resurrection. I said: Everything is possible. The servant takes upon himself the task of lightening the reckoning for himself through righteous deeds. The reckoning in the Hereafter will only be lightened for the one who held himself accountable in this world. Third: Ibn Abbas said about the Almighty’s saying: Those will have a share of what they have earned: He is the man who takes money to perform Hajj on behalf of someone else, so he will have a reward. It was narrated from him about this verse: A man said: O Messenger of God, my father died and did not perform Hajj, so should I perform Hajj on his behalf? The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: If your father had a debt and I paid it, would that not be sufficient? He said: Yes. He said: Then the debt of God is more deserving of being paid. He said: Do I have a reward? Then God, the Most High, revealed: For those, there is a share of what they have earned. Meaning, whoever performs Hajj on behalf of a dead person, the reward is shared between him and the dead person. Abu Abdullah Muhammad bin Khuwaiz Mandad said in his rulings: The statement of Ibn Abbas is similar to the statement of Malik, because the implication of Malik’s school of thought is that the one on whose behalf Hajj is performed gets the reward for spending, and the Hajj is for the pilgrim, so it is as if he gets the reward for his body and deeds, and the one on whose behalf Hajj is performed gets the reward for his money and spending. For this reason we said: There is no difference in this ruling for someone who performs Hajj on his own behalf, the Hajj of Islam, or does not perform Hajj, because the actions that are performed by representation do not differ from the ruling for the one who is represented, whether he has performed it on his own behalf or not, considering the religious and worldly actions. Do you not see that the one who owes zakat, expiation, or something else may pay it on behalf of someone else even if he does not pay it on his own behalf? Likewise, the one who does not take care of his interests in this world may act on behalf of someone else in something similar, so that it is completed for someone else even if it is not completed for himself, and he may marry someone else even if he does not marry himself.
2:203: The Almighty’s saying: And remember God during the appointed days contains six issues: The first: The Kufians said: The Alif and the Ta in (Ma'du'at) are for the least number, and the Basrans said: They are for the few and the many, based on the evidence of the Almighty’s saying: And they will be in the chambers, secure (Saba’: 37) and the chambers are many, and there is no disagreement among the scholars that the numbered days in this verse are the days of Manna, which are the days of Tashreeq, and that these three names apply to them, which are the days of stoning the Jamarat, and they apply to the three days from which the pilgrim hastens on the two days of sacrifice, so stop at that, and Al-Tha’labi said and Ibrahim said: The numbered days are the days of the ten, and the known days are the days of sacrifice, and likewise Makki and Al-Mahdun narrated that the numbered days are the days of the ten, and it is not correct for what we mentioned of consensus, according to what Abu Omar bin Abdul Barr and others transmitted, Ibn Atiyah said: This is either from a typo in the copy, or he means the ten days after sacrifice, and there is something wrong with that. Second: God Almighty commanded His servants to remember Him on the appointed days, which are the three days after the Day of Sacrifice, and the Day of Sacrifice is not one of them, because of the consensus of the people that no one should set out on the Day of Sacrifice, which is the second Day of Sacrifice. If the Day of Sacrifice were among the appointed days, it would be permissible for anyone who wanted to set out in haste on the Day of Sacrifice, because it has taken two days from the appointed days. Al-Daraqutni, Al-Tirmidhi, and others narrated on the authority of Abd al-Rahman ibn Ya`mar al-Dayli: “Some people from Najd came to the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, while he was in Arafat and asked him. He ordered a crier to call out: ‘The Hajj is Arafat. Whoever comes on the night of Jumu’ah before dawn has reached it. The days of Mina are three. Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him, and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him.’” That is, whoever hastens in two days of Mina, his stay will be three days until the Day of Sacrifice, and all his stoning will be forty-nine pebbles, and the stoning on the third day will be dropped from him. Whoever does not leave it until the end of the third day, he will have a four-day stay in Mina for the Day of Sacrifice, and he will have completed the number in stoning, as will be explained. Among the evidence that the days are three - in addition to what we have mentioned - is the statement of Al-Arji: We only meet three times a day before the group separates us The days of stoning are numbered, and the days of sacrifice are known. Nafi’ narrated on the authority of Ibn Umar that the numbered days and the known days are collected into four days: the day of sacrifice and the three days after it. The day of sacrifice is known but not numbered, and the two days after it are known but numbered, and the fourth day is numbered but not known. This is the doctrine of Malik and others. And it was like this because the first was not one of the days that are specific to Mina in the words of God Almighty: And remember God during the appointed days, nor one of those that the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, specified in his words: The days of Mina are three, so it was known, because God Almighty said: And let them mention the name of God on the appointed days over what He has provided for them of cattle (al-Hajj 22:28). There is no disagreement that what is meant by it is the sacrifice, and the sacrifice was on the first day, which is the day of sacrifice, and the second and third, and there was no sacrifice on the fourth by consensus of our scholars, so the fourth was not meant in the words of God Almighty: Informed, because no sacrifice is made on it and it was one of the days in which stoning is done, so it became numbered for the sake of stoning, not known because there is no sacrifice on it. Ibn Al-Arabi said: The truth about it is that the day of sacrifice is numbered by stoning and known by slaughter, but according to our scholars it is not meant in the words of God Almighty: And remember God during the appointed days. Abu Hanifa and Al-Shafi’i said: The known days are the ten from the first day of Dhul-Hijjah, and the last of them is the day of sacrifice. Their statement did not differ in That, and they narrated that from Ibn Abbas, and Al-Tahawi narrated from Abu Yusuf that the known days are the days of sacrifice. Abu Yusuf said: That was narrated from Omar and Ali, and I agree with him, because God Almighty said: And let them mention the name of God on known days over what He has provided for them of cattle (al-Hajj 22:28). Al-Karkhi narrated from Muhammad ibn Al-Hasan that the known days are the three days of sacrifice: the day of Al-Adha and the two days after it. Al-Kaya Al-Tabari said: According to Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, there is no difference between the known and the counted days, because the counted days mentioned in the Qur’an are the days of Tashreeq without dispute, and no one doubts that the counted days do not include the ten days, because God Almighty says: But whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him, and there is no ruling in the ten that relates to two days without the third, and it was narrated from Ibn Abbas that the known days are the ten, and the counted days are the days of Tashreeq, and this is the opinion of the majority. I said: Ibn Zayd said: The known days are the ten days of Dhul-Hijjah and the days of Tashreeq. There is something wrong with this, because of what we mentioned, and the apparent meaning of the verse refutes it. God made the remembrance in the numbered and known days, indicating the opposite of what He said, so there is no point in being preoccupied with it. Third: There is no disagreement that the one addressed by this remembrance is the pilgrim. He is addressed with the takbir when throwing the pebbles, and upon the animals he has been provided with during the specified days, and at the end of the prayers without the talbiyah. Is the non-pilgrim included in this or not? The opinion of the jurists of the regions and the famous Companions and Followers is that what is meant by takbir is everyone - especially at the times of prayers - so he says takbir at the end of each prayer - whether the worshipper is alone or in a group - with an apparent takbir during these days, following the example of the righteous predecessors may God be pleased with them. In al-Mukhtasar: Women do not say takbir after the prayers, and the first is more famous, because the ruling of ihram applies to her like a man, as stated in al-Mudawwana. Fourth: If someone forgets to say the takbir after a prayer, he should say it if he is close by, and if he is far away, then nothing is upon him. This was stated by Ibn al-Jalab. Malik said in al-Mukhtasar: He should say the takbir as long as he is in his seat, and if he gets up from his seat, then nothing is upon him. In al-Mudawwanah, from the words of Malik: If the imam forgets to say the takbir, if he is close by, he should sit and say the takbir, and if he is far away, then nothing is upon him. If he leaves and does not say the takbir and the people are sitting, then let them say the takbir. Fifth: The scholars differed regarding the two ends of the duration of the Takbir. Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn Abbas said: He should say Takbir from the Fajr prayer on the Day of Arafah until the Asr prayer on the last day of Tashreeq. Ibn Masoud and Abu Hanifa said: He should say Takbir from the morning of Arafah until the Asr prayer on the Day of Sacrifice. Their companions disagreed with them and said the first opinion, the opinion of Umar, Ali and Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them, so they avoided starting but not ending. Malik said: He should say Takbir from the Dhuhr prayer on the Day of Sacrifice until the Fajr prayer on the last day of Tashreeq. Al-Shafi’i said the same, and it is also the opinion of Ibn Umar and Ibn Abbas. Zaid ibn Thabit said: He should say Takbir from the Dhuhr prayer on the Day of Sacrifice until the last day of Tashreeq. Ibn al-Arabi said: As for those who said: He should say Takbir on the Day of Arafah and cut off the Asr prayer on the Day of Sacrifice, they have deviated from the apparent meaning, because God Almighty said: In appointed days, and the days are three. These people said: He should say Takbir on two days, so they left the apparent meaning without evidence. As for those who said the Day of Arafah and the days of Tashreeq, they said: He said: And when you depart from Arafat [Al-Baqarah].: 198], so the mention of (Arafat) is included in the mention of the days. This would have been correct if he had said: He says the takbir from sunset on the day of Arafat, because the time of the ifada is then. As for before, the apparent meaning of the wording does not require it, and it is necessary for it to be from the day of tarwiyah when arriving in Mina. Sixth: They differed regarding the wording of the takbir. The well-known Maliki school of thought is that one should say three takbirs after each prayer. This was narrated by Ziyad ibn Ziyad on the authority of Malik. There is a narration in the school of thought: After the three takbirs, one should say: There is no god but God, God is greater, and to God be praise. In the summary, on the authority of Malik: God is greater, God is greater, there is no god but God, and God is greater, God is greater, and to God be praise. The Almighty’s saying: But whoever hastens to leave within two days, there is no sin upon him. There are twenty-one issues in it: The first: The Almighty’s saying: So whoever hastens: Hastening here is never except at the end of the day, and likewise on the third day, because the time for stoning on those days is only after noon, and they agreed that on the Day of Sacrifice no one should be stoned except Jamrat al-Aqabah, because the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, did not stone any other Jamrat on the Day of Sacrifice, and its time is from sunrise to noon, and they also agreed that the time for stoning the Jamrat on the days of Tashreeq is after noon to sunset, and they differed regarding the one who stoned Jamrat al-Aqabah before dawn or after dawn before sunrise, so Malik, Abu Hanifa, Ahmad and Ishaq said: It is permissible to stone it after dawn before dawn appears, and it is not permissible to stone it before dawn, so if he stoned it before dawn he repeats it, and Abu Hanifa and his companions said likewise: It is not permissible to stone it, and Ahmad and Ishaq said the same, and a group permitted stoning before dawn. It was narrated on the authority of Asma’ bint Abi Bakr that she used to stone at night and say: We used to do this during the time of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace. Narrated by Abu Dawud. This statement was narrated on the authority of Ata’, Ibn Abi Malekah, and Ikrimah ibn Khalid. Ash-Shafi’i said the same when the stoning is after midnight. A group said: He should not stone until the sun rises. This was said by Mujahid, An-Nakha’i, and Ath-Thawri. Abu Thawr said: If he stoned it before sunrise, then if they differed about it, it is not valid. If they agreed, or there was a Sunnah in it, it is valid. Abu ‘Umar said: As for the statement of Ath-Thawri and those who followed him, his proof is that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, stoned the Jamarat after sunrise and said: Learn from me your rituals. Ibn al-Mundhir said: The Sunnah is not to throw stones until after sunrise, and throwing stones before dawn is not sufficient. If he throws stones, he must repeat it, because the one who does so is disobeying the Sunnah of the Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace, for his nation. And whoever throws stones after sunrise does not have to repeat it, because I do not know of anyone who said that it is not sufficient for him. Second - Muammar narrated that Hisham bin Urwa told me on the authority of his father who said: “The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, ordered Umm Salamah to go to Mecca on the Day of Sacrifice, and it was her day.” Abu Omar said: There is disagreement about Hisham regarding this hadith. A group narrated it on the authority of Hisham on the authority of his father, as a mursal, as Muammar narrated it. Others narrated it on the authority of Hisham on the authority of his father on the authority of Aisha, may God be pleased with her, that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, ordered Umm Salamah to do that, as a mursal. And others narrated it on the authority of Hisham on the authority of his father on the authority of Zainab bint Abi Salamah on the authority of Umm Salamah with a chain of transmission also, and all of them are trustworthy, and it indicates that she threw the pebbles at the Jamarat in Mina before dawn, because the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, ordered her to go to Mecca on the Day of Sacrifice, and this would not have happened unless she had thrown the pebbles at Mina at night before dawn, and God knows best. And Abu Dawud narrated it, he said: Harun bin Abdullah told us, he said: Ibn Abi Fadik told us on the authority of Ad-Dahhak bin Uthman on the authority of Hisham bin Urwah, on the authority of his father on the authority of Aisha, may God be pleased with her, that she said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, sent Umm Salamah on the night of Sacrifice, and she threw the pebbles at the Jamarat before dawn, then she sucked her saliva and performed the Ifadah, and that was the day when the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, was with her, and if it is proven, then throwing pebbles at night is permissible for whoever does it, and the choice is from sunrise to noon. Abu Omar said: They agreed that the time of choice in throwing pebbles at Jamarat Al-Aqabah is from sunrise to noon, and they agreed that if he threw them before sunset on the Day of Sacrifice, then he has done so. It is sufficient for him and nothing is upon him, except Malik, who said: It is recommended for him if he leaves the Jamrat al-Aqabah until evening, to shed blood and bring it from the sanctuary. They differed about the one who did not throw it until the sun set, so he threw it at night or the next day. Malik said: He must offer a blood sacrifice. He argued that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, set a time for throwing the Jamrat, which is the Day of Sacrifice. So whoever throws it after sunset has thrown it after its time has passed, and whoever does something in the Hajj after its time has a blood sacrifice. Al-Shafi’i said: He does not have a blood sacrifice. This is the opinion of Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, and Abu Thawr said the same, because “the questioner said to the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace: O Messenger of God, I threw it after evening, so he said: There is no blame.” Malik said: Whoever forgets to throw the Jamrat until evening, let him throw it at any time he remembers of the night or day, just as he prays at any time he remembers, and he should only throw what he missed specifically. If it is one Jamrat, he throws it, then throws whatever Jamrat he threw after it, because the order in the Jamrat is obligatory, so it is not permissible to start in Throwing a pebble until the first pebble is completed, like the rak’ahs of prayer. This is the well-known view of the school of thought. It has been said that the order is not obligatory for the validity of the throwing, but rather if the entire throwing is done at the time of performance, it is sufficient. Third: If the days of stoning have passed, then there is no stoning. If he remembers after he sets out while he is in Mecca or after he leaves it, then he must offer a sacrifice. Whether he left out all the Jamarat, or one Jamarat from it, or a pebble from a Jamarat until the days of Mina have passed, then he must offer a blood sacrifice. Abu Hanifa said: If he leaves out all the Jamarat, then he must offer a blood sacrifice. If he leaves out one Jamarat, then he must feed a poor person half a Sa’ for each pebble from the Jamarat, until he reaches a blood sacrifice, in which case he must feed as much as he wants, except for the Jamarat al-Aqaba, in which case he must offer a blood sacrifice. Al-Awza’i said: He must give charity if he leaves out a handful. Al-Thawri said: He must feed for one, two, or three pebbles. If he leaves out four or more, then he must offer a blood sacrifice. Al-Layth said: There is a blood sacrifice for one pebble, and this is one of the two opinions of al-Shafi’i. The other opinion, which is the well-known, is that there is a mudd of food for one pebble, two mudds for two pebbles, and three pebbles, there is a blood sacrifice. Fourth: According to everyone, there is no way to throw the pebbles that he missed during the days of Tashreeq until the sun sets at the end of them, and that is the fourth day of the days of sacrifice, which is the third day of the days of Tashreeq, but blood or feeding the poor is sufficient for him according to what we mentioned. Fifth: It is not permissible to spend the night in Mecca or elsewhere, other than in Mina, on the nights of Tashreeq, because that is not permissible according to everyone except for the shepherds and those in charge of providing water from the family of Abbas. Malik said: Whoever does not spend the night in Mina on a night other than the shepherds and those in charge of providing water, then he must offer a blood sacrifice. Al-Bukhari narrated on the authority of Ibn Umar. “Al-Abbas asked the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, for permission to spend the nights of Mina in Mecca in order to provide water for the Hajj pilgrims, and he gave him permission.” Ibn Abd al-Barr said: Al-Abbas used to oversee the watering and take care of it, and he would provide the pilgrims with its drink during the season. Therefore, he was given permission to spend the night in Mina, just as he gave permission to camel herders because of their need to graze their camels and their necessity to take them out to pastures far from Mina. Mina was named Mina because of the blood that is shed there. Ibn Abbas said: It was named Mina because Gabriel said to Adam, peace be upon him: Wish. He said: Wish for Paradise. So it was named Mina. He said: It was named Jam’ because Eve and Adam, peace be upon them, met there. Jam’ is also Muzdalifah, which is the sacred monument, as mentioned above. Sixth: The jurists agreed that spending the nights of Mina in Mina for the pilgrim other than those who were permitted to spend the nights of Mina is one of the rituals and rites of Hajj. The view requires that every pilgrim who misses his ritual must offer a blood sacrifice, by analogy with the rest of Hajj and its rituals. In Al-Muwatta’, Malik narrated from Nafi’ from Ibn Umar who said: Umar said: No pilgrim should spend the nights of Mina beyond the Aqaba. The Aqaba behind which Umar forbade anyone from spending the nights of Mina is the Aqaba at the Jamarat that people throw stones at on the Day of Sacrifice, which is near Mecca. It was narrated by Ibn Nafi’ from Malik in Al-Mabsut. He said: Malik said: Whoever spends the nights of Mina beyond it must pay a ransom, because he spent the nights of Mina outside of Mina, and it is a permissible overnight stay in Hajj. So the blood sacrifice is required for leaving it, like spending the night in Muzdalifah. And with the ransom here according to Malik is the sacrificial animal. Malik said: It is a sacrificial animal that is driven from the permissible area to the Haram. Seventh: Malik narrated on the authority of Abdullah bin Abi Bakr bin Muhammad bin Amr bin Hazm on the authority of his father, “that Abu al-Badah bin Asim bin Adi informed him that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, gave permission to camel herders to stay outside Mina and throw stones on the Day of Sacrifice, then throw stones on the next day, and the day after the next day for two days, then throw stones on the Day of Departure.” Abu Omar said: Malik did not say that this hadith is based on it. He used to say: They throw stones on the Day of Sacrifice - meaning Jamrat al-Aqabah - then they do not throw stones the next day. If it is the day after the next day, which is the second of the days of Tashreeq, which is the day on which the group of people who want to hasten or who are permitted to hasten should throw stones for the two days of that day and the day before it, because they are making up what was due on them, and no one should make up anything with him until after it is obligatory on him. This is the meaning of what Malik explained this hadith with in his Muwatta’. Others say: There is nothing wrong with all of that according to what is in the hadith of Malik, because they are all days of throwing stones. Rather, according to Malik, it is not permissible for the shepherds to advance the throwing because it is not permissible for non-shepherds to throw any of the stones on the days of Tashreeq before noon. If they throw before noon, they repeat it. They do not have to advance it, but they are permitted to do so on the second to third day. Ibn Abd al-Barr said: What Malik said on this issue is found in the narration of Ibn Jurayj, who said: Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr ibn Muhammad ibn Amr ibn Hazm informed me on the authority of his father that Abu al-Badah ibn Asim ibn Adi informed him that the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, permitted the shepherds to take turns, so they throw stones on the Day of Sacrifice, then leave a day and a night and then throw stones the next day. Our scholars said: The throwing of the third Jamarat is dropped for the one who is in a hurry. Ibn Abi Razin said: He throws it on the first day of departure when he wants to hurry. Ibn Al-Mawaz said: The one who is in a hurry throws twenty-one pebbles in two days, each Jamarat with seven pebbles, so his total throwing becomes forty-nine pebbles, because he threw seven pebbles at Jamarat Al-Aqabah on the Day of Sacrifice. Ibn Al-Mundhir said: The throwing of the third day is dropped. Eighth: Malik narrated on the authority of Yahya bin Saeed on the authority of Ata bin Abi Rabah that he heard him mention that he permitted shepherds to throw stones at night. He said, In the early times. Al-Baji said: “His statement in the early times necessitates that it be general in the time of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, because it was the first time of this legislation. Based on this, it is mursal, and it is possible that he meant by it the first time that Ata was aware of, so it is suspended.” And God knows best. I said: It is attributed to: The hadith of Amr ibn Shu`ayb on the authority of his father on the authority of his grandfather on the authority of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, was narrated by al-Daraqutni and others. We have mentioned it in al-Muqtabas in the explanation of the Muwatta` of Malik ibn Anas. They were permitted to throw stones at night because it is easier for them and more cautious in what they are trying to do with grazing camels, because the night is a time when they do not graze or spread out, so they throw stones at that time. They differed about the one who missed throwing stones until the sun sets. `Ata` said: There is no throwing stones at night except for camel herders, but not for merchants. It was narrated on the authority of Ibn `Umar that he said: Whoever missed throwing stones until the sun sets should not throw stones until the sun rises the next day. Ahmad and Ishaq said the same. Malik said: If he leaves it during the day, he throws them at night, and he must offer a blood sacrifice according to the narration of Ibn al-Qasim. It was not mentioned in the Muwatta` that he must offer a blood sacrifice. Al-Shafi`i, Abu Thawr, Ya`qub and Muhammad said: If he forgets to throw stones until evening, he throws them and there is no blood sacrifice on him. Al-Hasan al-Basri permitted throwing stones at night, and Abu Hanifa said: He throws them and there is nothing on him. If he does not remember it until the next day, he must throw it and must offer a blood sacrifice. Al-Thawri said: If he delays throwing it until the night, forgetfully or intentionally, he must offer a blood sacrifice. I said: As for the one who throws stones at a camel herder or a water-carrier at night, no blood money is due, according to the hadith. But if he is not one of them, then looking requires blood money, but only if he did it intentionally, and God knows best. Ninth: It has been proven that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, threw the pebbles at Jamrat al-Aqaba on the Day of Sacrifice on his mount. Malik and others preferred that the one who threw them should be riding. Ibn Umar, Ibn al-Zubayr, and Salim threw them while they were walking. He threw twenty-one pebbles every day of the three, saying Allahu Akbar with each pebble. He would face the Kaaba while throwing, and he would arrange the pebbles and gather them together, not separate them or turn them over. He would start with the first pebble and throw seven pebbles at it, not placing them down. This is what Malik, al-Shafi’i, Abu Thawr, and the people of opinion said. If he threw them down, it is permissible according to the people of opinion. Ibn al-Qasim said: It is not sufficient in both of the two opinions, and this is the correct view, because the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, would throw them, and they would not throw two pebbles or more at once. If he did, he would count them as one pebble. When he finished, he would advance in front of them and stand for a long time to supplicate with whatever he could. Then he would throw the second, which is the middle one, and turn away from it to the left in the valley, and he would stand for a long time at it to supplicate. Then he throws the third one at the place of Jamrat al-Aqaba with seven pebbles also, throwing them from below it and not stopping at it, and if he throws them from above it, it is sufficient for him, and he says Allahu Akbar in all of that with every pebble he throws, and the Sunnah of dhikr in stoning the Jamarat is to say Allahu Akbar without any other dhikr, and he throws it walking unlike the Jamrat on the Day of Sacrifice, and all of this is a hadith narrated by al-Nasa’i and al-Daraqutni on the authority of al-Zuhri that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, “When he threw the Jamarat that is next to the mosque - the mosque of Mina - he would throw it with seven pebbles, saying Allahu Akbar every time he threw a pebble, then he would advance in front of it and stand facing the qiblah, raising his hands and supplicating, and he would stand for a long time, then he would come to the second Jamarat and throw it with seven pebbles, saying Allahu Akbar every time he threw a pebble, then he would go down to the left from what is next to the valley and stand facing the qiblah, raising his hands and supplicating, then he would come to the Jamarat that is next to al-Aqaba and throw it with a rosary of pebbles, saying Allahu Akbar every time he threw a pebble, then he would turn away and not stand.” Then, Al-Zuhri said: I heard Salim bin Abdullah narrating this on the authority of his father on the authority of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace. He said: And Ibn Omar used to do it. Al-Darqutni’s wording. Tenth: The ruling on the Jamarat is that it should be pure, not impure, and not from what was thrown. If he throws what was thrown, it is not permissible for him according to Malik. Ibn al-Qasim said about it: If it is with a single pebble, it is permissible for him. It was revealed to Ibn al-Qasim, so he issued a fatwa to him on this. Eleventh: The scholars recommended taking it from Muzdalifah, not from the pebbles of the mosque. If he takes more than what he needs and it remains in his hand after throwing, he should bury it and not throw it away. This was stated by Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others. Twelfth: It is not washed according to the majority, contrary to what Tawus said. It has been narrated that if he did not wash the impure pebbles or threw what he had thrown, he has done wrong and it is sufficient for him. Ibn al-Mundhir said: It is disliked to throw what he had thrown, and it is sufficient if he threw it, because I do not know of anyone who made it obligatory for the one who did that to repeat it, and we do not know in any of the reports that came from the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, that he washed the pebbles or ordered that they be washed. We have narrated from Tawus that he used to wash them. Thirteenth: Neither mud nor anything other than stones are acceptable for the Jamarat. This is the opinion of Al-Shafi’i, Ahmad and Ishaq. The People of Opinion said: It is permissible to use dry clay, and likewise anything thrown from the ground is acceptable. Al-Thawri said: Whoever throws with pottery or mud does not repeat the throwing. Ibn Al-Mundhir said: Throwing is not acceptable except with pebbles, because “the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: ‘Use pebbles for throwing,’ and the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, threw pebbles.” Fourteenth: There is a difference of opinion regarding the size of the pebbles. Al-Shafi’i said: It should be smaller than the length and width of a fingertip. Abu Thawr and the people of opinion said: It should be the size of a throwing pebble. We have narrated on the authority of Ibn Umar that he used to throw pebbles at the Jamrah with the size of sheep dung. There is no meaning to Malik’s statement: I prefer something larger than that, because the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, prescribed throwing pebbles the size of a throwing pebble. It is permissible to throw with something that is called a pebble, and following the Sunnah is better, as Ibn al-Mundhir said. I said: It is the correct one and it is not permissible to contradict it for the one who is guided and follows his example. Al-Nasa’i narrated: “On the authority of Ibn Abbas, he said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said to me on the morning of Al-Aqabah while he was on his mount: ‘Bring me the pebbles.’ So I picked up pebbles for him, which were pebbles for throwing stones. When I put them in his hand, he said: ‘With the likes of these. And beware of extremism in religion, for it was extremism in religion that destroyed those who came before you.’ So his statement: ‘And beware of extremism in religion,’ indicates the undesirability of throwing the large pebbles, and that this is from extremism, and God knows best.” Fifteenth: If someone has a pebble left in his hand and does not know which pebble it is, he should make it one of the first, and then throw the middle and last pebbles. If it takes a long time, he should start all of them again. Sixteenth: Malik, Al-Shafi’i, Abdul-Malik, Abu Thawr and the people of opinion said about someone who performs one Jamrah after another: unless he throws it in succession. Al-Hasan, Ata’ and some people said: It is sufficient for him. Some people used as evidence the saying of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace: Whoever performs one ritual before another, there is no blame on him. He said: This does not happen to more than one man who has prayers or fasts combined and he performs some before others. The first is more cautious, and God knows best. Seventeenth: They differed regarding throwing stones at the sick person and throwing stones on his behalf. Malik said: He throws stones on behalf of the sick person and the boy who is not able to throw stones, and the sick person should be careful when throwing stones at them, so he should say seven takbirs for each pebble, and he must offer a sacrificial animal. If the sick person recovers during the days of throwing stones, he throws stones on his own behalf, and he must also offer a blood sacrifice according to Malik. Al-Hasan, Al-Shafi’i, Ahmad, Ishaq, and the people of opinion said: He throws stones on behalf of the sick person, and they did not mention a sacrificial animal. There is no disagreement regarding the boy who is not able to throw stones, that he throws stones on his behalf, and Ibn Umar used to do that. Eighteenth: Al-Darqutni narrated on the authority of Abu Saeed Al-Khudri, who said: We said, O Messenger of God, these are the pebbles that are thrown every year, and we think that they are decreasing. He said: No lifting from them is accepted, and if it were not for that, you would have seen them like mountains. Nineteenth: Ibn al-Mundhir said: The scholars agreed that whoever wants to leave from the pilgrim from Mina, heading to his country outside the sanctuary and not residing in Mecca in the first departure, should leave after the sun has passed its zenith if he has stoned the Jamarat on the day following the Day of Sacrifice before evening, because God Almighty said: But whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him. So whoever wants to leave should leave as long as there is some time left in the day. We have narrated from al-Nakha’i and al-Hasan that they said: Whoever is overtaken by the afternoon prayer while he is in Mina on the second day of the days of Tashreeq should not leave until the next day. Ibn al-Mundhir said: It is possible that they said that as a recommendation, and we say the first opinion, based on the apparent meaning of the Book and the Sunnah. Al-Muwaffiyah twentieth: They differed about the people of Mecca, whether they should set out for the first group. We narrated on the authority of Omar bin Al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, that he said: Whoever among the people wants to set out for the first group, except for the family of Khuzaymah, they should not set out except for the second group. Ahmad bin Hanbal used to say: I do not like for whoever sets out for the first group to stay in Mecca. He said: The people of Mecca are lighter. Ahmad and Ishaq made the meaning of Omar bin Al-Khattab’s statement except for the family of Khuzaymah to be that they are the people of the sanctuary. Malik used to say about the people of Mecca, whoever has an excuse, he may hasten in two days. If he wants to make things easier for himself from the matter of Hajj, then no. So he saw hastening for those who have not yet reached their destination. A group said: The verse is general, and the concession is for all people, the people of Mecca and others. He meant the one who leaves Mina to stay in Mecca or to go to his country. Ata’ said: It is for all people in general. Ibn Al-Mundhir said: It is similar to the doctrine of Al-Shafi’i, and we say the same. Ibn Abbas, Al-Hasan, Ikrimah, Mujahid, Qatadah, and Al-Nakha’i said: Whoever sets out for the first group The second day of the numbered days, there is no blame, and whoever delays until the third, there is no blame, so the meaning of the verse is that all of that is permissible, and it was expressed with this division as a concern and emphasis, since there were some Arabs who condemned the one who was hasty and vice versa, so the verse was revealed lifting the wing in all of that, and Ali bin Abi Talib, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Masoud, and Ibrahim Al-Nakha’i also said: The meaning of whoever is hasty is forgiven, and whoever is late is forgiven, and they used as evidence the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: Whoever performs Hajj to this House and does not utter obscenities or commit sins, will emerge from his sins as on the day his mother bore him, so his saying: There is no sin upon him, is a general negation and an absolute acquittal. Mujahid also said: The meaning of the verse is that whoever is hasty or late, there is no sin upon him until the next year, and a trace was attributed to this saying, and Abu Al-Aaliyah said about the verse: There is no sin upon him for whoever fears God for the rest of his life, and the pilgrim is forgiven absolutely, meaning his sin is completely gone if he fears God for the rest of his life, and Abu Salih and others said: The meaning of the verse is there is no sin upon whoever fears killing game And what he must avoid during Hajj. He also said: Whoever is pious during his Hajj and performs it completely will be accepted. Twenty-first: (from) in His statement: So whoever hastens is raised by the subject, and the predicate, there is no sin upon him, and it is permissible in other than the Qur’an, there is no sin upon them, because the meaning of (from) is a group, as the Almighty said: And among them are those who listen to you (Yunus 10:42) and likewise And whoever delays, there is no sin upon him, and the lam in His statement: For whoever fears God, is related to forgiveness, the meaning is forgiveness for whoever fears God, and this is according to the interpretation of Ibn Masoud and Ali. Qatada said: It was mentioned to us that Ibn Masoud said: Forgiveness was only made for whoever fears God after his departure from Hajj from all sins, and Al-Akhfash said: The meaning is that for whoever fears God, and some of them said: For whoever fears God, meaning killing game during ihram and in the sanctuary, and it was said that the meaning is permission for whoever fears God, this was narrated from Ibn Omar, and it was said: Safety is for whoever fears God, and it was said: It is related to the remembrance in the statement of the Almighty: And remember, meaning the remembrance, and Salim bin Abdullah read (there is no sin upon him) with a connection The letter Alif is used to make it easier, and Arabs may use it. The poet said: If I don't fight, cover me with a burqa. Then God Almighty commanded piety and mentioned the gathering and standing.
2:204: God Almighty says: And among the people is he whose speech about worldly life pleases you, and he calls God to witness as to what is in his heart, yet he is the most hostile of opponents. There are three issues: The first: The Almighty’s saying: And among the people is he whose speech pleases you, when He mentioned those whose ambitions were limited to this world, in His saying: And among the people is he who says, ‘Our Lord, give us in this world,’ and the believers who asked for the best of the two abodes, He mentioned the hypocrites, because they showed faith and concealed disbelief. Al-Suddi and other commentators said: It was revealed about Al-Akhns bin Shuraiq, whose name was my father, and Al-Akhns was a nickname given to him, because he withdrew on the day of Badr with three hundred men from his allies from Banu Zuhrah from fighting with the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, as will be explained in (Al-Imran), and he was a man of sweet speech and appearance, so he came after that to the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, and showed Islam and said: God knows that I am truthful, then he fled after that, and passed by a farm belonging to a group of Muslims and by donkeys, so he burned the farms and hamstrung the donkeys. Al-Mahdawi said: And about him were revealed: And do not obey every worthless swearer, a slanderer, going about with calumnies (Nun: 10, 11) and Woe to every slanderer and backbiter (Al-Humazah: 1), he said: Ibn Atiyah: It has never been proven that Al-Akhns converted to Islam. Ibn Abbas said: It was revealed about a group of hypocrites who spoke about those who were killed in the Battle of Raji’: Asim bin Thabit, Khubayb, and others. They said: The smell of these people, they did not stay in their homes, nor did they deliver the message of their master. So this verse was revealed about the characteristics of the hypocrites. Then he mentioned those who were martyred in the Battle of Raji’ in His statement: And among the people is he who sells himself, seeking the pleasure of God (al-Baqarah 2:207). Qatada, Mujahid, and a group of scholars said: It was revealed about every hidden disbelief, hypocrisy, lie, or harm, while he shows with his tongue the opposite of that, so it is general, and it is similar to what was mentioned in Al-Tirmidhi that in some of the books of God Almighty: “Indeed, among the worshippers of God are a people whose tongues are sweeter than honey and whose hearts are more bitter than aloes. They dress for people the skins of sheep out of softness. They buy the world with religion. God Almighty says: My father is deceived, and Ali They dare, so I swear by Me that I will make a trial for them that will make the forbearing among them an animal.” The meaning of and God bears witness is that he says: God knows that I say the truth. Ibn Muhaisin read: and God bears witness to what is in his heart with the opening of the ya’ and the ha’ in bears witness “God” in the nominative case. The meaning is, I am amazed by your statement: God knows from him the opposite of what he said. Its proof is His statement: And God bears witness that the hypocrites are liars (al-Munafiqun 63:1).
