The scholars of the principles of jurisprudence mentioned in this verse that when Abraham, peace be upon him, was described by God Almighty with what is His attribute of giving life and trustworthiness, but it is a matter for Him in reality and metaphorically, Abraham, peace be upon him, intended the reality, and Nimrod was frightened by the metaphor and deceived his people. So Abraham surrendered to him in a dialectical manner and moved with him from the example and came to him with a matter in which there is no metaphor. So the one who disbelieved was dumbfounded, meaning his argument was cut off and he was unable to say that I am the one who brought it from the east, because people of understanding would deny him. Second: This verse indicates the permissibility of calling a disbeliever a king if God has given him kingship, glory and elevation in this world. It indicates the establishment of debate, argument and establishing proof. There is much of this in the Qur’an and Sunnah for those who ponder it. God the Most High said: “Say: ‘Produce your proof, if you should be truthful.’” (al-Baqarah 2:111), Indeed, with you is some authority. (Yunus 10:68), meaning some proof. He described the dispute between Abraham, peace be upon him, and his people and his response to them regarding the worship of idols, as in Surat Al-Anbiya’ and others. He said in the story of Noah, peace be upon him: “They said: ‘O Noah, you have disputed with us and prolonged your dispute with us.’” (Hud 11:32), the verses up to His saying: And I am innocent of what you commit. (Hud 11:35), and likewise the argument of Moses with Pharaoh and other verses. It is all a teaching from God the Most High about questioning, answering and argumentation in religion, because the difference between truth and falsehood does not appear except by the appearance of the proof of truth and the refutation of the proof of falsehood. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, argued with the People of the Book and their people after the argument, as will be explained in Al Imran. Adam and Moses argued and Adam defeated him with the argument. The companions of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, argued on the day of Saqifah and pushed each other and decided and debated until the truth was revealed to its people. They debated after the pledge of allegiance to Abu Bakr regarding the apostates, and other things that are often mentioned. In the statement of God Almighty: Then why do you argue about that of which you have no knowledge? (Al Imran 3:66), there is evidence that arguing with knowledge is permissible and common for those who reflect. Al-Muzani, the companion of Al-Shafi’i, said: It is the right of debate that God Almighty is intended by it and that what is clear from it is accepted. They said: Debate is not valid and the truth is not revealed between the debaters until they are close or equal in one level of religion, reason, understanding and fairness, otherwise it is hypocrisy and stubbornness. Readings: Ali bin Abi Talib read (alam tar) with the jazm of the ra’, and the majority with its movement, and the ya’ was deleted for the jazm, (that God gave him the kingdom) in the accusative case, meaning because God gave him, or because God gave him, and the majority of the readers read (that I revive) by dropping the alif after the nun from (ana) in the connection, and Nafi’ and Ibn Abi Uways confirmed it, if you encounter a hamza in the entire Qur’an except in the saying of God the Almighty I am only a warner (al-A’raf 7:188), then he drops it in this place like the rest of the readers due to its scarcity, as it did not occur from it in the Qur’an except three places, he treated it as something after which there is no hamza due to its scarcity, so he deleted the alif in the connection. The grammarians said: The pronoun of the speaker is the noun in which there is a hamza and a nun, so if you say: ana or that, then the alif and the ha’ are to show the movement in the pause, and if the word is connected to something they are dropped, because the thing that the word is connected to takes the place of the alif, so you do not say: ana fa’alt by confirming The letter Alif is an exception in poetry, as the poet said: I am the sword of the tribe, so know me as Hamid, the one who has scattered the hump Al-Nahhas said: Nafi` confirmed the alif and read I give life and cause death and there is no basis for that. Makki said: The alif is redundant according to the Basrans, and the hidden noun according to them is the hamza and the nun, and the alif was added for emphasis. It was said: It was added for stopping to show the movement of the nun, and the noun according to the Kufians is ana in its entirety, so Nafi` confirmed the alif according to their saying according to the original, and the alif was only deleted from its deletion for ease, and because the fatha indicates it. Al-Jawhari said: As for their saying ana, it is a hidden noun and it is for the speaker alone, and it was built on the fatha to differentiate it from an which is a letter that erects the verb, and the last alif is only to show the movement in stopping, so if it is in the middle of the speech it is dropped except in a bad language as he said: I am the sword of the tribe, so know me as Hamid, the one who has scattered the hump The man was astonished, dazed, and dazed if he was cut off and remained silent, perplexed, from An-Nahhas and others. At-Tabari said: It was narrated from some Arabs in this meaning (baht) with the opening of the ba’ and the ha’. Ibn Jinni said: Abu Haywah read: (Fabhat al-Dhi kufr) with the opening of the ba’ and the damma of the ha’, and it is a dialect of (baht) with the kasra of the ha’. He said: Ibn Al-Sameeq read (Fabhat) with the opening of the ba’ and the ha’ with the meaning of (Fabhat Ibrahim al-Dhi kufr), so the one who is in the accusative case, he said: It is possible that bahat with the opening of the ba’ is a dialect of bahat. He said: Abu Al-Hasan Al-Akhfash narrated the reading (Fabhat) with the kasra of the ha’ like gharaq and dahash, he said: And the majority with the damma of the ha’. Ibn Atiyyah said: Some people interpreted the reading of those who read (Fabhat) with the opening of the ba’ that it means cursing and slandering, and that Nimrod is the one who cursed when he was cut off and he had no way out.
2:259: The Almighty said: "Or like the one who passed by a town and it was desolate on its roofs" Or for the purpose of conjunction based on the meaning and the estimation according to Al-Kisa'i and Al-Farra: Have you seen like the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord, or like the one who passed by a town? Al-Mubarrad said: The meaning is, have you not seen the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord, have you not seen who he is! Like the one who passed by a town. So he implied in the speech who he is. Abu Sufyan bin Hussein read or like the one who passed by with the opening of the waw, which is the waw of conjunction with the alif of interrogation entered on it, which means confirmation. The village was called a village because the people gathered in it, from their saying: I gathered the water, meaning I collected it, and it was mentioned before. Sulayman bin Buraydah, Najiyah bin Ka'b, Qatadah, Ibn Abbas, Al-Rabi', Ikrimah, and Al-Dahhak said that the one who passed by the village is Uzair. Wahb bin Munabbih, Abdullah bin Ubaid bin Umair, and Abdullah bin Bakr bin Mudar said: He is Jeremiah and he was a prophet. Ibn Ishaq said: Jeremiah is Al-Khidr, and Al-Naqqash narrated it on the authority of Wahb ibn Munabbih. Ibn Atiyyah said: This is as you see, unless it is a name that coincides with a name, because Al-Khidr was a contemporary of Moses, and the one who passed by the village was after him by some time from the tribe of Aaron, according to what Wahb ibn Munabbih narrated. I said: If Al-Khidr is Jeremiah, then it is not far-fetched that he is him, because Al-Khidr has been alive since the time of Moses until now, according to the correct view, as will be explained in Surat Al-Kahf. If he died before this story, then the statement of Ibn Atiyyah is correct, and God knows best. An-Nahhas and Makki narrated from Mujahid that he was an unnamed man from the Children of Israel. An-Naqqash said: It is said that he is the servant of Lot, peace be upon him. Al-Suhayli narrated from Al-Qutbi that he is Isaiah according to one of his two statements. The one who revived it after its destruction was Kushk the Persian. The village mentioned is Jerusalem according to Wahb bin Munabbih, Qatada, Ar-Rabi bin Anas and others. He said: He was coming from Egypt and his food and drink mentioned were green figs and grapes and a cup of wine. It was also said: juice. It was also said: a small water container was his drink. The one who evacuated Jerusalem at that time was Bukhtanasr, who was the governor of Iraq for Al-Harasib, then for Istasib bin Lahrasib, the father of Ispandiad. Al-Naqqash narrated that some people said: It is Al-Mu'tafika. Ibn Abbas said in the narration of Abu Salih: Nebuchadnezzar invaded the Children of Israel and captured many people from them and brought them, including Uzair bin Sharkhiya, who was one of the scholars of the Children of Israel. He brought them to Babylon. One day, he went out on some errand to the Monastery of Heraclius on the banks of the Tigris. He dismounted under the shade of a tree while riding his donkey. He tied the donkey under the shade of the tree and then went around the village. He did not see any inhabitants in it, and it was completely deserted. He said: How can God revive this after its death? It was said: It is the village from which thousands left, fearing death. This was said by Ibn Zayd. Ibn Zayd also said that the people who left their homes, thousands, fearing death, and God said to them, "Die." A man passed by them and they were rotten, sprouting bones. He stopped and looked and said: How can God revive this after its death? So God caused him to die for a hundred years. Ibn Atiyah said: This statement by Ibn Zayd contradicts the words of the verse, as the verse only includes an empty village with no inhabitants in it, and the reference with this is to the village. And its revival is only through construction and the presence of buildings and inhabitants. Wahb ibn Munabbih, Qatada, Ad-Dahhak, Ar-Rabi’ and Ikrimah said: The village is Jerusalem when it was destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar the Babylonian. And in the long hadith where the Children of Israel caused the events, Jeremiah or Ezra stopped at the village and it was like a great hill in the middle of Jerusalem, because Nebuchadnezzar ordered his soldiers to move the dirt to it until he made it like a mountain, and Jeremiah saw the houses whose walls had fallen on their roofs, so he said: How can God revive these after their death? Arish: the roof of a house. Everything that is prepared to provide shade or shelter is an arish, and from it is the arish of the grapevine, and from it is the saying of God the Almighty: And of what they erect. Al-Suddi said: He says it is fallen on its roof, meaning the roof fell and then the walls fell on it, and Al-Tabari chose it. And someone other than Al-Suddi said: Its meaning is empty of people and the houses are standing, and empty means vacant, and the origin of emptiness is emptiness, it is said: the house was khawt and khawyt khawwa khawwa extended and khawya: it was eaten, and likewise if it fell, and from it is the saying of God the Almighty: Then those are their houses, empty because of what they did wrong meaning empty, and it is said fallen, as He said: So they are empty on their thrones meaning fallen on their roof. Emptiness is hunger because the stomach is empty of food. The woman was khawt and khawyt also khawwa, meaning her stomach was empty at birth. And khawyt for her khawyat if you made a khawyah for her to eat and it is food. And khawy is the flat stomach of the ground on Fa’il. The camel prostrates when its belly is exposed to the ground while kneeling, and so does the man when he prostrates. God the Almighty said: How will God revive this after its death? Its meaning is from which path and by what reason? The apparent meaning of the wording is a question about reviving the village with construction and inhabitants, as is said now about ruined cities that are unlikely to be rebuilt and inhabited: How will this be rebuilt after its destruction? So this is as if this is the longing of someone who is standing and considering his city in which he knew his family and loved ones. And he gave him an example in himself of something greater than what he asked about, and the example that he gave him in himself may be that his question was only about reviving the dead of the sons of Adam, i.e. how will God revive its dead? At-Tabari narrated from some of them that he said: This statement was a doubt in God’s ability to revive! So that is why he gave him an example in himself. Ibn Atiyyah said: There is no doubt in God’s ability to revive a village by bringing construction to it, but doubt is conceivable from an ignorant person in the other aspect, and the correct thing is not to interpret the verse as doubt. The Almighty said: So God caused him to die for a hundred years. “A hundred” is an adverbial accusative. A year means a year. It is said: Years of floating which is an emphasis on the first, just as it is said: There was preoccupation between them. Al-Ajjaj said: Years of floating years have passed It is in the estimation a floating plural, except that it is not mentioned alone, because it is not a name but rather an emphasis, as stated by Al-Jawhari. Al-Naqqash said: The year is a source like the floating, this amount of time was named after it because it is a floating of the sun in the sky. And the floating is like the swimming, and God the Most High said: "Each in an orbit floats." Ibn Atiyah said: This is in the meaning of what Al-Naqqash said, and the year according to this is like the saying and the saying, and the apparent meaning of this death is that it is by removing the soul from the body. It was narrated in the stories of this verse that God the Most High sent to it a king from the kings to populate it and strive in that until its population was complete when the speaker was sent. It was said: When seventy years had passed since his death, God sent a great king from the kings of Persia called Kushk, and he populated it in thirty years. The Almighty’s saying: Then He resurrected him means He brought him back to life, and we have already discussed this. God the Almighty said: He said, ‘How long have you remained?’ There is a difference of opinion as to who said to him, How long have you remained? Some say, It was God, the Almighty, the Majestic. He did not say to him, If you are truthful, as the angels said, as mentioned above. It is also said, He heard a voice from the sky saying that to him. It is also said, Gabriel spoke to him. It is also said, A prophet. It is also said, A believing man from among those of his people who saw him when he died and lived until he was brought back to life. So he said to him, How long have you remained? I said: It is most apparent that the speaker is God, the Most High, because He said: And look at the bones - how We raise them up and then cover them with flesh Al-Bukhari and Muslim. And God knows best. The people of Kufa read kam labhat by assimilating the tha’ into the ta’ because of their proximity to it in articulation. Their articulation is from the tip of the tongue and the roots of the incisors and because they are both unvoiced. An-Nahhas said: It is better to pronounce it clearly because the articulation of the tha’ is different from the articulation of the ta’. It is said: This question was by the angel for the purpose of confirmation. kam is in the accusative case as an adverb. "He said, 'I stayed a day or part of a day.'" He only said this based on what he had and what he thought, and based on this he is not lying if he reported it. Similar to this is the statement of the People of al-Kahf 18:"They said, 'We stayed a day or part of a day.'" They only stayed three hundred and nine years - as will come - and they were not lying because they reported what they had, as if they had said: What we have and what we think is that we stayed a day or part of a day. Similar to this is the statement of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, in the story of Dhu al-Yadayn: I did not fall short and I did not forget. Some people say: It is a lie in the sense that there is a true lie in it, but he is not to be held accountable for it. Otherwise, lying is reporting something in a way that is different from what it is, and this does not differ based on knowledge or ignorance. This is clear in the view of the principles. Based on this, it is permissible to say: The prophets are not infallible from reporting something in a way that is different from what it is if it was not intentional, just as they are not infallible from forgetfulness and inattention. This is what is related to this verse, and the first statement is more correct. Ibn Jurayj, Qatadah, and al-Rabi’ said: God caused him to die in the morning, then he was sent before sunset, so he thought that this day was one, so he said: I stayed a day. Then he saw the rest of the sun and feared that he might be lying, so he said: Or part of a day. It was said: Rather, I stayed a hundred years. And he saw from the construction of the village, its trees, and its buildings what indicated that to him. God the Almighty said: Then look at your food, which is the figs he collected from the trees of the village he passed by. And your drink has not become stale. Ibn Masoud read: This is your food and your drink has not become stale. Talhah ibn Musarraf and others read: And look at your food and drink for a hundred years. The majority read with the ha’ in the connection, except for the two brothers, who delete it. There is no disagreement that the pause on it is with the ha’. Talhah ibn Musarraf also read: It has not become stale and look and assimilated the ta’ into the seen. According to the majority’s reading, the ha’ is original, and the damma was deleted for the jazm. It is derived from sunnah, meaning that the years have not changed it. Al-Jawhari said: “It is said: Sunun, and the sunnah is the same as “al-sanin,” and there are two opinions about its deficiency: one of them is the waw, and the other is the ha’. Its root is sanah like the forehead, because it is from sanahat an-nakhlah and tasnahat if the years come upon it. A palm tree sana’ means it bears one year and does not bear another, and sanaha also, some of the Ansar said: It is not a year of drought or a year of Rajab, but it is naked in the years of calamity. And I stayed with the Banu Fulan, I stayed with them, and I also stayed. And I hired him as a musanat and musanaha also. And in the diminutive saniya and saniha. An-Nahhas said: Whoever reads lam yatasna and look says in the diminutive: saniya and the alif is deleted for the jussive, and he stops on the ha and says: lam yatasnahu, the ha is to show the movement. Al-Mahdawi said: It is possible that its origin is from sanitu masanat, meaning I treated him year after year, or from sanahat with the ha, if it is from sanait then its origin is yatasanna so the alif was dropped for the jussive, and its origin is from the waw as evidenced by their saying sanawat and the ha in it is for the pause, and if it is from sanahat then the ha is the lam of the verb, and the origin of sanah according to this is sanah. And according to the first opinion sanwah. And it was said: It is from the water asan if it changes, and it should have been on this basis it is yatasna. Abu Amr Al-Shaibani: It is from his saying al-hama masnun so the meaning is it did not change. Glass, it is not like that, because his saying musnun does not mean it changes, but rather it means it is cast according to the year of the earth. Al-Mahdawi said: Its origin, according to Al-Shaibani, is yatasanna, then one of the two nuns was replaced with ya due to the dislike of doubling, so it became yatasanna, then the alif was dropped for the sake of jazm and the ha was added for the sake of sukoon. Mujahid said: lam yatasanna did not mean it stinks. Al-Nahhas said: The most correct thing that has been said about it is that it is from the year, meaning the years did not change it. It is possible that it is from the year and in drought, and from that is the saying of God Almighty: And We seized the people of Pharaoh with years and his saying, peace be upon him: O God, make them years like the years of Joseph. It is said: The people became barren, meaning they became dry. The meaning is that drought and famine did not change your food, or the years and decades did not change it, meaning it remained fresh and tender. God the Almighty said: And look at your donkey. Wahb ibn Munabbih and others said: Look at the connection of its bones and its revival, part by part. It is narrated that God revived it in this way until it became joined bones, then He clothed it with flesh until it became a complete donkey. Then an angel came to it and breathed the spirit into it, and the donkey stood up braying. This is the opinion of most of the commentators. It is narrated from Ad-Dahhak and Wahb ibn Munabbih also that they said: Rather, it was said to him: Look at your donkey standing in its tether, nothing has happened to it for a hundred years. The bones that he looked at were the bones of his own soul after God revived its eyes and head, while the rest of its body was dead. They said: And God blinded the eyes of Jeremiah and his donkey for this entire period. God the Almighty said: And We will make you a sign for the people. Al-Farra’ said: The waw was inserted in His statement And We will make you to indicate that it is a condition for a verb after it, meaning And We will make you a sign for the people, and to indicate the resurrection after death, We made that. If it is incorrect, the waw is made an inserted and redundant one. Al-A’mash said: The place where he is a sign is that he came as a young man in the same state as he was on the day he died, and he found his sons and grandsons old. Ikrimah: He was forty years old on the day he died. It was narrated on the authority of Ali, may God be pleased with him, that Uzair left his family and left his wife pregnant, and he was fifty years old, so God caused him to die for a hundred years, then He resurrected him and he returned to his family when he was fifty years old and he had a son after a hundred years, so his son was fifty years older than him. It was narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas that he said: When God revived Ezra, he rode his donkey and came to his camp. The people disapproved of him and they disapproved of him. He found in his house an old blind woman who had been their slave. Ezra left them when she was twenty years old. He said to her: Is this the house of Ezra? She said: Yes! Then she cried and said: Ezra parted from us such and such years ago! He said: I am Ezra. She said: We lost Ezra a hundred years ago. He said: God caused me to die for a hundred years and then resurrected me. She said: Ezra was the one whose prayers were answered for the sick and the afflicted, so he would recover, so pray to God to restore my sight. So he prayed to God and wiped her eyes with his hand and she recovered as if she had been freed from a shackle. She said: I bear witness that you are Ezra! Then she went to the leaders of the Children of Israel, among whom was the son of Ezra, an old man of one hundred and twenty-eight years, and his grandsons were old men. She said: O people, by God, this is Ezra! His son came to him with the people and his son said: My father had a black mole like a crescent moon between his shoulders. He looked at it and saw that it was Ezra. It was said: He came after everyone he knew had perished, so he was a sign for those of his people who were alive, as they were certain of his condition by hearing. Ibn Atiyyah said: In his death during this period and then his revival after that is the greatest sign, and his entire affair is a sign for the ages past, and there is no need to specify some of it over others. God the Almighty said: And look at the bones - how We resurrect them. The Kufians and Ibn Amir read it with a zay, and the rest read it with a ra’. Abaan narrated from Asim that We resurrect it with a fatha on the noon and a damma on the sheen and the ra’. Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, and Abu Haywah read it likewise. It was said: They are two languages for revival with one meaning, just as it is said: he returned and I returned it, the water subsided and I subsided it, and the animal lost and I lost it. However, what is known in the language is that God resurrected the dead, so they resurrected, meaning God revived them and they came to life. God the Almighty said: Then, if He wills, He will resurrect him. And resurrecting him is like spreading a garment. And resurrecting the dead, meaning he lived after death. Al-A’sha said: Until people say from what they saw, Oh, how strange is the dead man who spreads the report. So death is as if the bones and limbs are being folded, and revival is as if the limbs are being spread out to one another. As for the reading of nanshazha with a z, it means we raise it. Nashaz means that which is elevated from the ground. He said: You see the yearling fox in it, as if it were a well-dressed horse when it rises high. Al-Maki said: The meaning is: Look at the bones, how we raise some of them on top of others in the structure to revive them, because rising means rising, and from this comes the rebellious woman, who rises from the obedience of her husband, and from this is the saying of God the Almighty: And when it is said, ‘Arise,’ then rise meaning rise and join together. Also, the reading with the letter Ra’ means revival, and the bones do not come to life on their own until they join together, and the letter Zay is more appropriate for this meaning, as it means joining without revival. So what is described as revival is the man, not the bones on their own, and it is not said: This is a living bone, but rather the meaning is: Look at the bones, how we raise them from their places in the earth to the body of their owner to revive them. Al-Nakha’i read Nanshizuha with a fatha on the letter Noon and a damma on the letter Sheen and the letter Zay, and this was narrated from Ibn Abbas and Qatada. Abi bin Ka’b read Nanshiha with a Ya’. Clothing: what is covered of clothes, and meat is likened to it. Labid used it as a metaphor for Islam, saying: Until I acquired a garment of Islam The beginning of the Surah has been mentioned. God the Almighty said: And when it became clear to him, he said, ‘I know that God has power over all things.’ with the alif cut off. It has been narrated that God the Almighty revived part of him and then showed him how He revived the rest of his body. Qatada said that he began to look at how some of his bones were connected to each other, because the first thing God created from was his head, and it was said to him: Look, so he said at that time: I know, with the alif cut off, meaning I know this. At-Tabari said: The meaning of His statement And when it became clear to him is when what he had found strange in God’s power before he saw it became clear to him clearly, he said: I know. Ibn Atiyyah said: This is a mistake, because it required something that the wording does not require, and it was interpreted based on an anomalous statement and weak possibility. In my opinion, this is not an admission of what was before he denied it, as At-Tabari claimed, but rather it is a statement prompted by consideration, just as a believing person says when he sees something strange in the power of God the Almighty: There is no god but God, and the like. Abu Ali said: Its meaning is: I know this type of knowledge that I did not know. I said: We have mentioned this meaning from Qatada, and Makki, may God have mercy on him, said the same. Makki said: He spoke about himself when he witnessed the power of God Almighty in reviving the dead, so he was certain of that by witnessing, so he acknowledged that he knows that God is capable of everything, meaning I know this type of knowledge that I did not know with my own eyes. This is according to the reading of those who read I know by cutting off the alif, and they are the majority of the readers. Hamza and Al-Kisa’i read by connecting the alif, and it has two possible meanings: One of them is that the angel said to him: Know, and the other is that he puts himself in the position of the separate foreign addressee, so the meaning is: When it became clear to him, he said to himself: Know, O soul, this is the certain knowledge that you did not know with your own eyes. Abu Ali recited in a similar meaning: Farewell kitten, the caravan is leaving Didn't your eyes close on a sore night? Ibn Atiyah said: Abu Ali was comforted in this meaning by the poet’s saying: Remember who I am and where I drank it, he orders a psychic like this, the camel attack Al-Makki said: It is far-fetched that this is a command from God, the Most High, to him to know, because He has revealed to him His power, and shown him a command that he is certain of its truth and he has acknowledged the power, so there is no point in God commanding him to know that, rather he commands himself to do that and it is permissible and good. And in the letter of Abdullah there is what indicates that it is a command from God, the Most High, to him to know, in the sense of adhere to this knowledge when you have witnessed and become certain, and that is because in his letter it is said: Know, and also it is in agreement with what preceded it from the command in His statement: So look at your food and look at your donkey and look at the bones, so likewise and know that God, and Ibn Abbas used to recite it, it was said: Know, and he would say: Is he better or Abraham? When it was said to him: And know that God is Exalted in Might and Wise. So this shows that it is from the statement of God, the Most High, to him when he witnessed the revival.
2:260: People differed on this question, whether it was asked by Abraham out of doubt or not? The majority said: Abraham, peace be upon him, never doubted that God would revive the dead, but rather he asked to see it, because souls are eager to see what they have been told, and for this reason he, peace be upon him, said: Hearing is not like seeing it in person. Narrated by Ibn Abbas, and no one else narrated it. This was said by Abu Omar. Al-Akhfash said: He did not mean seeing with the heart, but rather seeing with the eyes. Al-Hasan, Qatada, Saeed bin Jubayr, and Al-Rabi’ said: He asked to increase his certainty to his certainty. Ibn Atiyyah said: Al-Tabari included in his interpretation the following: And others said that he asked his Lord for that, because he doubted the power of God Almighty. And he included under the translation the following on the authority of Ibn Abbas: There is no verse in the Qur’an that I have more hope for than it. And it was mentioned on the authority of Ata bin Abi Rabah that he said: Something entered the heart of Ibrahim, which enters the hearts of people, so he said: My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead. And he mentioned the hadith of Abu Hurairah that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: We are more deserving of doubt than Abraham, the hadith, then al-Tabari preferred this statement. I said: The hadith of Abu Hurairah was narrated by Al-Bukhari and Muslim on his authority that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: “We are more deserving of doubt than Abraham, when he said, ‘My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.’ He said, ‘Do you not believe?’ He said, ‘Yes, but [He said] that my heart may be reassured and that God may have mercy on Lot. He had sought refuge in a strong support. Had I remained in prison as long as Joseph remained, I would have answered the caller.’” Ibn Atiyyah said: “What Al-Tabari translated as is rejected in my opinion, and what was included in the translation is interpreted. As for the statement of Ibn Abbas: ‘It is the most hopeful sign,’ this is because it contains evidence of God the Most High and a request for life in this world, and this is not likely to be the case. It is permissible to say: ‘It is the most hopeful sign,’ because of his statement: ‘Do you not believe?’ meaning that belief is sufficient and does not require further investigation and research. As for the statement of Ata’: ‘Some of what enters the hearts of people entered Abraham’s heart,’ this means that it was witnessed, as mentioned above.” As for the saying of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace: We are more deserving of doubt than Abraham, its meaning is that if he had doubts, we would have been more deserving of him, and we do not doubt, so Abraham, peace be upon him, is more deserving of not doubting. The hadith is based on denying doubt from Abraham, and what was narrated in it from the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, is that he said: That is pure faith is only in thoughts that are not proven, as for doubt, it is a pause between two matters, neither of which has any advantage over the other, and that is what was denied from Abraham, peace be upon him. And the revival of the dead is only proven by hearing, and Abraham, peace be upon him, was the most knowledgeable about it, as indicated by his saying, My Lord is He who gives life and causes death. So doubt is far from someone whose footing is established in faith only, so how about the rank of prophethood and friendship? And the prophets are infallible from major and minor sins that contain vice, by consensus. And if you contemplate his question, peace be upon him, and the rest of the words of the verse, you will not give doubt, and that is because the question with how is only his question about the state of something existing and established in the questioner and the one being asked, and similar to your saying: How did Zaid know? And how was the garment woven? And the like of this. And when you say: How is your garment? And how is Zaid? The question is only about one of his states. How may be a predicate of something that can be asked about with how, such as your saying, However you wish, then be, and such as Al-Bukhari’s saying: How was the beginning of revelation? The how in this verse is only a question about the form of revival, and revival is established, but since we find that some of those who deny the existence of something may express their denial by asking about the state of that thing which they know is not correct, it follows from that that the thing in itself is not correct. An example of that is when a claimant says: I will raise this mountain, and the one who denies him says: Show me how you will raise it! This is a metaphorical way of expression, and its meaning is dialectical submission, as if he is saying: Suppose you raise it, then show me how you will raise it! So when the expression of Abraham, peace be upon him, was with this metaphorical ambiguity, God made it clear to him and led him to show him the truth, so He said to him: Do you not believe? He said: Yes. So the matter was completed and he was freed from all doubt, then he, peace be upon him, explained his question with reassurance. I said: This is what Ibn Atiyah mentioned and he is an adult, and such doubt is not permissible for the prophets, may God’s prayers be upon them, because it is disbelief, and the prophets agree on belief in the resurrection. God Almighty has informed us that Satan has no power over His prophets and saints, so He said: Indeed, My servants - over them you have no authority. And the accursed one said: Except for Your sincere servants among them. And if He has no authority over them, how can He make them doubt? Rather, he asked to see how the parts of the dead are gathered after they are separated and how the nerves and skins are joined after they are torn apart. So he wanted to ascend from the knowledge of certainty to the knowledge of certainty, so his saying: Show me how is a request to see the how. Some of the scholars of meaning said: Abraham only wanted his Lord to show him how He revives hearts, and this is corrupt and rejected by what follows from the explanation, mentioned by Al-Mawardi. And the alif in His statement: Have you not believed is not an alif of interrogation, but rather it is an alif of affirmation and confirmation, as Jarir said: Aren't you better than riding mounts? The letter waw is the letter waw of state. And the meaning of to believe is absolute faith, which includes the virtue of reviving the dead. He said, Yes, but so that my heart may be reassured. That is, I asked you so that my heart may be reassured by the difference between what is known by evidence and what is known by sight. Tranquility: moderation and stillness. Tranquility of the limbs is well-known, as he, peace be upon him, said: “Then bow until you are at peace while bowing.” The hadith. Peace of mind is for the mind to be at peace with the thing believed in. And thinking in the form of revival is not forbidden, just as we today can think about it, since it is a thought in it that is expressed, so Al-Khalil wanted to see, so his mind went in the form of revival. Al-Tabari said: The meaning of “for my heart to be at peace” is to be certain. Something similar was narrated from Saeed bin Jubair, and it was narrated from him to increase in certainty, and Ibrahim and Qatada said the same. Some of them said: To increase in faith with my faith. Ibn Atiyyah said: There is no increase in this meaning except to be at peace with thought, otherwise certainty is not divisible. Al-Suddi and Ibn Jubair also said: Do you not believe that you are my friend? He said: Yes, but so that my heart may be at peace with friendship. It was said: He asked to be shown how He revives the dead so that he may know whether his prayer will be answered, so God said to him: Do you not believe that I will answer your prayer? He said: Yes, but so that my heart may be at peace that you answer my prayer. There is a difference of opinion about what motivated him to do that. It was said: God promised him that He would take him as a friend, so he wanted a sign for that. This was said by Al-Sa’ib bin Yazid. It was also said: Nimrod’s saying: I give life and cause death. Al-Hasan said: He saw a corpse, half of it on land, distributed by wild beasts, and half of it in the sea, distributed by sea creatures. When he saw it dispersed, he wanted to see it come together, so he asked it to reassure his heart by seeing how it was gathered as he saw how it was dispersed. So it was said to him: Take four birds. It was said: They are the rooster, the peacock, the pigeon, and the crow. This was mentioned by Ibn Ishaq from some of the people of knowledge, and it was said by Mujahid, Ibn Jurayj, Ata bin Yasar, and where is Zaid? Ibn Abbas said the crane instead of the crow, and from him also the eagle instead of the pigeon. So he took these birds as he was ordered, slaughtered them, then cut them into small pieces, and mixed the flesh of some with the flesh of others, with the blood and feathers, so that it would be more amazing. Then he made a part of that mixed group on every mountain, and he stood where he could see those parts and held the heads of the birds in his hand, then he said: Come, by the permission of God. So those parts flew away, and the blood flew to the blood and the feathers to the feathers until they were united as they were before and remained without heads. Then he repeated the call, and they came to him running, that is, running on their legs. And a bird is not said to run if it flies except as an example, said An-Nahhas. And if Ibrahim pointed to one of them without its head, the bird would move away, and if he pointed to it with its head, it would come closer until every bird met its head, and they flew by the permission of God. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: Then make a part of each one on every mountain. Abu Bakr read from Asim and Abu Ja`far, Jaz`an with a doubling of the letter Zay. And from Abu Ja`far also, Jaz`an with a shaddah on the letter Zay. The rest are hamzat al-fadhah, and they are languages, and its meaning is the share. Seek and know is accusative in the state. And sarhin means to cut them, as stated by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Abu Ubaidah, and Ibn al-Anbari. It is said: sar al-shay’ yasawwaruhu meaning to cut it, and Ibn Ishaq said it. And on the authority of Abu al-Aswad al-Du’ali: In Syriac, it means to cut. Tobah ibn al-Humayr said, describing it: When I pulled the rope, its web creaked with the ends of the sticks, the straps of which were very strong. So the reasons brought me closer until I reached it with my rise, and my ascent almost depicted it. That is, he cuts them. And the word as-Suwar means to cut. Ad-Dahhak, Ikrimah, and Ibn Abbas said in some of what was narrated from him: It is a Nabataean word meaning to cut them. And it was said: The meaning is I hope them to you, that is, gather them and gather them to you. It is said: A man is asawur if his neck is inclined. And you say: I am yearning for you, meaning longing and inclined. And a woman is asawra’, and the plural is aswad like aswad and sawd. The poet said: God knows that we will look around on the day of separation at our neighbors His saying to you according to the interpretation of cutting is related to take and there is no need for an implied subject, and according to the interpretation of inclination and damma is related to sarahinna and in the speech there is something left out: so he inclined them to you then cut them off. And there are five readings for it: two in the seven and they are damma on the sad and kasra on it and softening the ra. And some people read fasrahinna with damma on the sad and stressed open ra, as if he is saying fashadhinna, and from it is the purse of dinars. And some people read fasrahinna with kasra on the sad and stressed open ra, and its meaning is shout them, and from your saying: sara the door and the pen if it makes a sound, narrated by al-Naqqash. Ibn Jinni said: It is a strange reading, and that is that the verb with kasra on the 'ayn in the transitive doubled is rare, and its root is yaf'al with damma on the 'ayn, like shadd yashudd and the like, but from it came the hadith namm yanmuhum yanmuhum, and the war yaharha yaharha, and from it is the verse of al-A'sha. Let the words haunt you until you destroy them And so on in a few letters. Ibn Jinni said: As for the reading of Ikrimah with a damma on the sad, it is possible for the word ra’ to be damma, fatha, or kasra, such as madd and shaddah, and the face is to have a damma on the ra’ because of the damma on the ha’ after it. The fifth reading is:صرهنwith the first letter sad open and the second letter ra stressed and broken. Al-Mahdawi and others narrated it on the authority of Ikrimah, meaning so detain them, from their saying: سرري سرسىif he detained, and from it the wordالسررر َسة means to detain. Here is an objection mentioned by Al-Mawardi, which is: How was Abraham answered to the signs of the Hereafter but not Moses in his saying: My Lord, show me, that I may look at You? There are two answers from him: The first is that what Moses asked is not valid while the obligation remains, and what Abraham asked was specific and valid while the obligation remains. The second is that circumstances differ, so it is better at some times to answer, and at other times to prevent what has not been previously permitted. Ibn Abbas said: God Almighty commanded Abraham to do this before he was born to him and before the scriptures were sent down to him, and God knows best.
2:261: It has five issues: First: When God Almighty narrated the proofs in it, He urged people to fight, and He made it known that whoever fights after this proof that only a prophet can bring, then he will have a great reward for his fight. Al-Basti narrated in his Sahih Musnad on the authority of Ibn Umar, who said: When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: O Lord, increase my nation. Then the verse was revealed: Who is it that will loan God a goodly loan so He may multiply it for him many times over? The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: O Lord, increase my nation. Then the verse was revealed: The patient will be given their reward in full, without account. This verse is a statement of an example of the honor and beauty of spending in the way of God, and it includes an encouragement to do so. In the speech, an adjective is omitted, the meaning of which is like the spending of those who spend their wealth in the way of God, like a seed. Another way: The example of those who spend their wealth is like that of a farmer who sows a seed in the ground, and the soil produces seven ears, meaning it produces seven ears, and in each ear there is a hundred grains. So the one who gives charity is like the farmer and the charity is like the seed, so God gives him for every charity seven hundred good deeds. Then God Almighty said: And God multiplies for whom He wills, meaning over seven hundred. So the example of the one who gives charity is like the farmer, if he is skilled in his work, and the seed is good and the land is prosperous, the crops will be more. Likewise, the one who gives charity if he is righteous and the money is good and he puts it in its place, then the reward will be greater, contrary to the one who said: There is no multiplication over seven hundred in the verse, as we will explain, God willing. Second: It was narrated that this verse was revealed regarding Uthman bin Affan and Abd al-Rahman bin Awf, may God be pleased with them: “When the Messenger of God (peace and blessings of God be upon him) urged people to give charity when he wanted to go out for the Battle of Tabuk, Abd al-Rahman came to him with four thousand and said: O Messenger of God, I had eight thousand, so I kept four thousand for myself and my family, and I lent four thousand to my Lord. The Messenger of God (peace and blessings of God be upon him) said: May God bless you in what you kept and in what you gave.” Uthman said: O Messenger of God, I have to provide for someone who has no provision, so this verse was revealed about them. It was said that it was revealed about voluntary spending. It was said that it was revealed before the verse on zakat and then abrogated by the verse on zakat. There is no need to claim abrogation, because spending in the way of God is recommended at all times. The paths of God are many, and the greatest of them is jihad so that the word of God may be supreme. Third: The Almighty’s saying: Like a seed. Seed is a generic name for everything that the son of Adam plants and eats. The most famous of this is wheat, so it is often meant as grain. From this, Al-Mutalammis said: I swear that the love of Iraq will feed me for a lifetime, and that love will eat me in the village of Licorice. The heart seed: its black part, and it is said its fruit, and that is it. The seed with a kasra on the ha: the seeds of legumes that are not food. In the hadith of intercession: They will grow as the seed grows in the silt of a torrent. The plural is habb. Habbah with a damma on the ha is the animal. It is said: yes, habbah, and karama. Love is affection, and so is love with a kasra. Love is also the beloved, like khudn and khudhayn. An ear of corn is a sandal from asbal al-sowt if the ear of corn is in it, meaning it is extended by the ear of corn as a curtain is extended by hanging it down. It was said: its meaning is that there is a hidden seed in it as a thing is covered by hanging its curtain down on it. The plural is sanabil. Then it was said: what is meant is the ear of millet, which is that which has this number in the ear of corn. I said: This is nothing, because the ear of millet comes in one ear more than this number by two times or more, as we have seen. Ibn Atiyyah said: It may be found in an ear of wheat what has a hundred grains, but in other grains it is more, but the example is this amount. At-Tabari said about this verse: His saying: In every ear a hundred grains means if that is found, otherwise it is on the assumption, then he narrated from Ad-Dahhak that he said: In every ear a hundred grains meaning every ear produced a hundred grains. Ibn Atiyyah said: At-Tabari made Ad-Dahhak’s statement similar to what he said, and that is not necessarily from Ad-Dahhak’s statement. Abu Amr Ad-Dani said: Some of them read one hundred in the accusative case, estimating that it produced a hundred grains. I said: Yaqub Al-Hadrami said: Some of them read in each ear a hundred grains on the basis of: It produced a hundred grains, and likewise some of them read And for those who disbelieve in their Lord is the punishment of Hell on the basis of: And We have prepared for them the punishment of the Blaze and We have prepared for those who disbelieve the punishment of Hell. Abu Amr, Hamzah and Al-Kisa’i read: It produced seven ears of wheat with the assimilation of the ta’ into the seen, because they are both unvoiced. Don’t you see that they follow one another? Abu Amr recited: May God curse the sons of Al-Sa’la’ Amr bin Maimun, the vile ones People wanted to change the letter seen to a taa. The rest of them pronounced it with izhar based on the original because they are two words. Fourth: The Qur’an states that the good deed in all righteous deeds is rewarded tenfold, and this verse requires that the good deed spent in jihad is rewarded seven hundredfold. Scholars differed regarding the meaning of His statement, And God multiplies for whom He wills. A group said: It explains and confirms what was mentioned previously about the seven hundred, and there is no multiplication above the seven hundred. A group of scholars said: Rather, it is an announcement that God, the Most High, multiplies for whom He wills more than seven hundred times. I said: This statement is more authentic because of the hadith of Ibn Umar mentioned at the beginning of the verse. Ibn Majah narrated that Harun ibn Abdullah al-Hammal told us, Ibn Abi Fadik told us, on the authority of al-Khalil ibn Abdullah, on the authority of al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Abi Talib, Abu al-Darda’, Abdullah ibn Umar, Abu Umamah al-Bahili, Abdullah ibn Amr, Jabir ibn Abdullah, and Imran ibn Husayn, all of them narrating on the authority of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, that he said: “Whoever sends money in the cause of God and stays in his house, he will receive seven hundred dirhams for every dirham. And whoever fights in the cause of God and spends in His cause, he will receive seven hundred thousand dirhams for every dirham - then he recited this verse - and God multiplies for whomever God wills.” It was narrated from Ibn Abbas that the multiplication ends with two thousand thousand for whomever God wills. Ibn Atiyyah said: This is not a proven chain of transmission from him. Fifth: In this verse there is evidence that farming is one of the highest professions that people do and the earnings that workers engage in, and therefore God gave an example of it and said: The example of those who spend their wealth verse. And in Sahih Muslim on the authority of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace: There is no Muslim who plants a tree or sows a seed and a bird, a person or an animal eats from it, but that it is considered a charity for him. Hisham bin Urwah narrated on the authority of his father on the authority of Aisha, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: Seek provision in the hidden recesses of the earth, meaning crops. Narrated by Al-Tirmidhi. The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said about palm trees: They are those that are firmly rooted in the mud and have good roots in the soil. This was done in a commendable manner. Agriculture is a communal obligation, so the Imam must force people to do it, as well as planting trees. Abdullah bin Abdul Malik bin Shihab met Al-Zuhri and said: Guide me to money that I can work with. Ibn Shihab began to say: I said to Abdullah when I met him, as he had saddled up the mounts, heading east Follow the secrets of the earth and call upon its King, perhaps one day you will be answered and provided for. He will give you abundant wealth, a reward when the waters of the earth flow. It was narrated on the authority of Al-Mu`tadid that he said: I saw Ali bin Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, in a dream, handing me a hoe and saying: Take it, for it is the key to the treasures of the earth.
2:262: There are three issues: First: The Almighty’s saying: Those who spend their wealth in the way of God. It was said that it was revealed about Uthman ibn Affan, may God be pleased with him. Abd al-Rahman ibn Samurah said: “Uthman came with a thousand dinars in the army of hardship and poured it into the lap of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace. I saw him put his hand in it and turn it over and say: ‘Whatever Ibn Affan does after today will not harm him. O God, do not forget this day for Uthman.’” Abu Saeed Al-Khudri said: “I saw the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, raising his hands and supplicating for Uthman, saying: ‘O Lord, Uthman, I am pleased with Uthman, so be pleased with him.’” He continued to supplicate until dawn broke, and then the verse was revealed: Those who spend their wealth in the way of God and do not follow up what they have spent with [an accusation of] corruption or injury. Second: As mentioned in the verse before spending in the way of God in general, it was made clear in this verse that this ruling and reward is only for the one who does not follow up his spending with a favor or harm, because favor and harm nullify the reward of charity as God the Almighty informed us in the verse after this. Rather, a person should seek the pleasure of God the Almighty and His reward by spending on the one he spends on, and he should not expect anything from him or consider his circumstances in any case other than taking into account his entitlement. God the Almighty said: We desire from you neither reward nor thanks. And whenever he spends in order to seek a reward from the one he spends on in any way, then he has not sought the pleasure of God. This is if he fails to expect from him his spending and causes harm. Likewise, whoever spends out of necessity, paying a fine, either because of a favor from the one he spends on or because of another indication of the care of the one who cares, then he has not sought the pleasure of God. Rather, what he gave for God is accepted, and most of his intention was seeking what is with God, like what was narrated from ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab may God be pleased with him that a Bedouin came to him and said: Oh Omar, may you be rewarded with Paradise. Dress my daughters and mother them. And be for us a paradise from time, I swear to God that you will do it Omar said: If I don't do it, what will happen? He said: So Abu Hafs, I will take him away He said: If I go, what will happen? He said: You will be asked about my condition on the day when the gifts are here The position of the person responsible for them is either Hell or Heaven. Omar cried until his beard was wet, then he said: Boy, give him this shirt of mine for that day, not for his hair, by God I do not own anything else. Al-Mawardi said: If giving in this manner is devoid of seeking reward or thanks, and devoid of gratitude and spreading it, then that is more honorable for the giver and more pleasant for the recipient. As for the giver, if he seeks reward through his giving, and seeks thanks and praise through it, then he is a person of reputation and hypocrisy, and in these two there is blame that contradicts generosity. If he seeks reward, then he is a profitable merchant who does not deserve praise or commendation. Ibn Abbas said about the verse of God the Almighty: {And do not bestow favors, expecting a greater reward} meaning, do not give a gift seeking a better one. Ibn Zayd believed that this verse is only about those who do not go out for jihad, but rather spend while sitting, and that the verse before it is about those who go out by themselves. He said: Therefore, it was stipulated for these and not for the first two. Ibn Atiyyah said: There is a problem with this statement, because there is arbitrariness in it. Third: The Almighty’s saying: Benefits and no harm. Manna: mentioning the blessing in the sense of enumerating it and rebuking it, such as saying: I have been good to you and given you comfort and the like. Some of them said: Manna: talking about what was given until it reaches the one who was given and harms him. Manna is one of the major sins, as proven in Sahih Muslim and others, and that it is one of the three whom God will not look at nor purify and for them is a painful punishment. Al-Nasa’i narrated on the authority of Ibn Umar that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: “There are three people whom God will not look at on the Day of al-Qiyamah 75:the one who is disobedient to his parents, the woman who imitates men, and the cuckold. And there are three people who will not enter Paradise: the one who is disobedient to his parents, the one who is addicted to alcohol, and the one who boasts about what he has given.” In some versions of Muslim: Al-Mannan is the one who gives nothing without a favor. Harm is cursing and complaining, and it is more general than a favor, because a favor is a part of harm, but it was mentioned specifically because it occurs frequently. Ibn Zayd said: If you think that your greeting will be burdensome to the one on whom you have spent for the sake of God, then do not greet him. A woman said to him: O Abu Usamah, guide me to a man who truly goes out in the cause of God, for they only go out to eat fruits, for I have arrows and a quiver. He said: May God not bless your arrows and your quiver, for you have harmed them before you gave them. Our scholars, may God have mercy on them, said: Whoever spends in the cause of God and does not follow it with a favor or harm, such as saying: How persistent you are, and God has delivered us from you, and the like, God has guaranteed him a reward, and the reward is Paradise, and He has removed from him fear after his death for what will come, and sadness over what has passed of his worldly life, because he rejoices in his Hereafter, so He said: For them is their reward with their Lord, and no fear will there be concerning them, nor will they grieve. This is enough of a virtue and honor for spending in the way of God Almighty. It is an indication of those who prefer the rich over the poor, as will be explained, God willing.
2:263: God Almighty says: “A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury. And God is Free of need and Forbearing.” There are three issues: First: The Almighty’s saying: A good word is a beginning and the predicate is omitted, meaning a good word is better and more appropriate, as mentioned by An-Nahhas and Al-Mahdawi. An-Nahhas said: It is possible that a good word is a predicate of an omitted beginning, meaning that what you have been commanded to do is a good word. A good word is supplication, comfort, and hope for what is with God, better than a charity that is apparently a charity but in reality is nothing, because mentioning a good word has a reward, while there is no reward in this. The Prophet, may God’s prayers and peace be upon him, said: A kind word is charity, and it is a form of kindness to meet your brother with a cheerful face. Narrated by Muslim. The beggar is greeted with joy and welcome, and he is met with cheerfulness and kindness, so that he will be thanked if he gives and excused if he refuses. Some wise men have said: Meet the one in need with joy, for if you do not thank him, you will not be without an excuse. Ibn Lankak narrated that Abu Bakr ibn Duraid went to one of the ministers to ask him about a need that he did not fulfill, and he appeared annoyed with him, so he said: Do not let the one who asks you become bored with you, for the best thing in your life is to see someone who is asked. Do not answer them with a hopeful face, for the continuation of your glory is to see what is hoped for. You receive a generous person and you are guided by his cheerful face, but you see the frown on the mean person as evidence. Know that you will soon become report, so be report that pleases and is beautiful. It was narrated on the authority of Omar, may God be pleased with him, that the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: “If someone asks a question, do not interrupt him until he has finished, then respond to him with dignity and gentleness, or with a small gift or a nice response, because someone who is neither human nor jinn may come to you and look at your actions in what God Almighty has given you.” I said: Its evidence is the hadith of a leper, a bald man and a blind man, narrated by Muslim and others. That is because an angel appeared in the form of a leper once, a bald man another time and a blind man another time, as a test for the one being asked. Bishr ibn al-Harith said: I saw Ali in a dream and said: O Commander of the Faithful, tell me something that will benefit me from God. He said: How beautiful is the kindness of the rich towards the poor out of desire for the reward of God the Most High, and better than that is the arrogance of the poor towards the rich out of trust in the promise of God. So I said: O Commander of the Faithful, tell me more. He turned away saying: You were dead and now you are alive, and soon you will be dead again. So, destroy a house in the house of mortality and build a house in the house of eternity. Second: The Almighty’s saying: And forgiveness. Forgiveness here means covering up the shortcomings and bad condition of the needy. From this is the saying of the Bedouin - when he asked some people in eloquent speech, someone said to him: Who is this man? He said to him: O God, forgiveness. Bad earnings prevent one from being related. It was said: The meaning is to overlook the questioner if he is persistent, rude, and harsh, better than giving him charity along with favors and harm. Al-Naqqash said its meaning. Al-Nahhas said: This is problematic and is clarified by grammar. Forgiveness is raised by the subject and the predicate is better than charity. The meaning is, and God knows best, and an action that leads to forgiveness is better than charity followed by harm. Its meaning in Arabic is and the action of forgiveness. It is permissible to say something like: God’s favor upon you is greater than the charity that you are hoping for, meaning God’s forgiveness is better than this charity that you are hoping for. Third: The Almighty’s saying: And God is Rich and Forbearing. The Almighty informed us about His absolute richness, that He is independent of the charity of His servants, and that He only commanded it to reward them, and about His forbearance, that He does not hasten to punish anyone who causes harm because of his charity.
2:264: There are three issues: First: The Almighty’s statement: with favor and injury. The meaning of this has already been presented. The Almighty expressed the lack of acceptance and deprivation of reward with the word nullification. What is meant is the charity that is bestowed with favor and injury, and nothing else. The belief is that bad deeds do not nullify or cancel out good deeds, so favor and injury in one charity do not nullify another charity. The majority of scholars said about this verse: The charity that God knows that its giver will either do good or cause harm is not accepted. It was also said: Rather, God gave the angel a sign about it, so he does not write it down, and this is good. The Arabs say about what is given as a favor: a black hand. And about what is given without being asked: a white hand. And about what is given upon being asked: a green hand. Some of the eloquent people said: Whoever does good, his gratitude is lost, and whoever is pleased with his work, his reward is lost. And some of the poets said: And a friend who I had loaned a favor to was slow to repay me, so he turned against me. When he was certain that time was against me, he expressed regret for what he had done to me. Another said: You spoiled the good you had given me with your generosity. Generous people are not generous when they give. Abu Bakr Al-Warraq said, and he said it well: Better than all good at all times and places A well-mannered creation free from favors Ibn Sirin heard a man say to another man: I did this to you and this, so he said to him: Be quiet, for there is no good in kindness if it is counted. It was narrated on the authority of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, that he said: Beware of showing gratitude for something good, for it nullifies gratitude and eliminates the reward. Then he recited: Do not nullify your charitable deeds by showing off or causing harm. Second: Our scholars, may God have mercy on them, said: Malik disliked, based on this verse, that a man should give his obligatory charity to his relatives lest he be compensated with praise and commendation from them, and his favor would be apparent to them and they would reward him for it, so it would not be purely for the sake of God Almighty. He preferred that he give it to strangers, and he also preferred that someone else be appointed to distribute it if the imam is not just, lest it be nullified by favors, harm, thanks, praise, and reward for service from the giver. This is unlike secret voluntary charity, because if its reward is nullified, it is saved from the threat and becomes like someone who did not do it, and if the reward of an obligatory charity is nullified, the threat is directed at it because it is like someone who did not do it. Third: The Almighty’s saying: Like one who spends his wealth to be seen by people. The Kaf is in the accusative case, meaning to nullify like the one who, so it is an attribute of the omitted source. It is also permissible for it to be in the position of a state. God Almighty likened the one who bestows favors and harms with his charity to the one who spends his wealth to be seen by people, not for the sake of God Almighty, and to the disbeliever who spends to be called generous and to be praised with various kinds of praise. Then He also likened this spender to a rock covered with dirt, so the one who thinks it is good, fertile soil, but when a downpour of rain falls on it, the dirt is removed and it remains solid. So the same is true of this hypocrite. So favors, harm, and showing off reveal the intention in the hereafter, so the charity is nullified, just as a downpour reveals a rock, which is a large, smooth stone. It was said: What is meant by the verse is to nullify the favor without the reward, so the one who intends to show off with his spending is not rewarded like the disbeliever, because he did not intend by it the sake of God Almighty, so he deserves the reward. The one who shows favor and harms others with the intention of seeking the face of God, who deserves His reward - even if he repeats his gift - and nullifies His favor. It has been said: The reward of his charity is only nullified by the time he shows it and harms others, and whatever comes before that is recorded for him and multiplied. So if he shows favor and harms others, the multiplication is cut off, because charity grows for its giver until it becomes greater than a mountain. So if it leaves the hand of its giver purely in the prescribed manner, it is multiplied. So if he shows favor and harms others, it stops there and the increase in multiplication is cut off. And the first statement is more apparent, and God knows best. And as-Safwan is the plural of safwanah, as Al-Akhfash said. And some of them said: Safwan is one, like a stone. And Al-Kisa’i said: Safwan is one, like a stone. And Al-Kisa’i said: Safwan is one, and its plural is Safwan and Safi and Safi. Al-Mubarrad denied it and said: Safi is the plural of safa like qaf and qaf, and from this meaning is as-Safwa and as-Safa, and it has been mentioned. And Sa’id ibn al-Musayyab and al-Zuhri read Safwan with a fat-ha on the fa’, and it is a language. And Qutrab narrated Safwan. An-Nahhas said: Safwan and Safwan may be plural or singular, except that it is better for it to be singular, because God Almighty said: Upon him was dust, and a downpour struck him. Although it is permissible to make the plural masculine, something does not go beyond its category except with conclusive evidence. As for what Al-Kisa’i narrated about the plural, it is not correct based on the true view, but Safwan is the plural of saffan and saffan with the meaning of safwan, and similar to it are warl and warlan, brother and brothers, and den and karwan, as the poet said: We have a day and the nightingale has a day when the wretched ones fly away, and there is no equal. The weak word in Arabic is Karawan, plural of Karawan, and Safi, plural of Safa, like a stick. Al-Wabil is heavy rain. The sky has become wet, and the earth has become wet. Al-Akhfash said: And from this is the saying of God Almighty: So We seized him with a severe seizure, meaning severe. And a severe strike, and a severe torment, meaning severe. And the solid... is the smooth of stones. Al-Kisa’i said: “Salad, salidu, salidan, with a moving lam, is sulud, with a sukoon, and it is everything that does not grow anything, and from this is a solid forehead, and Al-Asma’i recited for Ru’bah: Shining forehead of the noble Al-Naqqash said: As-salad al-ajrad is the language of Hudhayl. The meaning of “they are not able” means the hypocrite, the disbeliever, and the one who shows off on anything meaning on benefiting from the reward of something from their spending, which is their earnings when they need it, since it was for someone other than God. So spending was expressed as earnings, because they intended earnings by it. It was said: This was given as an example for the hypocrite in nullifying his reward, and for the one who shows off and causes harm in nullifying his favor. Al-Mawardi mentioned this.
2:265: The Almighty said: And the parable of those who spend their wealth seeking the pleasure of God and for strengthening themselves Seeking is an object for which. And for strengthening themselves is in apposition to it. Makki said in Al-Mushkil: Both are objects for which. Ibn Atiyyah said: It is rejected, and it is not correct in thabtiban that it is an object for which, because spending is not for strengthening. And striving is an accusative of the source in the place of the state, and the accusative of the object for which would be directed, but the accusative of the source is correct in terms of the apposition of the source which is stabtiban to it. And when God the Almighty mentioned the description of the charity of the people whose charity has no morals, and forbade the believers from doing anything similar to that in any way, He followed this verse by mentioning the expenditures of the people who purified their charity, since it was in accordance with the Shari'ah and its purpose. And striving means asking. And maradat is a source of radhi to be pleased, yardi. The meaning of and confirming is that they verify where they put their charity, as stated by Mujahid and Al-Hasan. Al-Hasan said: If a man intended to give charity, he would confirm it. If it was for the sake of God, he would carry it out, but if doubt mingled with him, he would hold back. It was also said that it means believing and being certain, as stated by Ibn Abbas. Ibn Abbas and Qatada also said: Its meaning is and in anticipation of reward from themselves. Al-Sha’bi, Al-Suddi, Qatada, Ibn Zayd, Abu Salih and others said: The meaning of and confirming is and being certain, meaning that their souls have insights, so they confirm them in spending in obedience to God, the Most High, with confirmation. These three statements are more correct than the statement of Al-Hasan and Mujahid, because the meaning they have adopted is that and confirming is a source other than the source. Ibn Atiyyah said: This is not permissible except with mentioning the source and clarifying the previous action, like the statement of God the Most High: And God has caused you to grow from the earth with a growth Al-Baqarah 2:176, And devote yourself to Him with a complete devotion. If the verb is not explicitly stated, then you cannot bring a source with a meaning other than its meaning and then say: I carry it on the meaning of such and such, for a verb that was not mentioned before. Ibn Atiyyah said: This is the generality of the speech of the Arabs as far as I know. Al-Nahhas said: If it were as Mujahid said, then it would be wa-tabattan from tabatabat like takramat takramaan. Qatadah’s statement: ta-hasban is not known unless it means that their souls confirm them, expecting reward, and this is far-fetched. Al-Sha’bi’s statement is good, meaning confirming from themselves for them to spend that in the obedience of God, the Almighty. It is said: Tabatat so-and-so in this matter, meaning I corrected his resolve and strengthened his opinion in it. Tabtahu thabta, meaning their souls are certain of God’s promise to confirm them in that. It was said: And confirming from themselves means they acknowledge that God, the Almighty, confirms it, meaning confirming from themselves for its reward, unlike the hypocrite who does not expect the reward. God the Almighty said: Like a garden on a height. Garden is an orchard, which is a piece of land where trees grow until they cover it. It is taken from the word jinn and jinn for their concealment. It has been mentioned before. A hill is a slightly elevated place, with mostly dense soil, and whatever is like this has better vegetation, and that is why He specifically mentioned a hill. Ibn Atiyyah said: The gardens of sadness are not from this as al-Tabari claimed, rather those are the gardens attributed to Najd, because they are better than the gardens of Tihamah, and the plants of Najd are more fragrant, and its breeze is cooler and more gentle, and Najd is called sadness. The air of Tihamah is rarely suitable except at night, and that is why a Bedouin woman said: My husband is like the night of Tihamah. Al-Suddi said: On a hill, meaning on a hill, which is a low part of the land. Ibn Atiyyah said: This is a weak expression, and the word hill is taken from riba yarbu if it increases. I said: Al-Suddi’s statement is nothing, because the construction of rab and its meaning is increase in the speech of the Arabs, and from it is the word ribu for the high soul. Rabaa yarbu if it is taken by asthma. And the horse rabaa if it is taken by asthma from an enemy or fright. Al-Farra’ said about the Almighty’s saying: So he seized them with a heavy seizure meaning an increase, like you say: arbait if you take more than you give. And rabutu in the Banu Fulan and rabayt means I grew up among them. Al-Khalil said: A hill is a high, good land, and God specifically mentioned that in which no water flows according to the custom in the lands of the Arabs, so he gave them an example of what they sense and perceive. Ibn Abbas said: A hill is a high place in which rivers do not flow, in which there is hot water, and he did not mean the type of place in which rivers flow, because God Almighty mentioned a hill with a place of settlement and a spring. What is known from the speech of the Arabs is that a hill is that which is higher than what is adjacent to it, whether water flows in it or not. It has five languages: Rabwah with a damma on the ra’, and this is how Ibn Kathir, Hamza, Al-Kisa’i, Nafi’, and Abu Amr read it. Rabwah with a fatha on the ra’, and this is how Asim, Ibn Amir, and Al-Hasan read it. Rabwah with a kasra on the ra’, and this is how Ibn Abbas and Abu Ishaq Al-Subai’i read it. Rabawah with a fatha, and this is how Abu Ja’far and Abu Abd Al-Rahman read it. The poet said: From my home in Rawdat Barbawah among the palm trees to Baqi' al-Gharqad? And Rabawa with the kasra, and this is how Al-Ashhab Al-Uqaili read it. Al-Farra’ said: It is also said Barbawah and Barbawa, and both are from the hillock, and its verb is rabaa yarbu. The Almighty said: It struck it meaning the hill. Half-load means heavy rain. The poet said: What a green, lush garden of sadness, upon which a downpour poured down It brought means it gave. Its food with a damma on the hamza: the fruit that is eaten, and from this is the saying of God Almighty: It yields its fruit at all times. And the thing that is eaten of anything is called food. And food: a morsel, and from this is the hadith: If the food is little, let him put in his hand a bite or two of it, meaning a morsel or two. Narrated by Muslim. Adding it to Paradise is an addition of specificity, like the saddle of a horse or the door of a house. Otherwise, the fruit is not from what Paradise eats. Nafi’, Ibn Kathir, and Abu Amr read akalha with a damma on the hamza and a sukoon on the kaf, and likewise everything added to a feminine. Abu Amr differed from them in what was added to a masculine, such as akalhu or was not added to anything, such as akal khmat, so Abu Amr made it heavy and they made it light. Asim, Ibn Amir, Hamzah, and Al-Kisa’i read it with a heavy emphasis in all that we mentioned. It is said: akal and akal mean the same thing. Douafeen means it gave twice the fruit of other lands. Some of the scholars said: it brought forth twice a year, and the first is more, meaning it produced from the crops what others produce in two years. The Almighty’s saying: But if no downpour hits it, then dew. This is an emphasis from the Almighty to praise this hill, that if no downpour hits it, then dew. It is sufficient for her and replaces the downpour in producing fruit twice as much, due to the generosity and goodness of the land. Al-Mubarrad and others said: Its meaning is that it is a dew that is sufficient for her. Al-Zajjaj said: What falls on it is dew. Dew is the weak, thin rain from the light drop, as stated by Ibn Abbas and others, and it is well-known in the language. Some people, including Mujahid, said: Dew is the rain. Ibn Atiyyah said: It is a metaphor and a simile. Al-Nahhas said: The linguists narrated: Wabalat and Wabbalat and Wabalat and Talat and Atallat. In Al-Sahah: Dew is the weakest rain, and the plural is Talal. You say from it, the land was dewed and the dew covered it, so it is Mutallool. Al-Mawardi said: The crops of dew are weaker than the crops of rain and produce less fruit, and in it - even if it is little - there is cohesion and benefit. Some of them said: There is an inversion in the verse, and its meaning is like a garden on a hill that is hit by a downpour, but if it is not hit by a downpour, then dew, so it produces fruit twice as much. It means that the leaves of the garden turned green and its fruit came out twice as much. I said: The first interpretation is more correct and there is no need to advance or delay.
