So the Almighty likened the growth of the expenditures of these sincere people whose charity God increases like the growth of a foal or young camel to the growth of the plants of Paradise on the described hill, unlike the rock whose soil has been exposed and remains solid. Muslim and others narrated on the authority of Abu Hurairah, may God be pleased with him, on the authority of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace: “No one gives in charity a date from his lawful earnings except that God takes it in his right hand and raises it as one of you raises his foal or young camel, until it becomes like a mountain or larger.” Also narrated by Al-Muwatta. The Almighty says: And God is Seeing of what you do. It is a promise and a threat. Al-Zuhri read they do with a ya as if he meant all people, or he meant only the spenders, so it is a pure promise.
2:266: To Him the Almighty: Would any of you like to have a garden of palm trees and grapevines? The verse. Al-Tabari narrated on the authority of Al-Suddi that this verse is another example of hypocritical spending, and he preferred this statement. I said: It was also narrated from Ibn Abbas who said: This is like the slap of God on the hypocrites with their deeds, He will nullify them on the Day of Resurrection when they are most in need of them, like the slap of a man who had a garden and children who did not benefit him, then he grew old and a hurricane struck the garden, that is, a violent wind with fire in it, and it was burned, so he lost it when he was most in need of it. It was narrated from Ibn Zayd that he read the words of God the Most High: O you who have believed, do not invalidate your charities with reminders or injury (al-Baqarah 2:14), then he gave an example of that and said: Would any of you like to (al-Baqarah 2:14). Ibn Atiyyah said: This is clearer than what al-Tabari preferred, and this verse is not another example of hypocritical spending, this is what the context of the speech requires. As for the meaning in other than this context, it is like the state of every hypocrite or disbeliever who did an action thinking that he was doing well, but when the time of need came he found nothing. I said: It has been narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas that it is an example of someone who works for other than God, whether a hypocrite or a disbeliever, as will come, except that what is proven in Bukhari on his authority is contrary to this. Bukhari narrated on the authority of Ubayd ibn Umair who said: One day, Umar ibn al-Khattab said to the companions of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him): Why was this verse revealed: Would any of you like to have a garden of date palms and grapevines? They said: God and His Messenger know best. Umar became angry and said: “Say: We know or we do not know!” Ibn Abbas said: I have something in mind about it, O Commander of the Faithful. He said: O son of my brother, say it and do not belittle yourself. Ibn Abbas said: You have given an example of a deed. Umar said: What deed? Ibn Abbas said: The deed of a rich man who works in obedience to God, then God sends Satan to him, so he works in sins until he burns up his work. In another narration: So when his life is over and his end is near, he seals it with a miserable deed. Umar was pleased with that. Ibn Abi Malekah narrated that Umar recited this verse and said: This is an example of a man who does a good deed until, at the end of his life, he is most in need of it, and he does a bad deed. Ibn Atiyyah said: This is a view that applies the verse to everything that falls under its wording, and something similar was said by Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Rabi’ and others. He mentioned palm trees and grapes specifically because of their honor and superiority over all other trees. Al-Hasan read gardens in the plural. Underneath which rivers flow was mentioned earlier. For him therein are all kinds of fruits meaning there is no fruit that does not grow therein. The Almighty’s saying: And old age has seized him is a past tense in apposition to a future tense, which is to be. It was also said: He would like. It was said: The meaning is: And old age has seized him. It was also said that it is based on the meaning, because the meaning is: Would any of you like that he had a paradise? It was also said: The and is the and of the state, and likewise in the Almighty’s saying: and for him. God the Almighty said: Then a whirlwind containing fire struck it, and it was burned. Al-Hasan said: A whirlwind containing fire means a wind with intense hail. Al-Zujaj: In the language, a whirlwind is a strong wind that blows from the earth to the sky like a column, and it is what is called a whirlwind. Al-Jawhari said: A whirlwind is a chief of the jinn, and from it the whirlwind was called a whirlwind. It is also said: Umm Zub’ah, and it is a wind that stirs up dust and rises to the sky like a column. It was also said: A whirlwind is a wind that stirs up clouds with thunder and lightning. Al-Mahdawi: It was called a whirlwind because it is twisted like a garment when it is squeezed. Ibn Atiyyah: This is weak. I said: Rather it is correct: because it is seen and felt, as it ascends a twisted column. It was said: The wind is called a hurricane because it squeezes the clouds, and the clouds are squeezed either because they are pregnant, so they are like the squeezed women, or because they are squeezed by the winds. Ibn Sidah narrated: The squeezes were interpreted by some people as the winds, not the clouds. Ibn Zayd: The hurricane is a violent and strong poisonous wind, and Al-Suddi said the same, the hurricane is the wind and the poisonous fire. Ibn Abbas: A wind in which there are strong poisonous winds. Ibn Atiyyah said: This happens in intense heat and in intense cold, and all of that is from the breath of Hell and its soul, as the saying of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, implies: If the heat becomes intense, then cool down before praying, for intense heat is from the heat of Hell. And: The Fire complained to its Lord. It was narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas and others: This is a parable that God the Almighty has given for the disbelievers and hypocrites, like the case of a man who planted a garden and it produced a lot of fruit, but he became old and had weak offspring - meaning boys and girls - and his livelihood and the livelihood of his offspring came from that garden. Then God sent a wind with fire in it and burned it, and he had no strength to plant it again, and his children had no good to turn back to their father. Likewise, the disbeliever and the hypocrite, when they come to God the Almighty on the Day of Resurrection, will not have a chance to be resurrected and returned a second time, just as this man has no strength to plant his garden again, and those who are in need of it when they are old and their offspring are weak will not have enough to do without it. God Almighty says: Thus does God make clear to you the signs that you may give thought. He means that you may return to My greatness and Lordship and not take guardians besides Me. Ibn Abbas also said: You may think about the passing of this world and its demise and the coming of the Hereafter and its permanence.
2:267: It contains eleven issues: First: The Almighty’s saying: O you who have believed, spend. This is addressed to the entire nation of Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace. Scholars differed about the intended meaning of spending here. Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ubaydah al-Salmani, and Ibn Sirin said: It is the obligatory zakat, and people are forbidden from spending bad in it instead of good. Ibn Atiyyah said: What appears from the words of al-Bara’ ibn ‘Aazib, al-Hasan, and Qatadah is that the verse is about voluntary charity, and they are encouraged not to volunteer except with good, chosen charity. The verse includes both aspects, but the one who gave zakat commented that it is commanded and the command is obligatory, and that he forbade bad charity, and that is specific to the obligatory charity. As for voluntary charity, just as a person can volunteer a little, so can he volunteer something that is lower in amount, and a dirham is better than a date. The proponents of encouragement held fast to the fact that the word af’al is suitable for encouragement because it is suitable for the obligatory charity, and bad charity is forbidden in voluntary charity just as it is forbidden in obligatory charity, and God is more deserving of being chosen for it. Al-Bara’ narrated: “A man hung up a straw rod, and the Messenger of God (peace and blessings of God be upon him) saw it and said: ‘What a bad thing he has hung up!’ So the verse was revealed. It was narrated by Al-Tirmidhi and will be mentioned in full. According to this statement, the matter is recommended, and they were recommended not to volunteer except with good and chosen things. The majority of commentators said: The meaning of “from good and chosen things” is what you have earned. Ibn Zayd said: Through what you have earned. Second: Earning is done through physical effort, which is hiring, and its ruling will come later, or by contracting in trade, which is selling, and its explanation will come later. Inheritance is included in this, because the non-inheritor has earned it. Sahl ibn Abdullah said: Ibn al-Mubarak was asked about a man who wants to earn and intends by his earnings to maintain kinship ties, to strive and do good deeds, and he enters into the dangers of earning for this purpose. He said: If he has enough to live on, enough to keep himself away from people, then leaving this is better, because if he seeks what is lawful and spends in what is lawful, he will be asked about it, about his earnings, and about his spending, and leaving that is asceticism, because asceticism is in leaving what is lawful. Third: Ibn Khuwaiz Mandad said: And because of this verse, it is permissible for the father to eat from his son’s earnings, because the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: Your children are from your good earnings, so eat from your children’s wealth in peace. Fourth: The Almighty’s saying: And from what We have produced for you from the earth meaning plants, minerals, and treasure. These are three chapters included in this verse. As for plants, Al-Daraqutni narrated on the authority of Aisha, may God be pleased with her, who said: The Sunnah of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) is: There is no zakat on less than five wasqs. A wasq is sixty sa’s, so that is three hundred sa’s of wheat, barley, dates, and raisins. There is no zakat on vegetables that the earth produces. Some people have cited as evidence for Abu Hanifa the words of God the Most High: And of what We have produced for you from the earth, and that this is general in the little or much that the earth produces and in all other types. They saw the apparent meaning of the command as obligatory. This will be explained in full in Al-An’am. As for minerals, the imams narrated on the authority of Abu Hurayrah on the authority of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) that he said: The wound of a dumb animal is a compensation, the well is a compensation, the mine is a compensation, and there is a fifth in the treasure. Our scholars said: When the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: And there is a fifth of the treasure, it indicates that the ruling on minerals is not the same as the ruling on treasure, because the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, distinguished between minerals and treasure with the separating and. If the ruling on them were the same, he would have said: And the mine is a tyrant and there is a fifth in it. So when he said: And there is a fifth of the treasure, it is known that the ruling on treasure is not the ruling on the mine with regard to what is taken from it. And God knows best. The root of the word treasure in the language is that which is fixed in the ground of gold, silver and jewels. It is also the case with all the jurists, because they say that the rarity that is found in the mineral fixed in the ground and cannot be obtained by work, effort or toil, is subject to one-fifth, because it is a treasure. It was narrated from Malik that the ruling on the rarity in the mineral is the ruling on what requires work to be extracted from the mineral in the treasure. The first is the attainment of his doctrine and the fatwa of the majority of the jurists is based on it. Abdullah bin Saeed bin Abi Saeed Al-Maqburi narrated on the authority of his father on the authority of his grandfather on the authority of Abu Hurairah who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, was asked about treasure. He said: The gold that God created on the earth on the day He created the heavens and the earth. Abdullah bin Saeed’s hadith is rejected. This was mentioned by Ibn Abi Hatim. It was narrated through another chain of transmission on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, but it is not authentic. This was mentioned by Al-Daraqutni. According to a group of scholars, the burial of their wealth in the pre-Islamic era is also treasure, and they do not differ about it if it was buried before Islam from ordinary money. As for what was minted in Islam, its ruling according to them is the ruling on lost property. Fifth: They differed on the ruling on treasure if it is found. Malik said: Whatever is found buried during the time of ignorance in the land of the Arabs or in the deserts of the land that the Muslims owned without war, it belongs to its finder and a fifth is due on it. As for what is in the land of Islam, it is like a found object. He said: Whatever is found in the land of force is for the group who conquered it, not its finder. Whatever is found in the land of peace, it belongs to the people of that country, not the people, and the finder has nothing in it unless he is from the people of the house, in which case it is his, not them. It was said: Rather, it is for all the people of the peace. Ismail said: The ruling on treasure is the ruling on spoils of war because it is the property of an infidel that a Muslim found, so he treated it like someone who fought him and took his property, so he was entitled to four-fifths of it. Ibn al-Qasim said: Malik used to say about goods, gems, iron, lead, and the like that are found as treasure: There is a fifth in it. Then he changed his mind and said: I do not see anything in it. Then the last thing we left was that he said: There is a fifth in it. This is correct due to the generality of the hadith, and the majority of jurists agree with it. Abu Hanifa and Muhammad said about the treasure found in a house: It belongs to the owner of the house and not the finder, and it is subject to one-fifth. Abu Yusuf disagreed with him and said: It belongs to the finder and not the owner of the house, and this is the opinion of Al-Thawri. If it is found in the wilderness, it belongs to the finder according to all of them, and it is subject to one-fifth. They do not differentiate between the land of peace and the land of forced labor, and they consider the land of the Arabs and others the same. They allow the finder to keep one-fifth for himself if he is in need, and he may give it to the poor. Some of the people of Medina and the followers of Malik do not differentiate between any of that and they said: Whether the treasure is found in the land of forced labor or in the land of peace or the land of the Arabs or the land of war, if it is not owned by anyone and no one claims it, it is for the finder and it is subject to one-fifth according to the general meaning of the hadith, and this is the opinion of Al-Layth, Abdullah bin Nafi’, Al-Shafi’i and most of the scholars. Sixth: As for what is found from minerals and what is extracted from them, there is a difference of opinion regarding it. Malik and his companions said: There is nothing in what is extracted from minerals of gold or silver until it is twenty mithqals of gold or five ounces of silver. If they reach this amount, zakat is due on them, and what is more is calculated accordingly as long as there is a well in the mine. If it is cut off and then another well comes after that, then zakat begins on it in its place. And the treasure, according to them, is like a crop; zakat is taken from it at its time and a year is not waited for it. Sahnun said about a man who has mines: He does not add what is in one of them to the others and he does not pay zakat except on two hundred dirhams or twenty dinars in each one. Muhammad ibn Maslama said: Some of them are added to each other and zakat is paid on all of them like crops. Abu Hanifa and his companions said: The mineral is like the treasure, so whatever is found in the mineral of gold or silver after taking out the fifth, each one of them is considered, so whoever has in his possession what is obligatory for zakat, he pays zakat for the completion of a year if a year has passed on it and it is the nisab in his view, this is if he does not have gold or silver, then zakat is obligatory. If he has what is obligatory for zakat, he adds it to that and pays zakat. Likewise, according to them, every benefit is added in a year to the nisab of its kind and is zakatable for the original year, and this is the opinion of al-Thawri. Al-Muzani mentioned from al-Shafi’i that he said: As for what I am standing on of what is extracted from minerals, al-Muzani said: It is more appropriate for him according to his principle that what is extracted from the mineral is a benefit that is zakatable for a year after it is extracted. Al-Layth ibn Sa’d said: Whatever is extracted from minerals of gold and silver is like a benefit that is renewed for a year, and this is the opinion of al-Shafi’i in what al-Muzani obtained from his school of thought, and Dawud and his companions said this if a year has passed on it according to Malik, and the ownership is correct, because the Prophet (peace and blessings of God be upon him) said: Whoever acquires wealth, there is no zakat on it until a year has passed. Narrated by Al-Tirmidhi and Al-Darqutni. They also cited as evidence what was narrated by Abd Al-Rahman bin An’am bin Abi Sa’d Al-Khudri: “The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, gave gold in the soil of a group of people whose hearts were to be reconciled,” sent by Ali, may God be pleased with him, from Yemen. Ash-Shafi’i said: And those whose hearts were to be reconciled have a right to zakat. Thus, it is clear that the law of zakat on minerals is the law of zakat. Malik’s proof is a hadith on the authority of Rabi’ah ibn Abi Abd al-Rahman that the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, gave Bilal ibn al-Harith the Qibli minerals, which are in the direction of al-Far’. To this day, nothing is taken from those minerals except zakat. This hadith has an interrupted chain of transmission, and the scholars of hadith do not use it as evidence. However, it is a practice that they practice in Madinah. Ad-Darawardi narrated it on the authority of Rabi’ah on the authority of al-Harith ibn Bilal al-Muzani on the authority of his father. Al-Bazzar mentioned it, and Kathir ibn Abdullah ibn Amr ibn Awf narrated it on the authority of his father on the authority of his grandfather on the authority of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace: He gave Bilal ibn al-Harith the Qibli minerals, both their Jalisa and Ghori, and wherever it was suitable for cultivation in Quds, and he did not give him the right of a Muslim. Al-Bazzar also mentioned it, and many agree on its weakness. This is the ruling on what the earth produces, and the ruling on what the sea produces will come in Surat al-Nahl, as it is the divider of the earth. The meaning of his saying, peace be upon him, The wound of a dumb animal is repaired, will come in al-Anbiya’, each in its place, God willing. Seventh: The Almighty’s saying: And do not aim at that which is bad, spending [for yourselves]. “At-tammum” means intend. Evidence will come from the poetry of the Arabs that at-tammum is the sanctity of women, God willing. The verse indicates that earnings include good and bad. Al-Nasa’i narrated on the authority of Abu Umamah ibn Sahl ibn Hunaif regarding the verse in which God Almighty said: And do not aim at that which is bad, spending [for yourselves], he said: It is the ja’rur and the color of Habiq, so the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, forbade them to be taken in charity. Al-Darqutni narrated on the authority of Abu Umamah ibn Sahl ibn Hunaif on the authority of his father, who said: "The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) ordered his charity to be given, and a man came from this valley with some dates - Sufyan said: meaning shis - and the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) said: Who brought this?! No one would bring anything without it being attributed to the one who brought it. So the verse was revealed: "And do not give away that which is bad, spending it." He said: The Prophet (peace be upon him) forbade the ja'rur and the color of habeek from being taken in charity" - Az-Zuhri said: Two colors of dates from Madinah - and At-Tirmidhi included it from the hadith of Al-Bara' and authenticated it, and it will come. At-Tabari and An-Nahhas narrated that in the reading of Abdullah, and do not go to the mosque and they are two dialects. Muslim ibn Jundub read and do not go to the mosque with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the meem. Ibn Kathir read and do not go to the mosque with a shaddah on the ta'. There are dialects in the word, including I took the thing with a lightened first meem and I took it with a shaddah, and I took it to the mosque and I took it to the mosque and I took it to the mosque. Abu Amr narrated that Ibn Masoud read Do not lead yourselves in prayer with a hamza after the closed ta’. Eighth: The Almighty’s saying: From it you spend. Al-Jurjani said in his book Nazm Al-Quran: A group of people said: The speech was completed in the Almighty’s saying: The bad, then He began with a description of the bad, saying: From it you spend, and you do not take it except if you close your eyes, meaning you are lenient, as if this meaning is a rebuke and reprimand to the people. The pronoun in From it refers back to the bad, which is the lowly and the vile. Al-Jurjani said: Another group said: The speech is connected to His saying From it, so the pronoun in From it refers back to what you have earned, and You spend comes as if it is in the accusative case as a state, and it is like your saying: I am going out to fight in the way of God. Ninth: The Almighty’s statement: And you would not take it unless you close your eyes to it. That is, you would not take it in your debts and rights from people unless you are lenient in that and abandon some of your rights, and you hate it and are not pleased with it. That is, do not do with God what you would not be pleased with for yourselves. Al-Bara’ ibn ‘Aazib, Ibn ‘Abis, and Al-Dahhak said its meaning. Al-Hasan said: The meaning of the verse is: And you would not take it even if you found it being sold in the market unless you withhold some of its price. Something similar was narrated from ‘Ali, may God be pleased with him. Ibn ‘Atiyyah said: These two statements are similar to the verse being about obligatory zakat. Ibn al-‘Arabi said: If it were about an obligatory zakat, he would not have said: And you would not take it, because the bad and defective is not permissible to take in an obligatory zakat under any circumstances, neither with the assumption of closing eyes nor without it. Rather, it is taken without closing eyes in a voluntary zakat. Al-Bara’ ibn Aawb also said that its meaning is: And you would not take it even if it was given to you unless you close your eyes to it, meaning that you would be ashamed before the Mahdi and accept from him what you have no need for and which he does not value in himself. Ibn Atiyyah said: This is similar to the verse being about voluntary offerings. Ibn Zayd said: And you would not take what is forbidden unless you close your eyes to what is disliked. Tenth: The Almighty’s saying: Unless you close your eyes to it. This is how the majority read it. From aghma a man is lenient in a matter and is satisfied with some of his right and goes beyond it. From this is the saying of Al-Tirmaah: We were not tempted by the odd number of people, but we were given people who were satisfied with ignoring it. This is like ignoring something when it is disliked. Al-Naqqash mentioned this meaning in this verse and Makki referred to it - or from the saying of the Arabs: A man closed his eyes if he came to something obscure, as you say: Aaman, meaning he came to Oman, and A’raq, meaning he came to Iraq, and Anjad and Aghur, meaning he came to Najd and Al-Ghor, which is Tihamah, meaning he seeks interpretation for his taking. Al-Zuhri read it with a fatha on the ta’ and a kasra on the meem, lightened, and also from him: Taghamdu with a damma on the ta’ and a fatha on the ghayn and a kasra on the meem and stressed. The first is on the meaning that you will deprive the seller of its price from you, so he will deprive you. The second, which is the reading of Qatada according to what An-Nahhas mentioned, is that you will take it with a reduction. Abu Amr Ad-Dani said: The meaning of Az-Zuhri’s reading is until you take it with a reduction. Makki narrated from Al-Hasan, except that you close your eyes with a shaddah on the meem and a fatha. Qatada also read Taghamdu with a damma on the ta’ and a sukoon on the ghayn and a fatha on the meem, lightened. Abu Amr Al-Dani said: Its meaning is unless you close your eyes, and An-Nahhas narrated it from Qatada himself. Ibn Jinni said: Its meaning is that you find that you have closed your eyes to the matter through your interpretation or your leniency and you have gone in a way that is not previously in the souls. This is like saying: I praised the man and found him praiseworthy, and other examples. Ibn Atiyyah said: The reading of the majority is based on transgression and closing the eyes, because aghmad is like ghamd. And it means until you come to something ambiguous in interpretation and consideration in taking that, either because it is forbidden according to the opinion of Ibn Zayd, or because it is a guidance or taken in a religion according to the opinion of others. Al-Mahdawi said: And whoever reads taghmadhu, the meaning is that you close the eyes of your insights from taking it. Al-Jawhari said: And you closed your eyes to someone if you were lenient with him in a sale or purchase and closed your eyes, and God the Almighty said: And you would not take it except that you close your eyes to it. It is said: Close your eyes to me in what you sold me, as if you want to increase it due to its poor quality and reduce its price. An is in the accusative case, and the meaning is except that. Eleventh: The Almighty’s saying: And know that God is Free of need, Praiseworthy. The Almighty drew attention to the attribute of richness, meaning that He has no need of your charity. So whoever draws near and seeks reward, let him do so with what is of value and importance, for he only gives for himself. And Hamid means praised in every situation. We have already mentioned the meanings of these two names in the Most Sublime Book, and praise be to God. Al-Zajjaj said about His saying: And know that God is Free of need, Praiseworthy: meaning that He did not command you to give charity out of need, but rather without your knowledge, so He is Praiseworthy for that and for all His blessings.
2:268: God Almighty says: “Satan threatens you with poverty and orders you to immorality, while God promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty. And God is all-Encompassing and Knowing.” There are three issues: First: The Almighty’s saying: The devil has been mentioned previously in the meaning of the devil and its derivation, so there is no point in repeating it. And he threatens you with poverty, meaning with poverty lest you spend. So this verse is connected to what came before, and that the devil has a role in discouraging people from spending in the way of God, and in addition to that he commands immorality, which is sins and spending in them. And it was said: meaning that you do not give charity, lest you disobey and cut off relations. And poverty was read with a damma on the fa’, and this is a language. Al-Jawhari said: And poverty is a language for poverty, like weakness and weakness. Second: The Almighty’s saying: And God promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty. When a promise is used in general terms in the speech of the Arabs, it is for good. If it is restricted to what is promised, it may be for good or for evil, such as good report. So this verse is one of those in which a promise is restricted to both meanings. Ibn Abbas said: In this verse there are two from God Almighty and two from Satan. Al-Tirmidhi narrated on the authority of Abdullah ibn Masoud that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: “The devil has a touch with the son of Adam, and the angel has a touch. As for the touch of the devil, it is a threat of evil and a denial of the truth. As for the touch of the angel, it is a threat of good and a belief in the truth. Whoever finds that, let him know that it is from God. Whoever finds the other, let him seek refuge with God from the devil. Then he recited: The devil threatens you with poverty and orders you to immorality.” He said: This is a good and authentic hadith. It is permissible in other than the Qur’an to say and orders you to immorality without the ba. Sibawayh recited: I have commanded you to do good, so do what I have commanded you to do, for I have left you with wealth and lineage. Forgiveness is covering up for His servants in this world and the hereafter. Grace is provision in this world and expansion and bliss in the hereafter, and God Almighty has promised all of this. Third: Al-Naqqash mentioned that some people took comfort in this verse in that poverty is better than wealth because Satan only distances the servant from goodness, and by frightening him with poverty, he distances him from it. Ibn Atiyyah said: There is no conclusive evidence in the verse, rather the opposition to it is strong. It was narrated that in the Torah, My servant, spend from My provision, I will extend My bounty to you, for My hand is extended upon every outstretched hand. And in the Qur’an, its proof is His saying, And whatever you spend - He will replace it, and He is the Best of providers. Ibn Abbas mentioned: And God is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing. Its meaning was mentioned earlier. What is meant here is that He, glory be to Him, gives from His abundance and knows where He places it, and He knows the unseen and the seen. These are two of His names that we mentioned among the names in the Most Noble Book. All praise is due to God.
2:269: God the Almighty says: He gives wisdom to whom He wills meaning He gives it to whomever He wills of His servants. Scholars differed regarding wisdom here. Al-Suddi said: It is prophecy. Ibn Abbas said: It is knowledge of the Qur'an, its understanding, abrogation, clear and ambiguous verses, strange verses, its beginning and end. Qatada and Mujahid said: Wisdom is understanding the Qur'an. Mujahid said: Correctness in speech and action. Ibn Zayd said: Wisdom is reason in religion. Malik ibn Anas said: Wisdom is knowledge of the religion of God, understanding it and following it. Ibn Al-Qasim narrated from him that he said: Wisdom is contemplating the command of God and following it. He also said: Wisdom is obedience to God, understanding religion and acting upon it. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: Wisdom is fear of God. Ibrahim Al-Naha'i said: Wisdom is understanding the Qur'an, and so did Zayd ibn Aslam. Al-Hasan said: Wisdom is piety. I said: All of these sayings, except for the saying of al-Suddi, al-Rabi’ and al-Hasan, are close to each other, because wisdom is a source of rulings, which is perfection in a saying or action. So everything mentioned is a type of wisdom, which is the genus. So the Book of God is wisdom, and the Sunnah of His Prophet is wisdom, and everything mentioned of preference is wisdom. The origin of wisdom is that which prevents foolishness, so knowledge is called wisdom, because it prevents, and through it one knows how to prevent foolishness, which is every ugly action. And so is the Qur’an, and so is the Qur’an, reason and understanding. And in al-Bukhari: Whoever God intends good for, He gives him understanding in religion. And here He said: And whoever is given wisdom has certainly been given much good. And He repeated the mention of wisdom without implying it out of concern for it, and to draw attention to its honor and virtue, according to what was previously explained in His statement, But those who did wrong substituted another statement. And Ad-Darimi Abu Muhammad mentioned in his Musnad: Marwan bin Muhammad told us, Rafdah Al-Ghasani told us, Thabit bin Ajlan Al-Ansari told us, he said: It was said: God intends to punish the people of the earth, but when He hears the teacher teaching the children wisdom, He turns that away from them. Marwan said: He means by wisdom the Qur’an. God the Almighty says: “And he who has been given wisdom has certainly been given much good. And none will remember except those of understanding.” It is said that he who has been given wisdom and the Qur’an has been given the best of what has been given of the collection of knowledge of the books of the ancients from the scrolls and other things, because He said to them: And you have not been given of knowledge except a little. And He called this a great good because this is the essence of speech. Some of the wise men said: He who has been given knowledge and the Qur’an should know himself, and not humble himself before the people of this world for the sake of their world, for he has been given the best of what the people of this world have been given, because God the Almighty called the world a little enjoyment, as He said: Say, ‘The enjoyment of this world is little.’ And He called knowledge and the Qur’an a great good. The majority of scholars read and he who is given in the passive form of the verb. Al-Zuhri and Ya’qub read: and he who is given with a kasra on the ta’ meaning and he who is given God wisdom, so the subject is the name of God the Almighty. Min is the first object presented, and al-Hikmah is the second object. Al-Albab means the intellects, the singular of which is lab and it has been mentioned before.
2:270: God Almighty says: “Whatever you spend or vow, God knows it. And the wrongdoers will have no helpers.” Condition and its answer. Vows were a common practice among the Arabs, so God the Almighty mentioned the warning, what a person does voluntarily and what he does after obligating himself. In the verse there is the meaning of promise and threat, meaning whoever has a sincere intention will be rewarded, and whoever spends for show or for another meaning that earns him favor and harm and the like, he is unjust, his action goes in vain and he finds no supporter in it. The meaning of He knows it is that He counts it, said Mujahid. He made the pronoun singular and mentioned two things, so An-Nahhas said: The meaning is and whatever you spend of expenditure then God knows it, or whatever you vow of vow, then God knows it then he deleted. It is permissible for the meaning to be: and whatever you spend then God knows it and the ha’ refers to what as Sibawayh recited for Imru’ Al-Qais: It is clear that the drawing of the reading has not been erased because it was woven from the south and north. And or you have vowed a vow is connected to it. Ibn Atiyah said: The pronoun in He knows is singular, and he mentioned two things from where he intended what he mentioned or stated. I said: This is good, because the pronoun may mean all of the above, even if there are many. The true expression of a vow is to say: It is what the person responsible has made obligatory upon himself of acts of worship, which if he had not made it obligatory, it would not be binding upon him. You say: The man vowed such-and-such, if he committed himself to doing it. He vows with a silent dhal and he vows with a kasra. And it has rulings that will be explained in a different context, God willing.
2:271: The majority of commentators have said that this verse is about voluntary charity, because concealing it is better than revealing it, and likewise with all other acts of worship, concealing it is better in voluntary charity because there is no ostentation in it, but this is not the case with obligatory acts. Al-Hasan said: Showing zakat is better, and concealing voluntary charity is better, because it is more indicative that it is intended for God Almighty alone. Ibn Abbas said: God made secret voluntary charity better than its public, it is said seventy times, and He made the public charity of the obligatory charity better than its secret, it is said twenty-five times. He said: And likewise with all obligatory and voluntary acts in the things that have it. I said: Such a thing is not said from an opinion, but rather it is a revelation. In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, he said: The best prayer of a person is in his home, except for the obligatory prayer. This is because the obligatory prayers are not subject to hypocrisy, while the voluntary prayers are susceptible to that. Al-Nasa’i narrated on the authority of Uqbah ibn Amir that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: He who recites the Qur’an aloud is like he who gives charity aloud, and he who recites the Qur’an quietly is like he who gives charity quietly. In the hadith: Secret charity extinguishes the wrath of the Lord. Ibn al-Arabi said: There is no authentic hadith that indicates that public charity is better than secret charity, nor that secret charity is better than public charity, but it is the established consensus. As for voluntary charity, the Qur’an explicitly states that it is better to give it in secret than to give it publicly. However, our scholars said that this is the most common interpretation, and the truth is that the situation of charity differs according to the situation of the one who gives it, the one who is given it, and the people who witness it. As for the one who gives it, he benefits from it by showing the Sunnah and the reward of being an example. I said: This is for those whose condition is strong, whose intentions are good, and whose soul is safe from hypocrisy. As for those who are too weak for this level, then secrecy is more misleading for them. As for the one who is given it, keeping it secret is safer for him than people despising him, or accusing him of taking it despite being rich and not being chaste. As for the state of the people, keeping it secret from them is better than being public to them, because they may accuse the one who gives it of showing off and the one who takes it of being rich. They may also move hearts to give charity, but this is rare today. Yazid bin Abi Habib said: This verse was revealed about charity to the Jews and Christians, so he ordered that the zakat be distributed in secret. Ibn Atiyah said: This is rejected, especially among the righteous predecessors. Al-Tabari said: People agreed that making the obligation public is better. I said: Al-Kaya al-Tabari mentioned that this verse indicates the view that concealing charity is better in general, and that it is the right of the poor and that it is permissible for the owner of the wealth to distribute it himself, according to what is one of the two opinions of al-Shafi’i. According to the other opinion, they mentioned that what is meant by charity here is voluntary charity, not obligatory charity, which is better to show so that it does not attract suspicion. For this reason, it was said: Praying voluntary charity individually is better, and praying in congregation for obligatory charity is further from suspicion. Al-Mahdawi said: What is meant by the verse is the obligation of zakat and what is voluntary, so concealing it was better during the time of the Prophet, peace and blessings of God be upon him. Then people’s suspicions worsened after that, so the scholars approved of showing obligatory charity so that no one would be suspected of preventing it. Ibn ‘Atiyyah said: This opinion is contrary to the reports, and in our time it is similar to the idea that it is better to conceal obligatory charity, as the prohibitions on it have increased and its giving has become subject to ostentation. Ibn Khuwaiz Mandad said: It is possible that the verse refers to the obligatory and voluntary zakat, because he mentioned concealment and praised it, and revealed it and praised it, so it is possible that it refers to both of them. Al-Naqqash said: This is a verse that was abrogated by the Almighty’s statement: Those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and publicly Al-Ankabut 2:17. The Almighty’s saying: How excellent it is is a praise for showing charity, then He ruled that concealing it is better than that. Therefore, some of the wise men said: If you do a good deed, conceal it, and if it is done to you, spread it. Du’bal Al-Khuza’i said: If they take revenge, they announce it, and if they bestow favors, they bestow them in secret. Sahl bin Harun said: If you ever come to him to ask him, he will give you what he has, and he will be satisfied and apologize. He hides his good deeds, but God reveals them. If you hide a good deed, it will appear. Al-Abbas ibn Abdul Muttalib, may God be pleased with him, said: A good deed is not complete except with three characteristics: hastening it, minimizing it, and concealing it. If you hasten it, you will congratulate it. If you minimize it, you will magnify it. If you conceal it, you will complete it. A poet said it well: Your kindness to me has increased greatly, because you are a lowly and humble person. You forget about him as if he never came to you, but he is famous and dangerous among people. The reciters differed in his saying Fan'ama hi so what is it?. Abu Amr and Nafi' in the narration of Warsh and Asim in the narration of Hafs and Ibn Kathir read Fan'ama hi with a kasra on the noon and the 'ayn. Abu Amr also read and Nafi' in a narration other than that of Warsh and Asim in the narration of Abu Bakr and Al-Mufaddal read Fan'ama with a kasra on the noon and a sukoon on the 'ayn. Al-A'mash, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and Al-Kisa'i read Fan'ama with a fatha on the noon and a kasra on the 'ayn, and all of them sukoon the meem. It is permissible in places other than the Qur'an Fan'ama ma hi. An-Nahhas said: But in the black it is connected, so assimilation is required. The grammarians have narrated four languages for Na'am: Na'am al-rajul Zayd, this is the original. Na'am al-rajul, with a kasra on the noon and the 'ayn. Na'am al-rajul, with a fatha on the noon and a sukoon on the 'ayn, and the original is Na'am, the kasra was deleted because it is heavy. Na'am al-rajul, this is the most eloquent of the languages, and the original is Na'am. It occurs in every praise, so it was lightened and the kasra of the ‘ayn was changed to the nun and the ‘ayn was made sukun, so whoever reads Fananima hi has two possibilities: One of them is that he came with it in the language of the one who says Na’am. The other possibility is that it is in the good language, so the original is Na’am, then the ‘ayn was broken because of the meeting of two sukun letters. Al-Nahhas said: As for what was narrated from Abu Amr and Nafi’ about the sukun of the ‘ayn, it is impossible. It was narrated from Muhammad bin Yazid that he said: As for the sukun of the ‘ayn and the doubled meem, no one is able to pronounce it, but rather he aims for all of them between two sukun letters and moves them and does not care. Abu Ali said: Whoever reads with the sukun of the ‘ayn, his statement is not correct, because he combined two sukun letters, the first of which is not a letter of extension and softness, and this is only permissible according to grammarians if the first is a letter of extension, since the extension becomes a substitute for the movement, and this is like Daba and Dhawal and the like. Perhaps Abu Amr concealed the movement and stole it, as he took it with concealment in Bari'kum - and - Ya'murkum, so the listener thought the concealment was a sukoon for the subtlety of that in the hearing and its concealment. Abu Ali said: As for the one who read Na'ma with the fatha on the noon and the kasra on the 'ayn, he only came with the word in its original form, and from that is the saying of the poet: My feet did not bear them. They are indeed the best of those who strive for righteousness. Abu Ali said: “And what of the Almighty’s saying: ‘Blessings’ is in the accusative case, and His saying ‘it’ is an explanation of the implied agent before the mention, and the estimate is ‘Blessings’ is something to show it, and showing is what is specifically praised, except that the complement was deleted and the complement to it was put in its place. And what indicates this is His saying: ‘Then it is better for you’, meaning concealment is better. So just as the pronoun here is for concealment, not for the charity, so too, firstly the agent is showing it, and it is what the pronoun is connected to, so showing was deleted and the pronoun for the charity was put like it. ‘And if you conceal it’ is a condition, and that is why the nun was deleted. ‘And you give it’ is in apposition to it. The answer is: ‘Then it is better for you’. ‘And disbelieves’ the reciters differed in its recitation, so Abu ‘Umrah, Ibn Kathir, and ‘Asim in the narration of Abu Bakr, Qatadah, Ibn Ishaq recited ‘and disbelieves’ with the nun and raised the ra’. Nafi’, Hamza, and Al-Kisa’i recited with the nun and the jazm in the ra’, and something similar was also narrated from ‘Asim. Al-Husayn ibn Ali al-Ja'fi narrated from al-A'mash, Yakfir with the accusative of the ra. Ibn 'Aamer read it with the ya and the nominative of the ra. Hafs narrated it from Asim, and it was also narrated from al-Hasan, and it was narrated from him with the ya and the jazm. Ibn Abbas read Yakfir with the ta and the kasra of the fa and the jazm of the ra. Ikrimah read Yakfir with the ta and the fatha of the fa and the jazm of the ra. Al-Mahdawi narrated from Abu Hurmuz that he read Yakfir with the ta and the nominative of the ra. It was narrated from Ikrimah and Shahr ibn Hawshab that they both read it with the ta and the accusative of the ra. These are nine readings, the most obvious of which is Yakfir with the noon and the nominative. This is the opinion of al-Khalil and Sibawayh. Al-Nahhas said, Sibawayh said: The nominative here is the correct view, because the speech after the fa is similar to it in other than the reward. He permitted the jazm by carrying it on the meaning, because the meaning is And if you conceal it and give it to the poor, it will be better for you, and We will expiate for you. Abu Hatim said: Al-A'mash read Yakfir with a Ya without a Waw before it. An-Nahhas said: What was narrated by or Hatim from Al-A'mash without a Waw in the jussive mood is in the substitution as if it were in the place of Fa. What was narrated from Asim was Yakfir with a Ya and in the nominative case, its meaning is Wa kufr God, this is the opinion of Abu Ubaid. Abu Hatim said: Its meaning is Wa kufr al-i'ta. Ibn Abbas read Wa kufr, its meaning is Wa kufr al-dadaqat. In short, whatever of these readings is with a Nun is the Nun of majesty, and whatever of them is with a Ta is charity, so pay attention to it, except what was narrated from Ikrimah with a fatha on the Fa, because the Ta in that reading is for bad deeds, and whatever of them is with a Ya then God is the one who... The second is the separation and resumption. The conjunction waw is not for sharing, but it connects one sentence to another. We have already mentioned the meaning of the jussive reading. As for the accusative and wa nakfir, it is weak and it is based on the omission of an and it is permissible. We have already mentioned the meaning of the jussive reading. As for the accusative and wa nakfir, it is weak and it is based on the omission of an and it is permissible with distance. Al-Mahdawi said: It is similar to the accusative in the answer to a question, since the recompense requires something because something else is required, like a question. The jussive in the ra’ is the most eloquent of these readings, because it indicates the inclusion of takfir in the recompense and its being conditional if the concealment occurred. As for the nominative, it does not have this meaning. I said: This is contrary to what Al-Khalil and Sibawayh chose. The word “min” in his statement, of your bad deeds is for pure partiality. Al-Tabari reported from a group that it is redundant. Ibn Atiyyah said: This is a mistake on their part. And God is Aware of what you do is a promise and a threat.
2:272: The Almighty’s saying: You are not responsible for their guidance, but God guides whom He wills. There are three issues in this: First: The Almighty’s statement: You are not responsible for their guidance. This statement is connected to the mention of charity, so it is as if He explained in it the permissibility of giving charity to polytheists. Saeed bin Jubair narrated, without a chain of transmission, on the authority of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, regarding the reason for this verse, that the Muslims used to give charity to the poor of the People of the Covenant, and when the number of poor Muslims increased, the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: Do not give charity except to people of your religion. This verse was revealed permitting charity to those who are not Muslims. Al-Naqqash said: “The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, was given alms, and a Jew came to him and said: Give me. The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: You have nothing from the alms of the Muslims. The Jew went a short distance away, and this verse was revealed: ‘You are not responsible for their guidance.’ So the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, called him and gave him some.” Then God abrogated that with the verse on alms. Ibn Abbas narrated that he said: There were some people from the Ansar who had relatives from Banu Qurayzah and Banu Nadir, and they did not give them alms because they wanted them to convert to Islam if they were in need, so the verse was revealed because of those people. Some commentators narrated that Asma’, the daughter of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, wanted to connect with her grandfather Abu Quhafah, but she refused because he was a disbeliever, so the verse was revealed about that. Al-Tabari narrated that the purpose of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, in preventing alms was only so that they would convert to Islam and enter the religion, so God Almighty said: ‘You are not responsible for their guidance.’” It was said: You are not responsible for their guidance is not connected to what came before, so it is apparent in the alms and spending them on the infidels. Rather, it is possible that its meaning is the beginning of a statement. Second: Our scholars said: This charity that was permitted to them according to what these narrations included is voluntary charity. As for the obligatory charity, it is not permissible to give it to an unbeliever, because of his saying, peace be upon him: I have been commanded to take charity from your rich and give it to your poor. Ibn al-Mundhir said: All the scholars I have memorized from have agreed that a non-Muslim is not to be given any zakat on his wealth. Then he mentioned a group of those who explicitly stated this and did not mention any disagreement. Al-Mahdawi said: Muslims are permitted to give the obligatory charity to the polytheists from their relatives because of this verse. Ibn ‘Atiyyah said: This is rejected by consensus. And God knows best. Abu Hanifa said: Zakat al-Fitr should be given to them. Ibn al-‘Arabi: This is weak and has no basis. Our evidence is that it is an obligatory charity of purification, so it is not given to a non-Muslim like the charity on livestock and on cash. The Prophet (blessings and peace of God be upon him) said: Save them from asking about this day meaning the day of Eid al-Fitr. I said: This is because they are busy with the Eid and the Eid prayer, and this is not applicable to the polytheists. It may be permissible to give it to a non-Muslim according to the opinion of those who made it a Sunnah, and this is one of the two opinions in our view, and it is the opinion of Abu Hanifa according to what we mentioned, in view of the generality of the verse regarding righteousness, feeding the poor, and giving charity in general. Ibn Atiyyah said: This ruling is conceivable for Muslims with their dhimmis and with the enslaved from the belligerents. I said: In the revelation: And they give food, in spite of their love for it, to the poor, the orphan, and the captive. The captive in the land of Islam is none other than a polytheist. And God the Almighty said: God does not forbid you from those who do not fight you because of religion and do not expel you from your homes - from being righteous toward them and acting justly toward them. The apparent meaning of these verses necessitates the permissibility of giving charity to them in general, except that the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, singled out the obligatory zakat from it, “because of his saying, may God bless him and grant him peace, to Muadh: Take charity from their rich and give it to their poor.” And the scholars agreed on that, as mentioned above. So voluntary charity is given to them if they are in need, and God knows best. Ibn al-Arabi said: As for the sinful Muslim, there is no disagreement that the zakat al-fitr is given to him unless he abandons the pillars of Islam, such as prayer and fasting, in which case the charity is not given to him until he repents. As for all other sinners, the charity is given to those who commit sins because they are included in the name of Muslims. In Sahih Muslim it says: A man gave charity to a rich man, a thief, and an adulteress, and his charity was accepted, as will be explained in the verse on charity. Third: The Almighty’s saying: But God guides whom He wills, meaning He directs whom He wills. This is a refutation of the Qadarites and groups of the Mu’tazilites, as mentioned above. God the Almighty said: And whatever you spend of good is for yourselves, and you do not spend except seeking the countenance of God. This is a condition and its answer. The good in this verse is money, because it is coupled with the mention of spending, so this indication indicates that it is money. When it is not coupled with something that indicates that it is money, it is not necessary for it to mean money, like the Almighty’s saying: A better place to settle and His saying: An atom’s weight of good will see it. And so on. This is to avoid the saying of Ikrimah: Every good in the Book of God the Almighty is money. It was narrated that some scholars used to do a lot of good deeds and then swear that they did not do good to anyone, so he was asked about that and he would say: I only did it for myself, and he would recite: And whatever you spend of good is for yourselves. Then God the Almighty explained that the spending that is considered acceptable is that which was seeking His countenance. And seeking is for the one for whom it is done. It was said: It is a testimony from God Almighty to the Companions, may God be pleased with them, that they only spend seeking His face. This is an indication of preference and praise for them. According to the first interpretation, it is a condition for them, and the condition includes others from the nation. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said to Sa`d ibn Abi Waqqas: You will not spend anything seeking the pleasure of God Almighty without being rewarded for it, even what you put in your wife’s mouth. The Almighty says: And whatever you spend in good will be fully repaid to you, and you will not be wronged. “Will be fully repaid to you” is an emphasis and explanation of His saying: And whatever you spend in good will be for yourselves. And the reward for spending will be fully repaid to the spenders, and they will not withhold anything from it, for that withholding would be an injustice to them.
2:273: It contains ten issues: The first: The Almighty’s saying: For the poor. The lam is related to His saying: And whatever you spend of good. It was said: With an omitted word, the meaning of which is spending or charity for the poor. Al-Suddi, Mujahid and others said: What is meant by these poor are the poor emigrants from Quraysh and others, then the verse includes everyone who fell under the description of the poor throughout time. The poor emigrants were specifically mentioned because there were no one else there but them, and they were the people of the Suffa, and they were about four hundred men. This is because they used to present the poor to the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, and they had no family or money, so a Suffa was built for them in the mosque of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, and they were called: the people of the Suffa. Abu Dharr said: “I was one of the people of the Suffa, and when evening came, we would go to the door of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, and he would order each man to go with another man, and ten or less of the people of the Suffa would remain, and the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, would be brought his dinner, and we would eat dinner with him. Then when we finished, the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, would say: Sleep in the mosque.” Al-Tirmidhi narrated on the authority of Al-Bara’ bin Azib: And do not aim towards that which is bad therefrom, spending [in charity]. He said: It was revealed about us, the Ansar. We were owners of palm trees. A man would bring from his palm trees according to their abundance or scarcity, and a man would bring a large or small qanū and hang it in the mosque. The people of Suffah did not have food, so when one of them was hungry, he would bring a qanū and hit it with his stick, and some unripe dates would fall and he would eat. Some people who did not desire good would bring a qanū with husks and chaff in it, or a broken qanū and would hang it in the mosque. So God revealed: "O you who have believed, spend from the good things which you have earned and from that which We have produced for you from the earth. And do not aim towards that which is bad therefrom, spending [in charity] while you would not take it [in charity] except with closed eyes." He said: If one of you were given a gift equal to what he gave him, he would not take it except with closed eyes and shyness. He said: So after that, a man would bring the best of what he had. He said: This is a good, strange, and authentic hadith. Our scholars said: They may God be pleased with them were in the mosque out of necessity, and they ate from the charity out of necessity. When God granted victory to the Muslims, they no longer needed that condition and left, then they became kings and rulers. Then God, the Exalted, explained the conditions of those poor emigrants that necessitated compassion towards them, saying: Those who were confined in the cause of God, meaning they were confined and prevented. Al-Qatada said: Where is Zaid: Confined in the cause of God? They confined themselves from managing their livelihoods for fear of the enemy. That is why God, the Exalted, said: They are unable to travel throughout the land, because the entire country was complete disbelief. This was in the early days of Islam. Their actions prevented them from earning money through jihad, and the disbelievers’ denial of their Islam prevented them from engaging in trade, so they remained poor. It was said: The meaning of They are unable to travel throughout the land is because they had committed themselves to jihad. The first is more apparent. And God knows best. The second: The ignorant think them rich because of their self-restraint. That is, because of their shrinking, abandoning asking for, and relying on God, such that the ignorant thinks them rich. This is evidence that the term poverty may be given to someone who has valuable clothing, and this does not prevent zakat from being given to him. God Almighty’s command was decreed to give to these people, and they were among the emigrants who fought with the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, neither sick nor blind. Self-restraint is a verb, and it is an exaggerated construction from ‘afa ‘an al-shay’ if he refrained from it and refrained from seeking it. Qatada and others interpreted this meaning. Opening the seen and breaking it are two languages in yahisbahum. Abu ‘Ali said: Opening is more correct, because the ‘ayn of the past tense is broken, so its rule is to come open in the present tense. Reading with the kasra is good, because it is heard, even if it is an anomaly from the rule. The min in his statement: from self-restraint is for the beginning of the goal. It was said to clarify the type. Third: The Almighty’s statement: You will recognize them by their mark is evidence that the mark has an effect on the consideration of the one who appears to have that mark, so if we see a dead person in the land of Islam wearing a belt and he is not circumcised, he is not buried in the Muslim cemetery. This takes precedence over the ruling on the land according to the majority of scholars, including the statement of the Almighty: And you will surely recognize them by the tone of their speech. The verse indicates the permissibility of giving charity to someone who has clothes, clothing, and adornment. The scholars agreed on this, although they differed after that about the amount that he should take if he is in need. Abu Hanifa considered the amount on which zakat is due, al-Shafi’i considered the sustenance of a year, Malik considered forty dirhams, and al-Shafi’i does not give zakat to someone who earns a living. Seema short: the mark, and it can be extended to say seema. Scholars have differed in identifying it here. Mujahid said: it is humility and modesty. As-Suddi: the traces of poverty and need on their faces and the lack of blessings. Ibn Zayd: the shabbiness of their clothes. Some people said, and Makki narrated it: the trace of prostration. Ibn Atiyyah: this is good, because they were free and trusting, and had nothing to do in most cases except prayer, so the trace of prostration was on them. I said: This mark, which is the trace of prostration, was shared by all the Companions, may God be pleased with them, as God Almighty informed us at the end of the conquest with His saying: Their mark is on their faces from the trace of prostration. There is no difference between them and others. So nothing remains except that the mark is the trace of poverty and need, or the trace of prostration is greater, so they were known by the yellowness of their faces from standing at night and fasting during the day. And God knows best. As for humility, its place is in the heart and the rich and the poor share in it. So nothing remains except what we have chosen, and the Grantor of success is God. Fourth: The Almighty’s saying: They do not ask people insistently. A source in the place of a state, meaning swearing. It is said: al-hafā and ah-hafā are the same. It is also said: The jury has no such response The derivation of the word ilhaaf comes from the word lihaaf, and it was named thus because it includes all aspects of the request in the question, just as the word lihaaf includes covering. That is, this questioner asks everyone with his question, so he presses them. From this is the saying of Ibn Ahmar: He kept covering them with his cloak and covering them with his thick blanket. The male ostrich describes incubating eggs with its wings. Its wings are like a blanket, and it is soft yet thick. Al-Nasa’i and Muslim narrated on the authority of Abu Hurairah that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: “The poor man is not the one who is satisfied with one or two dates, or one or two mouthfuls. Rather, the poor man is the one who is too modest to ask people for anything.” Read if you wish, He does not ask people importunately. Fifth: The scholars differed regarding the meaning of his statement: They do not ask people insistently, with two opinions. Some of them, including al-Tabari and al-Zajjaj, said: The meaning is that they do not ask at all, and this is on the basis that they are completely abstaining from asking, and this is the opinion of the majority of commentators, and abstinence is a fixed characteristic of them, meaning that they do not ask people insistently or otherwise. Some of them said: What is meant is the negation of insistence, meaning that they ask without insistence, and this is what is understood first, meaning that they ask without being insistent. This is a warning about the bad state of those who ask people insistently. The imams narrated, and the wording is from Muslim, on the authority of Mu’awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: Do not insist in asking, for by God, if any of you asks me for something and I give him something from him while he is reluctant to do so, then he will be blessed in what I give him. In Al-Muwatta’, on the authority of Zaid bin Aslam, on the authority of Ata bin Yasar, on the authority of a man from Banu Asad, he said: “My family and I stopped at Baqi’ al-Gharqad and my family said to me: Go to the Messenger of God (peace and blessings of God be upon him) and ask him for something to eat for us. They started mentioning their need, so I went to the Messenger of God (peace and blessings of God be upon him) and found a man begging him and the Messenger of God (peace and blessings of God be upon him) said: I do not have anything to give you. The man turned away from him angry and said: By my life, you give to whomever you wish! The Messenger of God (peace and blessings of God be upon him) said: He gets angry with me if I do not have anything to give to whoever among you asks and has an ounce or its equivalent, he has asked persistently.” Al-Asadi said: I said: A she-camel is better for us than an ounce. Malik said: An ounce is forty dirhams. He said: So I went back and did not ask him. After that, he came to the Messenger of God (peace and blessings of God be upon him) with barley and raisins and he divided some of it for us. May God enrich us.” Ibn Abd al-Barr said: This is how Malik narrated it, and Hisham ibn Sa`d and others followed him. It is an authentic hadith. The ruling on a companion who is not named is not the same as the ruling on someone below him who is not named, according to the scholars, because the criticism is removed from all of them and their justice is proven. This hadith indicates that asking is disliked for someone who has an ounce of silver. So whoever asks and has this limit, number, and amount of silver or what takes its place and is equivalent to it, then he is being harsh. I do not know of any scholar who does not dislike asking for someone who has this amount of silver or its equivalent in gold, based on the apparent meaning of this hadith. And whatever comes to him without asking, it is permissible for him to eat it if it is not from zakat. This is something about which I do not know of any difference of opinion. If it is from zakat, then there is a difference of opinion about it, and its explanation will come in the verse on charity, God willing. Sixth: Ibn Abd al-Barr said: Among the best of what has been narrated from the answers of the jurists regarding the meanings of begging, its abhorrence, and the doctrine of the pious people regarding it is what al-Athram narrated on the authority of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, who said: A delegation was asked about begging, when is it permissible? He said: If he does not have what will provide him with lunch and dinner, according to the hadith of Sahl ibn al-Hanzaliyyah. It was said to Abu Abdullah: What if he is forced to beg? He said: It is permissible for him if he is forced. It was said to him: What if he refrains? He said: That is better for him. Then he said: I do not think anyone dies of hunger! May God provide for him. Then he mentioned the hadith of Abu Saeed al-Khudri: Whoever seeks chastity, God will grant him chastity. And the hadith of Abu Dharr on the authority of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, who said to him: Be chaste. Abu Bakr said: I heard him ask about a man who does not have anything. Should he ask people or eat carrion? He said: Should he eat carrion while he has someone to ask him? This is abhorrent. He said: And I heard him ask him: Can a man ask for someone else? He said: No, but he turns away. Like: The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said when some barefoot, naked, leopard-skinned people came to him, Give charity, and he did not say, Give them. Abu Omar said: The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: Intercede and you will be rewarded. This includes asking someone else for intercession. And God knows best. He said: Is there no man who will give charity to this man? Abu Bakr said: It was said to him - meaning Ahmad bin Junbal - What if a man mentions a man and says that he is in need? He said: This is an insinuation and there is nothing wrong with it. The point is that he should say, Give him. Then he said: I do not like it when a man asks for himself, so how about someone else? Insinuation here is more pleasing to me. I said: Abu Dawood, Al-Nasa’i, and others narrated: Al-Faraasi said to the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace: Ask, O Messenger of God? He said: No, and if you are a questioner, then ask the righteous. So the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, permitted asking people of virtue and righteousness when there is a need for that, and if he directs his need to God, then that is higher. Ibrahim bin Adham said: Asking people for needs is a veil between you and God, the Most High, so fulfill your need through the One who has the power to harm and benefit, and let your refuge be to God, the Most High, and God will suffice you from everything else, and you will live happily. Seventh: If something comes to him without him asking, then he has the right to accept it and not reject it, because it is a provision that God has provided for him. Malik narrated on the authority of Zaid bin Aslam on the authority of Ata bin Yasar: “The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, sent a gift to Umar ibn al-Khattab, but he returned it. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said to him: Why did you return it? He said: O Messenger of God, did you not tell us that it is better for one of us not to take anything? The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: That is only due to asking. As for what is not from asking, it is only a provision that God has provided for you.” Umar ibn al-Khattab said: By the One in Whose hand is my soul, I do not ask anyone for anything and he does not bring me anything without asking for it, so I take it. This is a clear text. Muslim narrated in his Sahih, and al-Nasa’i in his Sunan, and others, on the authority of Ibn Umar, who said: I heard Umar say: “The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, used to give me money, and I would say: Give it to someone who is in need of it more than me. Once he gave me money, and I said: Give it to someone who is in need of it more than me. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: Take it, and whatever of this money comes to you while you are not in need or asking, take it, and whatever does not, do not pursue it yourself.” An-Nasa’i added after his saying: Take it, and give it as a loan or give it in charity. Muslim narrated from the hadith of Abdullah ibn al-Sa’di al-Maliki: On the authority of Umar, the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said to me: If you are given something without asking, then eat and give in charity. This is a sound hadith of Malik, mursal. Al-Athram said: I heard Abu Abdullah Ahmad ibn Hanbal being asked about the saying of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace: What came to you without asking or seeking, which seeking did he mean? He said: If you seek it and say: Perhaps he is sending it to me in your heart. It was said to him: And if he does not present it? He said: Yes, it is in the heart. It was said to him: This is severe! He said: And if it is severe, then it is like this. It was said to him: If the man did not accustom me to sending something to me, but he presented it to my heart and I said: Perhaps he is sending it to me. He said: This is seeking. But if it came to you without you expecting it and it did not cross your heart, then now there is no seeking. Abu Omar said: Seeking in idle talk is raising the head to what is desired and desired, and that a person is cheerful and seeks it. What Ahmad said in interpreting seeking is restriction and severity, and in my opinion it is far-fetched, because God the Almighty has overlooked for this nation what their souls have spoken about as long as the tongue has not uttered it or need has done it. As for what the heart believes of sins, other than disbelief, then it is nothing until it is acted upon, and the thoughts of the soul are overlooked by consensus. Eighth: Insisting on a question and insisting on it when one does not need it is forbidden and not permissible. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: Whoever asks people for their money in order to increase it is asking for burning coals, so let him ask for little or ask for a lot. Narrated by Abu Hurairah and included by Muslim. On the authority of Ibn Umar, the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: The question will not cease to be with one of you until he meets God without a shred of flesh on his face. Narrated by Muslim as well. Ninth: If the questioner is in need, there is no harm in him repeating the question three times as an excuse and warning, but it is better to leave it. If the person being asked knows about that and is able to do what he asked for, then he must give it to him. But if he is ignorant of it, then he should give it to him for fear that he may be sincere in his question and he will not succeed in rejecting him. Tenth: If he was in need of something to perform the Sunnah prayer with, such as wearing a garment to wear on Eid and Friday prayers, Ibn al-Arabi said, “I heard a man in the Caliph’s Mosque in Baghdad say: ‘This is your brother who attends Friday prayers with you, but he does not have any clothes to perform the Sunnah prayer with on Friday.’ Then, on the next Friday, I saw other clothes on him, and it was said to me: ‘Abu al-Tahir al-Barsani gave him these clothes,’ and he was praised.”
2:274: God Almighty says: Those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and publicly, will have their reward with their Lord, and no fear will there be concerning them, nor will they grieve. There is one issue: It was narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas, Abu Dharr, Abu Umamah, Abu Darda, Abdullah bin Bishr Al-Ghafiqi and Al-Awza’i that it was revealed regarding the fodder of horses tied up in the way of God. Ibn Saad mentioned in Al-Tabaqat, saying: I was told on the authority of Muhammad bin Shuaib bin Shapur, who said: Saeed bin Sinan informed us on the authority of Yazid bin Abdullah bin Urayb on the authority of his father on the authority of his grandfather Urayb: “The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, was asked about the words of God Almighty: ‘Those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and publicly, will have their reward with their Lord. And no fear will there be concerning them, nor will they grieve.’ He said: They are the owners of horses.” And with this chain of transmission he said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: “He who spends on horses is like one who extends his hand in charity and does not withhold it. Their urine and dung will be before God on the Day of Resurrection like pure musk.” It was narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas that he said: This was revealed about Ali ibn Abi Talib may God be pleased with him. He had four dirhams, so he gave in charity one dirham at night and one dirham during the day, one dirham in secret and one dirham publicly. It was mentioned by Abd al-Razzaq who said: Abd al-Wahhab ibn Mujahid told us on the authority of his father on the authority of Ibn Abbas. Ibn Jurayj said: This was revealed about a man who did that, and he did not name Ali or anyone else. Qatada said: This verse was revealed about those who spend without being extravagant or stingy. The meaning of by night and by day is night and day. The fa was included in the statement of God the Almighty: for them because the statement has the meaning of reward. This has been mentioned before. Zayd is not permissible, so he is departing.
3:131: God Almighty says: “Those who consume interest cannot stand [on the Day of Resurrection] except as one stands who is being beaten by Satan into insanity. That is because they say, ‘Trade is [just] like interest.’ But God has permitted trade and has forbidden interest. So whoever receives an admonition from his Lord and desists may have what is past, and his affair rests with God. But whoever returns [to it] - those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.” God the Almighty said: And fear the Fire which has been prepared for the disbelievers. Many commentators said: This is a warning to those who consider usury permissible, and whoever considers usury permissible disbelieves and disbelieves. It was said that its meaning is: Beware of the action that strips you of faith and you deserve the Fire, because there are sins that require the doer to have faith stripped and he fears for it, such as disobeying parents. There is a report about that: A man was disobedient to his parents, and he was told when he was dying: Say there is no god but God, but he was not able to do that until his mother came to him and was pleased with him. Among those are severing family ties, consuming usury, and betraying a trust. Abu Bakr al-Warraq reported on the authority of Abu Hanifa that he said: What strips a person's faith most often occurs at death. Then Abu Bakr said: We looked into the sins that strip faith and we did not find anything that strips faith faster than oppressing people. This verse is evidence that Hell was created, in response to the Jahmites, because what is non-existent cannot be prepared.
2:276: God Almighty says: “God destroys interest and gives increase for charities. And God does not like every ungrateful sinner.”
2:277: God Almighty says: “Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous deeds and established prayer and given zakah will have their reward with their Lord, and no fear will there be concerning them, nor will they grieve.”
